title: ABM-SIRTEM: A Hybrid Agent-Based and Epidemiological Model for Pandemic Response
summary: The COVID-19 pandemic has had profound impacts on global health, social structures, and economies. It disproportionately affected lower socioeconomic groups and those reliant on interaction-based jobs. Regulatory bodies faced the challenge of designing policies that preserve public health while limiting disruption to economic stability and productivity. Epidemiological models such as SIR and agent-based models (ABMs) have been used to study disease dynamics and the socioeconomic impacts of disease and interventions. Population-level models often simplify individual heterogeneity, while detailed ABMs can become computationally expensive as the numbers of agents and interactions increase. We propose ABM-SIRTEM, a hybrid model that incorporates occupation categories, economic productivity, and welfare at the individual level while dynamically modeling compliance with government interventions. We calibrate the model against historical positive and negative test counts from four U.S. states and examine the resulting compliance dynamics. This framework provides a basis for studying the interaction between disease spread and socioeconomic behavior in pandemic-response planning.

AI.tldr: ABM-SIRTEM: A hybrid epidemiological model combining agent-based modeling with SIR dynamics, incorporating socioeconomic factors and policy compliance for pandemic response analysis.
AI.motivation: The COVID-19 pandemic disproportionately affected vulnerable groups and created policy challenges balancing public health with economic stability. Existing epidemiological models either oversimplify individual heterogeneity (population-level models) or become computationally expensive (detailed ABMs) when modeling socioeconomic impacts and intervention compliance.
AI.method: Proposed ABM-SIRTEM, a hybrid model that incorporates occupation categories, economic productivity, and welfare at individual level while dynamically modeling compliance with government interventions. The model was calibrated against historical test count data from four U.S. states.
AI.result: The model successfully calibrated against historical COVID-19 test data and examined resulting compliance dynamics, providing insights into how disease spread interacts with socioeconomic behavior during pandemic response.
AI.conclusion: The ABM-SIRTEM framework provides a valuable basis for studying the complex interactions between disease spread and socioeconomic behavior, offering policymakers a tool for better pandemic-response planning that considers both public health and economic factors.

title: Social Laws for Multi-agent Coordination in Stochastic Environments
comment: Appeared at the RIPL Workshop as part of ICAPS 2026
summary: In multi-agent environments, coordinating agents to prevent interference and ensure robust individual performance is a critical challenge. Previous research on social laws for multi-agent systems has primarily focused on deterministic, goal-based settings. This paper extends the concept of social laws to stochastic, reward-based environments, proposing a formalism for defining and verifying their robustness under various conditions. We introduce the notion of $α$-robustness, a measure of the guaranteed utility each agent retains while pursuing its optimal single agent policy, assuming all agents obey the social law. We then present an approach for robustness verification of social laws in stochastic settings, based on a reduction to solving a series of Markov decision processes. Empirical evaluations on toy environments illustrate the potential of our framework.

AI.tldr: Extends social laws from deterministic to stochastic multi-agent settings, introduces α-robustness measure, and provides verification methods using MDP reductions.
AI.motivation: Previous social law research focused on deterministic, goal-based multi-agent systems, but real-world environments are often stochastic and reward-based. There's a need to prevent interference between agents while ensuring robust individual performance in these more complex settings.
AI.method: Proposes a formalism for defining social laws in stochastic, reward-based environments. Introduces α-robustness measure to quantify guaranteed utility when agents follow optimal single-agent policies under the social law. Provides verification approach based on reduction to solving series of Markov Decision Processes.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on toy environments demonstrate the framework's potential. The approach enables formal analysis of social law robustness in stochastic multi-agent systems.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully extends social law concepts to stochastic settings, providing formal tools for analyzing and verifying multi-agent coordination mechanisms that ensure individual agent performance while preventing interference in complex environments.

title: ERPBench: A State-Grounded Evaluation Paradigm for Computer-Use Agents in Enterprise Software
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables, submitted for review to 2027 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing (ICASSP)
summary: Computer-use agents that operate through screenshots and simulated actions are advancing rapidly, yet their evaluation remains anchored to general desktop and web tasks. Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems run the finance, procurement, inventory, and customer operations of organizations worldwide, and pose distinct challenges for computer-use agents: dense interfaces, coordinated multi-step interactions, and errors that alter persistent business records rather than surfacing on screen. Existing enterprise benchmarks rely on proprietary platforms or on simulated approximations of such software. We introduce ERPBench, a benchmark that evaluates screenshot-only agents on a live and reproducible ERP system and scores each task against ground-truth values in its database. Beyond the benchmark, we present a production-grade harness that gates agent actions behind human approval for safe deployment, which ERPBench runs autonomously. Evaluating six closed and open-source agents, we demonstrate that strong general GUI performance does not transfer to enterprise reliability. Even when an agent reaches the right form and saves it, the stored record is often wrong: some agents save in up to 85% of runs but write the correct value in as few as 3%. We further characterize failure modes specific to enterprise workflows.

AI.tldr: ERPBench: A new benchmark for evaluating screenshot-only agents on live ERP systems, showing that general GUI performance doesn't translate to enterprise reliability despite agents saving forms.
AI.motivation: Current computer-use agent evaluations focus on general desktop/web tasks, but ERP systems pose distinct challenges with dense interfaces, multi-step interactions, and persistent data changes that aren't visible on screen. Existing enterprise benchmarks use proprietary platforms or simulations rather than live systems.
AI.method: Introduced ERPBench benchmark that evaluates screenshot-only agents on a live, reproducible ERP system, scoring tasks against ground-truth database values. Also developed a production-grade harness with human approval gating for safe deployment. Evaluated six closed and open-source agents.
AI.result: Strong general GUI performance doesn't transfer to enterprise reliability. Agents can save forms in up to 85% of runs but write correct values in as few as 3%. Characterized specific failure modes in enterprise workflows.
AI.conclusion: ERPBench addresses a critical gap in evaluating agents for real enterprise systems, revealing significant reliability issues not captured by current benchmarks. The benchmark and safety harness enable safer, more realistic evaluation of enterprise automation agents.

title: Where Should Agents Live? Energy-Memory Characterization of Agentic AI for the Edge-Cloud Continuum
summary: As telecommunication networks evolve toward autonomous 5G-Advanced and 6G operations, agentic artificial intelligence (AI) workflows, where large language models (LLMs) execute multi-step reasoning, invoke diagnostic tools, retrieve domain knowledge, and coordinate across agent teams, are increasingly embedded across the edge-cloud continuum. While the biological brain accomplishes complex cognition on an exceptionally modest metabolic power budget of approximately 20W contemporary LLMs are profoundly energy- and memory-intensive, making sustainable lifecycle orchestration a critical operational priority. However, existing AI lifecycle metrics evaluate only isolated, single-model inferences or overlook multi-agent execution graphs entirely. Consequently, network operators lack foundational models to determine whether distributed agent communication incurs meaningful energy costs and where across edge-cloud tiers agent teams should physically reside. To address this gap, we introduce agentic-eCAL, generalizing the Energy Cost of AI Lifecycle (eCAL) metric to directed multi-agent workflows by coupling a closed-form two-rate single-call energy model (compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode) with 7-layer OSI data transport. Grounded in hundreds of GPU benchmark configurations on NVIDIA A100 and H100, 16 open-weight models and 8 orchestration topologies, we validate components of the metric and study workflow placement implications. Our findings demonstrate that inter-agent text transport incurs 0.25% of workflow energy across 5G RAN, metro, and optical links. Therefore in edge-cloud agent placement the dominant energy cost of distribution is often not the transmission of inter-agent text itself, but the additional inference and context processing induced by that communication.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces agentic-eCAL, a generalized energy cost metric for multi-agent AI workflows that models both computation energy (prefill/decode phases) and 7-layer OSI transport energy, revealing that agent communication energy is negligible compared to the additional inference overhead it causes.
AI.motivation: As 5G-Advanced/6G networks adopt agentic AI workflows with LLMs across edge-cloud continuum, there's a critical gap: existing AI lifecycle metrics only evaluate single-model inferences and ignore multi-agent execution graphs, leaving network operators without tools to assess distributed agent communication energy costs and optimal agent placement.
AI.method: The authors generalize the Energy Cost of AI Lifecycle (eCAL) metric to directed multi-agent workflows by combining a two-rate single-call energy model (compute-bound prefill and memory-bound decode phases) with 7-layer OSI data transport modeling, validated through extensive benchmarking on NVIDIA A100/H100 GPUs with 16 open-weight models and 8 orchestration topologies.
AI.result: Inter-agent text transport incurs only 0.25% of total workflow energy across 5G RAN, metro, and optical links, indicating that the dominant energy cost in distributed agent placement is not the communication itself but the additional inference and context processing required by that communication.
AI.conclusion: The introduced agentic-eCAL metric provides network operators with a foundational model to evaluate multi-agent AI workflow energy costs, revealing that agent placement optimization should focus on minimizing the inference overhead triggered by inter-agent communication rather than the communication transport energy itself.

title: Making AI-Assisted Claims Independently Challengeable: Publication Authority and a Protocol for Falsifiable Publication Records
comment: Main article: 24 pages, 4 figures; supplementary material: 13 pages. Preprint; not peer-reviewed. Yifei Dong is the corresponding author
summary: AI-assisted claims can appear authoritative when evidence, analysis, human authorization, presentation, and correction history refer to different states. Provenance, attestation, and transparency expose history but alone do not specify the publication transition examined here. We develop Publication Authority as an exact-state, non-transferable, single-use publication capability and instantiate it in PAC-2026 (Publication-Accountability Calculus), a machine-readable AIJIM Protocol candidate. We evaluate its fourth bounded semantic freeze (SF-4), a fixed-profile specification designed for replaceable bindings. Six obligations govern evidence, runs and artifacts, measurement disclosure, authorization, surface correspondence, and lifecycle continuity. Each yields a target-bound witness, localized counterexample, or localized unverifiability; none can compensate for another. Only a fresh, complete all-pass record derives the permit consumed by one atomic publication transition. We use identity vectors, adversarial cases, finite models, and historical implementations. Ten models explored 110,764 safe reachable states; 76 unsafe configurations produced the expected violation or observer countermodel. A reader surface passing its correspondence check cannot authorize publication unless the accepted record admits that surface. SF-4 separates evidence horizon from verification time and rejects an authentic but causally invalid authorization. A historical predecessor path reproduced 17 frozen authorization-successor outcomes. A later in-house, instance-blind test of known case classes matched all 183 scored expectations; same-host package execution reproduced its 240 archived observations. Results support internal coherence, bounded safety, fault sensitivity, and limited constructibility, but not factual truth, general refinement, blind interoperability, field efficacy, or standards status.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Publication Authority - an exact-state, non-transferable, single-use publication capability for AI-assisted claims, implemented as PAC-2026 protocol. It ensures claims refer to same evidence/analysis/authorization states via six obligations that produce target-bound witnesses or counterexamples.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted claims can appear authoritative when different components (evidence, analysis, authorization, presentation, correction history) refer to different states, creating misleading authority. Current provenance/attestation/transparency approaches don't address the specific publication transition problem.
AI.method: Developed Publication Authority concept and instantiated it in PAC-2026 (Publication-Accountability Calculus), a machine-readable AIJIM Protocol candidate. Evaluated its fourth bounded semantic freeze (SF-4) using six obligations governing evidence, runs, measurement disclosure, authorization, surface correspondence, and lifecycle continuity. Used identity vectors, adversarial cases, finite models, and historical implementations for analysis.
AI.result: Analyzed 110,764 safe reachable states across ten models; 76 unsafe configurations produced expected violations. SF-4 separates evidence horizon from verification time, rejects causally invalid authorizations. Historical predecessor path reproduced 17 frozen outcomes; later tests matched 183 scored expectations; execution reproduced 240 archived observations. Supports internal coherence and bounded safety but not factual truth or general interoperability.
AI.conclusion: Publication Authority provides a framework for ensuring AI-assisted claims have consistent state references across all components. The approach demonstrates internal coherence and fault sensitivity but doesn't guarantee factual truth, general refinement, blind interoperability, field efficacy, or standards status - it's a bounded safety mechanism for publication transitions.

title: Pay Only for Disagreement: Certified No-Regression Verdicts for Model Updates with Matching Label-Complexity Bounds
summary: Every production model is updated, by retraining, fine-tuning, quantization, or a silent vendor swap, and each update risks being worse than what it replaced. We formalize update promotion as certified paired risk-difference auditing. Our starting point is a support identity: the risk difference between two models lives on the inputs where they disagree, observable without labels. We build DISCERN, a sequential two-tier protocol. A zero-label tier certifies benign updates whose disagreement rate is below tolerance from unlabeled traffic alone. An audited tier labels only sampled disagreements through an anytime-valid confidence sequence, valid at every stopping time and under any label-routing rule, even an adversarial judge. We prove finite-sample validity and matching label-complexity bounds of order rho^2/eps^2 at the rate level, so exploiting free disagreement provably saves a factor 1/rho over any pairing-blind auditor, and the guarantee composes across an unbounded sequence of promotions from one error budget. Across 14,000+ replayed audit streams over 785 update pairs, including LoRA fine-tunes of language models up to 1.4B parameters, miscoverage is 0.0002 (nominal 5%), power 0.986 with zero false alarms, and 56% of benign updates certify with zero labels. Each audit emits a machine-checkable evidence record for post-market monitoring.

AI.tldr: A method called DISCERN provides certified auditing for model updates without requiring labels for benign updates, using disagreement rates on unlabeled data and sampling only when models disagree.
AI.motivation: Model updates (retraining, fine-tuning, quantization, vendor swaps) can degrade performance, but traditional evaluation requires extensive labeled data. There's a need for efficient, certified auditing that minimizes labeling cost while ensuring updates don't worsen performance.
AI.method: DISCERN uses a two-tier sequential protocol: 1) Zero-label tier certifies benign updates when disagreement rate on unlabeled traffic is below tolerance; 2) Audited tier labels only sampled disagreements using anytime-valid confidence sequences that work under any stopping time and even adversarial label routing. The method exploits that risk differences only matter where models disagree.
AI.result: Theoretical: Finite-sample validity with label complexity bounds of ρ²/ε², saving factor 1/ρ over blind auditors. Empirical: On 14,000+ audit streams over 785 update pairs including 1.4B parameter LoRA fine-tunes, miscoverage 0.0002 (nominal 5%), power 0.986 with zero false alarms, and 56% of benign updates certified with zero labels.
AI.conclusion: DISCERN provides efficient, certified model update auditing with minimal labeling, provably exploiting disagreement patterns, and generates machine-checkable evidence records for post-market monitoring while maintaining statistical validity across unlimited update sequences.

title: Compositional Policy Violations: When Step-Level Compliance Fails In Agentic AI Workflows
summary: Agentic workflows now make consequential decisions in regulated settings, and the governance placed around them is almost entirely step-scoped: input-output classifiers, per turn rails, and span-level evaluators. The policies organizations actually hold, such as referral thresholds, authority limits, and review requirements, are properties of the whole execution rather than of any one step. This mismatch admits a failure mode we call a Compositional Policy Violation (CPV): every individual step passes its own check while the composed execution violates the governing policy. A predicate over a single step cannot evaluate a property that step does not determine, so no improvement in the accuracy of the step-scoped monitors detects this class. We define CPVs as the failure of step-level compliance to compose, and present a taxonomy of four types: Authority Creep, Threshold Laundering, Cumulative Sum Violation, and Context Collapse. We show that the correct repair for each class is dictated by where the guarded quantity mutates. We then introduce a provenance-aware runtime architecture that evaluates policies over complete execution traces, recomputing guarded quantities from raw provenance rather than the pipeline's derived representation.

AI.tldr: Step-level compliance monitors fail to detect policy violations that emerge from composed executions, requiring runtime architecture with full execution trace analysis.
AI.motivation: Current AI governance focuses on step-level checks, but real organizational policies (referral thresholds, authority limits, review requirements) are properties of entire executions. This mismatch creates undetectable failures where each step passes but the composition violates policy.
AI.method: 1. Define Compositional Policy Violations (CPVs) as failure of step-level compliance to compose. 2. Develop taxonomy of four CPV types: Authority Creep, Threshold Laundering, Cumulative Sum Violation, and Context Collapse. 3. Analyze correct repairs based on where guarded quantity mutates. 4. Introduce provenance-aware runtime architecture that evaluates policies over complete execution traces using raw provenance data.
AI.result: A framework identifying four types of undetectable policy violations in agentic workflows and a proposed architecture that recomputes guarded quantities from raw provenance rather than pipeline-derived representations to properly enforce policies.
AI.conclusion: Step-scoped monitoring is insufficient for enforcing execution-level policies in agentic workflows. Organizations need provenance-aware runtime architectures that analyze complete execution traces to detect and prevent Compositional Policy Violations that emerge from composed but individually-compliant steps.

title: EvolveTrade: Experience-Driven Policy Refinement for Self-Evolving LLM Trading Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) trading agents can combine market data, news, and executable analysis, but their behavior is often controlled by static hand-written tool-use policies that are fixed before deployment. This limits their ability to adapt how they gather evidence, invoke tools, verify signals, and manage risk under changing market regimes. We introduce EvolveTrade, a self-evolving framework that treats the system prompt of a tool-using trading agent as a text-parameterized policy. After each update interval, a Policy Agent revises this policy using accumulated decision traces and realized portfolio feedback, while keeping the backbone LLM fixed. The updated policy is then used for the next batch of trading decisions, enabling the agent to refine its information-acquisition and portfolio-construction procedure over time. Experiments across multiple market regimes and two LLM backbones show that EvolveTrade often improves Sharpe Ratio and Cumulative Return over fixed-policy LLM baselines, achieving the improved SR and CR in most evaluated settings. Behavioral analyses further show that self-evolved policies increase code-mediated analysis and activate regime-relevant computations; case-level policy-to-return attributions trace how policy-induced allocation changes contribute to realized return differences. These results suggest that adapting the reusable procedure governing tool use is a key direction for building more robust LLM trading agents.

AI.tldr: EvolveTrade: A self-evolving framework for LLM trading agents that dynamically updates their system prompt/policy based on feedback, outperforming static policies across market regimes.
AI.motivation: Current LLM trading agents use static hand-written tool-use policies fixed before deployment, limiting their ability to adapt evidence gathering, tool invocation, signal verification, and risk management under changing market conditions.
AI.method: Treats the system prompt of a tool-using trading agent as a text-parameterized policy. After each update interval, a Policy Agent revises this policy using accumulated decision traces and realized portfolio feedback while keeping the backbone LLM fixed.
AI.result: EvolveTrade improves Sharpe Ratio and Cumulative Return over fixed-policy LLM baselines across multiple market regimes and two LLM backbones. Self-evolved policies increase code-mediated analysis and activate regime-relevant computations, with policy-induced allocation changes contributing to realized return differences.
AI.conclusion: Adapting the reusable procedure governing tool use is a key direction for building more robust LLM trading agents. Self-evolving prompt policies enable agents to refine their information-acquisition and portfolio-construction procedures over time.

title: Beyond Static RAG: An Adaptive, Tri-Metric Routing Framework for Efficient Long-Context Inference on Commodity GPUs
comment: This Paper is accepted and presented at ICML Scale Workshop 2026. https://scale-icml-2026.github.io/accepted_papers.html (Paper ID :72)
summary: Deploying retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on commodity GPUs such as the NVIDIA T4 (16 GB VRAM) exposes a practical failure mode we call the Compression Paradox: neural prompt compression can add key-value (KV) cache contention and preprocessing latency that outweigh generation-time savings, while skipping compression can cause out-of-memory (OOM) failures on long contexts. We identify two distinct failure mechanisms when a vLLM-served LLM and a PyTorch-based compressor are co-deployed under tight memory budgets, and introduce the Tri-Metric Router, a deterministic, training-free policy that selects among Raw, Neural (LLMLingua-2), and Lexical (BM25) pipelines. The router uses three CPU-side signals: spatial complexity ($L$), syntactic density ($ρ_{key}$), and type-token ratio (TTR). Unlike prior semantic-only adaptation, our dispatch signal is hardware-physical, based on VRAM headroom and a latency crossover point. Thresholds are calibrated from profiling on LongBench qasper, yielding an operating crossover near 4,332 words on T4; our contribution is this calibration methodology rather than a hardware-specific constant. On out-of-distribution holdouts, the method achieves 0% OOM failures, 88.5 $\pm$ 4.4% oracle alignment, and 49.3% Combined F1, improving over always-on lexical compression by 5.2 points without additional VRAM or training cost.

AI.tldr: A deterministic routing system called Tri-Metric Router solves GPU memory limitations in RAG systems by dynamically selecting between raw, neural, or lexical compression pipelines based on hardware-physical signals, eliminating out-of-memory failures while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Deploying retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on commodity GPUs like NVIDIA T4 (16GB VRAM) faces the "Compression Paradox": neural prompt compression adds KV cache contention and preprocessing latency that may outweigh savings, while skipping compression causes out-of-memory failures on long contexts.
AI.method: Introduces Tri-Metric Router, a training-free policy that selects among Raw, Neural (LLMLingua-2), and Lexical (BM25) pipelines using three CPU-side signals: spatial complexity (L), syntactic density (ρ_key), and type-token ratio (TTR). The dispatch signal is hardware-physical, based on VRAM headroom and latency crossover points calibrated from profiling on LongBench qasper.
AI.result: On out-of-distribution holdouts, achieves 0% OOM failures, 88.5 ± 4.4% oracle alignment, and 49.3% Combined F1, improving over always-on lexical compression by 5.2 points without additional VRAM or training cost. Identifies operating crossover near 4,332 words on T4 GPU.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces a practical solution to the Compression Paradox in RAG deployment, providing a calibration methodology rather than hardware-specific constants. The Tri-Metric Router enables reliable deployment on resource-constrained GPUs by making intelligent compression decisions based on hardware-physical signals rather than semantic content alone.

title: One Axis, No Brake: Self-Knowledge Limits the Filtering of Harmful Peer Conformity in LLMs
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems are expected to be more reliable because agents can catch each other's mistakes. But peer pressure cuts both ways: the same correction that fixes a wrong answer can overturn a right one. The tempting safeguard is a brake that keeps the beneficial revisions and blocks the harmful ones. We show this brake is hard to build, for a simple reason: a revision is harmful exactly when the original answer was right, so deciding whether to block it is the same as knowing whether the model was already correct. This turns the open-ended hunt for a brake into one measurable quantity, the model's self-knowledge: any brake built from a deploy-time signal is a correctness probe in disguise, and self-knowledge is far from perfect (AUROC $\approx 0.64$--$0.89$ across six model families). We call this ceiling the wall. Even white-box steering of the model's own correctness direction does not breach it: it changes how often the model revises, but harmful and beneficial revisions move together. At population scale the wall becomes the cliff: when most agents start wrong, debate amplifies the shared mistake into a confident, wrong consensus. In our multiple-choice societies, more agents, more model diversity, and a stronger member do not fix it. What helps is adding information before the revision, not filtering after it. Local agreement is not global correctness.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent LLM systems face a fundamental limit: effective error correction requires knowing which answers are already correct, which is hindered by imperfect self-knowledge in models.
AI.motivation: To understand why multi-agent LLM systems, which should be more reliable through peer correction, often fail to improve performance and can even degrade it through harmful revisions of correct answers.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis showing that building an effective "brake" to filter harmful revisions is equivalent to having perfect self-knowledge of correctness. Empirical measurement of models' self-knowledge using AUROC across six model families, and analysis of how steering mechanisms affect revision behavior.
AI.result: Models have limited self-knowledge (AUROC ≈ 0.64-0.89), creating a fundamental "wall" that prevents effective revision filtering. Steering mechanisms change revision frequency but don't separate harmful from beneficial revisions. At scale, this becomes a "cliff" where debate amplifies shared mistakes into confident wrong consensus. Traditional fixes (more agents, diversity, stronger members) don't work.
AI.conclusion: The fundamental limitation of multi-agent correction is that filtering harmful revisions requires knowing correctness, which models lack. Solutions must focus on adding information before revisions rather than filtering after them, as local agreement doesn't guarantee global correctness.

title: One Color Preprocessing Improves DSATUR
summary: The Graph Coloring Problem (GCP) is NP-hard and DSATUR stands as one of the fastest heuristics for it despite producing colorings that typically use more colors than state-of-the-art coloring algorithms. We propose SSLD (Semidefinite Spectral Learning with DSATUR), which improves DSATUR by preprocessing a first good color class before letting DSATUR complete coloring the rest of the given graph. We obtain this color class from a Semidefinite Programming (SDP), similar to an SDP used to compute the Lovász theta number. To the best of our knowledge, SSLD is the first approach to improve DSATUR by preprocessing through fixed color classes. We evaluate SSLD against DSATUR and against a naive 1-color-class preprocessing algorithm on DIMACS instances, random graphs (Erdős--Rényi, Watts-Strogatz, Barabási--Albert), Frequency Assignment and Job Shop Scheduling instances. SSLD matches or beats DSATUR in almost every case across over 1600 benchmark instances, and out performs the naive GISD baseline, allows us to confirm the value brought by the SDP-guided choice of the first color class. This quality comes at a runtime cost of roughly 195 times slower that DSATUR, but demonstrating that SDP-guided preprocessing of a first color class is a direction for future improvements.

AI.tldr: SSLD improves DSATUR by preprocessing a first color class via semidefinite programming before letting DSATUR complete coloring, achieving better results but with higher runtime cost.
AI.motivation: DSATUR is fast for graph coloring but typically uses more colors than state-of-the-art algorithms. The authors aim to improve DSATUR's coloring quality while maintaining its efficiency.
AI.method: SSLD combines DSATUR with SDP preprocessing: first computes a good initial color class using a semidefinite programming approach similar to Lovász theta number, then lets DSATUR complete the coloring of the remaining graph.
AI.result: SSLD matches or beats DSATUR in almost every case across 1600+ benchmark instances (DIMACS, random graphs, Frequency Assignment, Job Shop Scheduling), outperforming a naive baseline. However, it's ~195 times slower than DSATUR.
AI.conclusion: SDP-guided preprocessing of a first color class successfully improves DSATUR's coloring quality, demonstrating a promising direction for future improvements despite the computational cost increase.

title: Where Grokking Happens: Distributed Utility and Fourier Recoding Without a Module Switch
summary: Where in a Transformer is the change from memorization to generalization functionally expressed? We introduce Transition Games--behavior-aligned exact activation games with paired non-generalizing controls--and find distributed utility gain with a prospective block-0 attention bias; selected degree-two modes account for 67--92% of its addition contrast across replacement games, and a disjoint exact path study confirms that block-1 MLP mediates more of their effect than all other tested downstream paths in 12/12 pairs. The sharper "MLP memorizes, attention generalizes" prediction instead reverses (-.331 bits/example at the memory anchor; 0/12 in the predicted direction), while routing onset, global rank collapse, and a prime-invariant architecture ridge also fail, identifying grokking here as spectral recoding of an existing distributed circuit rather than a module switch.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates where in a Transformer the transition from memorization to generalization occurs, finding it's a distributed circuit transformation rather than a module switch, with specific attention and MLP components playing complementary roles.
AI.motivation: To identify where in a Transformer architecture the functional change from memorization to generalization (grokking phenomenon) is expressed, challenging the common "MLP memorizes, attention generalizes" hypothesis.
AI.method: Introduced Transition Games - behavior-aligned exact activation games with paired non-generalizing controls; used two complementary studies: 1) exact activation games with replacement controls, 2) disjoint exact path analysis to trace causal contributions of different architectural components.
AI.result: Found distributed utility gain with prospective block-0 attention bias; degree-two modes account for 67-92% of addition contrast; block-1 MLP mediates more effect than all other tested downstream paths in 12/12 pairs; "MLP memorizes, attention generalizes" hypothesis reversed (-.331 bits/example at memory anchor, 0/12 in predicted direction); grokking identified as spectral recoding of existing distributed circuit rather than module switch.
AI.conclusion: Grokking (transition from memorization to generalization) in Transformers is expressed as spectral recoding of an existing distributed circuit involving specific attention and MLP components working together, not as a switch between different modules or functions.

title: Flag Game: A Toy Model for Mechanistic Swarm Interpretability
summary: Emergent coordinated behaviors of AI agents are starting to present critical safety risks. A key phenomenon driving these behaviors is the rapid formation and spread of beliefs about the world, and mechanistic understanding is crucial for collective alignment. To this end, we introduce the Flag Game, a toy model for studying the mechanisms of collective belief formation. Concretely, a hidden country flag defines the ground truth, and each bounded agent directly observes only a private crop but can exchange beliefs and weigh social evidence from peers. Despite its simplicity, the Flag Game reproduces rich collective phenomenology: non-monotonic scaling of performance with population size, accuracy gains from social-awareness prompting and team diversity, and strong effects of organizational structure. In particular, we identify that collective belief collapse at small population sizes turns into collective belief polarization as the population grows. This polarization causes the performance decline at large population sizes, but creates diversity in collective beliefs. Finally, we dissect the mechanisms underlying collective belief collapse and polarization with two complementary approaches. We first introduce social circuit attribution, a technique to predict which agent, and what view, matters most to collective dynamics, and verify its predictions by causal interventions on agents, tracing how agent patching changes collective outcomes. However, the efficacy of causal interventions on agents decreases as the population grows. We therefore develop a statistical mechanical theory for larger populations and verify that it matches the empirical phase diagram. Together, these results take a first step toward mechanistic swarm interpretability, a science of how the properties of individual agents and their communication give rise to emergent collective behavior.

AI.tldr: Researchers introduce the Flag Game, a toy model to study collective belief formation in AI agents, revealing phenomena like non-monotonic scaling with population size, belief collapse at small scales turning into polarization at large scales, and demonstrating analytical tools for mechanistic swarm interpretability.
AI.motivation: Emergent coordinated behaviors of AI agents present critical safety risks, and understanding the mechanisms of collective belief formation is crucial for collective alignment. Current systems lack mechanistic understanding of how beliefs form and spread in agent collectives.
AI.method: Introduced the Flag Game: a toy model where a hidden country flag defines ground truth, agents observe private crop information and exchange beliefs/weigh social evidence. Used two complementary approaches: 1) Social circuit attribution to identify influential agents/views with causal interventions, 2) Statistical mechanical theory for larger populations to match empirical phase diagrams.
AI.result: The Flag Game reproduces rich collective phenomenology: non-monotonic scaling of performance with population size, accuracy gains from social-awareness prompting and team diversity, strong effects of organizational structure. Collective belief collapse at small population sizes turns into polarization as population grows, causing performance decline but creating diversity in beliefs. Social circuit attribution effectively predicts influential agents in small populations, but efficacy decreases as population grows.
AI.conclusion: The study takes a first step toward mechanistic swarm interpretability - understanding how individual agent properties and communication give rise to emergent collective behavior. The Flag Game provides a foundational model for studying collective belief formation mechanisms in AI agent systems.

title: Physics-Constrained Digital Twins for Sensor Integrity in Urban Pedestrian Flow: Detecting Stealthy False Data Injection with Conformal Guarantees
summary: City pedestrian counting systems now feed economic indicators, planning decisions and safety operations, yet the twins built on top of them treat the incoming stream as ground truth. We study what happens when it is not. We formalise stealthy false data injection for city-scale pedestrian sensing, where the map from latent flow to observation is far more rank deficient than in the power and water networks for which stealth has been characterised. Our twin estimates directed flows on the pedestrian street graph, assimilates counts through a learned graph-localised gain, and is trained against a flow conservation residual that couples metered and unmetered segments. Detection combines the innovation with that residual, and the alarm threshold is set by adaptive conformal calibration rather than by hand. To measure what the physics buys, we define the attack margin, the relative reduction in worst-case corruption of the estimated flow field, achieved against a white-box adversary that optimises directly through the twin. On six years of Melbourne data the margin reaches 0.54 against a single compromised device and falls to 0.19 when a third of the fleet is compromised, on a network where only 1.18 per cent of walkable segments are metered. Replacing the street graph by a distance graph collapses it to 0.09, which shows that the gain comes from the conservation law rather than from locality.

AI.tldr: A method to detect stealthy false data injection attacks on city pedestrian counting systems using flow conservation laws and adaptive conformal calibration.
AI.motivation: Current city pedestrian counting systems treat sensor data as ground truth, but these systems can be vulnerable to false data injection attacks. There's a need to understand what happens when sensor data is compromised, especially since pedestrian networks are more rank-deficient than power/water networks where stealth attacks have been studied.
AI.method: Formalizes stealthy false data injection for city-scale pedestrian sensing. Uses a twin estimator for directed flows on pedestrian street graphs, assimilates counts through learned graph-localized gain, and trains against flow conservation residuals. Detection combines innovation with residual, with alarm threshold set by adaptive conformal calibration rather than manual setting.
AI.result: On six years of Melbourne data, achieves attack margin (relative reduction in worst-case corruption) of 0.54 against single compromised device, falling to 0.19 when a third of fleet is compromised. Network has only 1.18% of walkable segments metered. Replacing street graph with distance graph collapses margin to 0.09, showing conservation law (not just locality) provides detection capability.
AI.conclusion: The physics of flow conservation laws provides significant detection capability against false data injection attacks in pedestrian counting systems, even with sparse sensor coverage. Adaptive conformal calibration offers automated threshold setting, and the method shows resilience particularly when leveraging the structural properties of street networks.

title: Disentangling Algorithmic Bias from Archival Artifacts: A Controlled Audit of Vision-Language Model Valuation in Metropolitan Museum Archives
summary:
Auditing vision-language models (VLMs) for societal bias requires distinguishing direct algorithmic valuation disparities from confounders embedded within archival metadata. In this study, we audit Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) models using historical artwork metadata from the Metropolitan Museum of Art Open Access collection (N = 1,500 total objects; N = 743 attributed works: Male n = 534, Female n = 209; n = 618 anonymous).
  We establish a quantitative audit framework evaluating zero-shot CLIP logit differential scores across three semantic prompt pairs (masterpiece, quality, and influence). Unadjusted evaluations demonstrate high score convergence without a statistically significant main gender effect under OpenAI CLIP (mu_F = -0.0067 vs mu_M = -0.0035, p = 0.1829) or OpenCLIP (mu_F = 0.0171 vs mu_M = 0.0237, p = 0.1224). Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) confirm statistical equivalence across Cohen's d >= 0.25 bounds (pTOST < 0.005).
  Multivariate OLS regression controlling for artwork medium, creation era, and aspect ratio (R^2 < 0.02) confirms that artist gender has no statistically significant conditional effect (p > 0.20). High residual embedding variance (R^2 < 2%) indicates that global zero-shot valuation metrics operate near an embedding noise floor, showing that broad zero-shot prompt logit differentials are a coarse measurement instrument rather than proving absolute model fairness.
  We highlight two key caveats: (i) macro-level score equivalence reflects metric insensitivity to fine-grained visual-semantic features and does not preclude localized micro-level visual biases, and (ii) excluding 41.2% unattributed holdings reflects institutional survival bias. These results demonstrate the necessity of multivariate confound control, equivalence testing, and archival provenance auditing when assessing AI fairness in cultural heritage collections.

AI.tldr: CLIP models show no statistically significant gender bias in evaluating historical artworks when controlling for metadata confounders like medium and era, suggesting current zero-shot valuation metrics are too coarse to detect fine-grained visual biases.
AI.motivation: The study aims to audit vision-language models (CLIP) for societal bias in cultural heritage contexts, distinguishing between genuine algorithmic bias and confounders embedded in archival metadata from museum collections.
AI.method: Researchers created a quantitative audit framework using the Met Museum Open Access collection (1,500 artworks, with 743 attributed works: 534 male, 209 female artists). They evaluated zero-shot CLIP logit differentials across three semantic prompts (masterpiece, quality, influence) and conducted statistical analyses including Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) and multivariate OLS regression controlling for medium, creation era, and aspect ratio.
AI.result: Unadjusted evaluations showed no statistically significant gender effect for either OpenAI CLIP or OpenCLIP. TOST confirmed statistical equivalence within Cohen's d ≥ 0.25 bounds. Multivariate regression controlling for confounders showed artist gender has no significant conditional effect, with R² < 0.02 indicating minimal explanatory power of these factors on model outputs.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that macro-level score equivalence in zero-shot valuation metrics doesn't prove model fairness, as these metrics operate near an embedding noise floor and are insensitive to fine-grained visual-semantic features. The findings highlight the necessity of multivariate confound control, equivalence testing, and considering archival provenance biases when assessing AI fairness in cultural heritage applications.

title: Cognitive Extensions for Dual-Process Language Agents: Memory and Self-Reflection in Interactive Environments
summary: Language agents remain brittle in interactive environments, where success requires long-horizon state tracking, valid action execution, and recovery from failed steps. We extend SwiftSage, a dual-process agent that combines a fast action proposer with a slower planner, using two modular cognitive extensions: an Adaptive Memory Module (AMM) for salience-gated episodic storage and trigger-driven retrieval, and a Self-Reflection Module (SRM) for bounded execution-time validation and corrective intervention. Both modules are implemented as feature-flagged extensions over the same execution substrate, enabling controlled ablations on ScienceWorld. Across four configurations---baseline, baseline+AMM, baseline+SRM, and the full system---the full system achieves the best mean final score (64.62), success rate (43.17%), and successful-step efficiency (19.33 steps), while SRM is the strongest standalone contributor. The results suggest that execution-time control is the dominant bottleneck in this setting, while episodic memory becomes most useful once the runtime loop is stabilized.

AI.tldr: SwiftSage agent enhanced with Adaptive Memory Module and Self-Reflection Module achieves best performance in interactive environments through salience-gated episodic storage and execution-time validation.
AI.motivation: Language agents struggle in interactive environments requiring long-horizon state tracking, valid action execution, and recovery from failed steps. Current agents remain brittle and need improvements in memory and self-correction capabilities.
AI.method: Extended SwiftSage dual-process agent with two modular cognitive extensions: 1) Adaptive Memory Module (AMM) for salience-gated episodic storage and trigger-driven retrieval, and 2) Self-Reflection Module (SRM) for bounded execution-time validation and corrective intervention. Both are implemented as feature-flagged extensions over the same execution substrate.
AI.result: Tested across four configurations on ScienceWorld. Full system achieved best mean final score (64.62), success rate (43.17%), and successful-step efficiency (19.33 steps). SRM was the strongest standalone contributor.
AI.conclusion: Execution-time control is the dominant bottleneck in interactive environments, while episodic memory becomes most useful once the runtime loop is stabilized. The modular extensions significantly improve agent robustness and performance.

title: What You Can't See Is Still What You Learn: A Preregistered Sixty-Society Confirmation That Evidence Masking Drives Compositional Generalization
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Preregistered fresh-world confirmation of arXiv:2608.20054; related companion study: arXiv:2609.11365
summary: Restricting what a module can read may improve what a system learns to compute. We test this in a preregistered confirmation with sixty four-cell systems sharing a frozen language-model backbone and communicating through learned continuous packets. Five conditions vary evidence masking, ownership markers, and replacement of foreign evidence with neutral filler, across six initialization clusters, each with two data orders, on one fresh task world. With markers available in both regimes, masking improved accuracy on held-out two- and three-operation compositions by median paired differences of 0.846 and 0.859; all twelve pairs cleared the required margins, and the full preregistered behavioral criterion passed. The unmarked replication also passed. No globally visible system passed the marker-following check, so the effect of usable role information remains unresolved. The filler condition yielded seven full generalizers, but its decomposition criteria were inconclusive. Packet interventions in all eighteen audited masked systems followed the predicted intermediate-value changes on eligible cases; these finite, success-conditioned audits do not establish mediation. The results confirm a large advantage of the tested masking regime, while leaving its finer attribution and generality open. Protocols, results, and checkpoints are public.

AI.tldr: The study confirms that restricting what neural modules can read (masking evidence) significantly improves learning to compute compositions in multi-module systems, but the mechanisms and generality require further investigation.
AI.motivation: To test whether restricting information access between modules (evidence masking) can improve what a computational system learns to compute, based on the hypothesis that limiting module visibility may enhance learning.
AI.method: Used 64-cell systems with frozen language model backbones communicating through learned continuous packets. Tested five conditions varying evidence masking, ownership markers, and foreign evidence replacement with neutral filler. Conducted across six initialization clusters with two data orders on a fresh task world, following preregistered protocols.
AI.result: Masking with markers available improved accuracy on held-out 2- and 3-operation compositions by median differences of 0.846 and 0.859 respectively. All 12 paired comparisons cleared required margins, passing the preregistered behavioral criterion. No system passed marker-following checks. The filler condition produced 7 full generalizers but decomposition analysis was inconclusive. Packet interventions showed predicted intermediate-value changes but don't establish mediation.
AI.conclusion: The study confirms a significant advantage of the tested masking regime for learning compositions, but leaves open questions about finer attribution, generality, and whether systems actually use available role information (markers). The effect of usable role information remains unresolved despite observed performance improvements.

title: Temperon: Full-Time SAM Quality at a Third Less Wall-Clock
summary: Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) doubles the cost of every training step, yet its benefit concentrates where training ends. We study where an expensive training mode should be spent and propose Temperon: a plain-SGD explorer for the first 43% of the epoch budget, then one scheduled hand-off that gives the entire final cosine anneal to a SAM-wrapped Muon refiner. On CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and Tiny ImageNet (five seeds, times reported as epochs-to-target times an idle-GPU-calibrated epoch cost), Temperon matches the best full-time-SAM recipe on accuracy everywhere while reaching the hardest common target 35%, 34% and 32% sooner on three of the four, and sits a tier above the published SAM+SGD recipe at level cost. Ablations make the attribution exact: the Muon refiner is worth +0.85pp with everything else fixed; the explorer's shape and its restarts are worth nothing, and we withdraw them as contributions. Re-running the closest rival, late-phase SAM, at matched budget shows the frontier: it is fastest to every mid-level target, but the tier the Muon refiner buys (0.83 on CIFAR-100, 0.97 on CIFAR-10) is reached by no SGD-refined method in any seed, and on Tiny ImageNet, where Muon buys no tier, the rival simply wins -- the measured boundary of the method. The allocation law transfers to GPT-2 pretraining (full-SAM quality at -29% wall-clock) and GLUE fine-tuning (never worse than full-time SAM at a third of its SAM cost). Two constants organize the economics: skipping SAM early buys a fixed credit, and a Muon epoch costs 1.50x a SAM+SGD epoch on all four datasets. Finally, the hand-off cannot be timed from the trajectory: under cosine schedules the accuracy curve is plateau-then-surge, so the information lives in the schedule, making the scheduled switch principled rather than convenient. Code and a pip-installable implementation are released.

AI.tldr: Temperon: A training strategy that uses plain SGD for the first 43% of epochs, then switches to a SAM-wrapped Muon refiner for the final cosine annealing phase, matching full-time SAM accuracy while being 29-35% faster.
AI.motivation: Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) doubles training cost but its benefits concentrate at the end of training. The authors aim to find where expensive training modes should be spent most effectively.
AI.method: Propose Temperon with two phases: 1) plain-SGD explorer for first 43% of epoch budget, 2) scheduled hand-off to SAM-wrapped Muon refiner for final cosine annealing phase. Allocation is principled based on schedule rather than trajectory observation.
AI.result: Matches full-time SAM accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, Tiny ImageNet while reaching hardest targets 32-35% sooner. On GPT-2 pretraining achieves full-SAM quality at -29% wall-clock time. Muon refiner provides +0.85pp improvement; switching timing cannot be determined from trajectory as accuracy follows plateau-then-surge pattern under cosine schedules.
AI.conclusion: Scheduled phase allocation (early SGD, late SAM-wrapped Muon) provides optimal training efficiency frontier. Two economic constants: skipping SAM early buys fixed credit, and Muon epoch costs 1.50x SAM+SGD epoch. The principled schedule-based switching outperforms trajectory-based timing.

title: CapMem: A Benchmark for Caption-Based Episodic Memory in Egocentric Video
summary: Wearable assistants require episodic memory over egocentric video, yet current vision-language models face bounded frame budgets, growing visual-token costs, and long-context retrieval failures. Under these practical constraints, we study whether textual captions can serve as reusable episodic memory. We define the Episodic Memory Video Caption QA task and introduce CapMem, a human-annotated benchmark with 75 videos totaling 33.7 hours, and 1,000 multiple-choice questions across 16 scenarios. On long videos (>20 min), full-coverage CaptionQA with 30s and 60s caption windows outperforms direct VideoQA for 10/12 and 8/12 models, respectively. On the same video subset, a matched-frame control across six Qwen models retains mean accuracy gains of 3.22 and 2.55 points, respectively. Our caption-guided retrieve-and-verify harness further improves accuracy by up to 5.3 points. These results support the effectiveness of caption memory for episodic reasoning over long egocentric video.

AI.tldr: Textual captions serve as effective episodic memory for long egocentric videos, outperforming direct video analysis under practical constraints and improving question answering accuracy through caption-guided retrieval.
AI.motivation: Wearable assistants need episodic memory for long egocentric videos, but current vision-language models face frame budget limitations, high visual-token costs, and long-context retrieval failures, creating practical constraints that need addressing.
AI.method: Introduces CapMem benchmark with 75 videos (33.7 hours) and 1,000 multiple-choice questions across 16 scenarios; compares caption-based QA (CaptionQA with 30s/60s windows) vs direct VideoQA; implements matched-frame controls across Qwen models and develops caption-guided retrieve-and-verify harness.
AI.result: On long videos (>20 min), CaptionQA with 30s/60s windows outperforms direct VideoQA for 10/12 and 8/12 models respectively; matched-frame controls show accuracy gains of 3.22 and 2.55 points; caption-guided retrieve-and-verify improves accuracy by up to 5.3 points.
AI.conclusion: Textual captions can serve as reusable episodic memory that effectively supports episodic reasoning over long egocentric videos, offering practical advantages over direct video analysis under current model constraints.

title: When the Gradient Sees Rank: Provable Necessity, Causal Recruitment, and Composition in Trained Matrix Memories
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Code and archived results: https://github.com/saml212/matrix-memories
summary: Can gradient-based training learn the rank needed to store and compose associations in a matrix memory? In our earlier study, we used a matrix-augmented reasoner on a task that admits a rank-1 solution, leaving this question open. We train matrix memories on $K$ fresh key-value bindings whose exact linear recovery requires $\mathrm{rank}(Z) \geq K$. A fixed linear readout queries a single matrix state without access to the original bindings. Experiments measure recovery by cosine similarity greater than 0.9, a threshold distinct from mathematical equality. Learned effective rank increases with $K$ across the tested grid (Spearman $ρ= 1.0$ at $d = 16$). Training-time rank caps produce a recovery transition near $k = K$: at $d = 8$, $K = 4$, rank 3 gives at most 0.0004 recovery and rank 4 gives 0.97. Four of five seeds retain at least 0.9996 recovery through 21-fold self-application of the trained operator. On the entity subspace, the learned operator has effective rank close to $K$ and approximates the ideal cycle. For the single converged seed capped below $K$, a calculation using the entity-subspace operator and ideal cycle predicts the measured cosine within 0.008 through seven applications. Extending training resolves several initial failures, but recovery still declines at larger matrix dimensions with encoder width fixed.

AI.tldr: Gradient-based training can learn the necessary rank to store and retrieve K key-value bindings in a matrix memory, with learned rank scaling with K and enabling composition through multiple applications.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether gradient-based training can learn the appropriate rank required for storing and composing associations in a matrix memory, building on previous work that used a rank-1 solution.
AI.method: Train matrix memories on K fresh key-value bindings where exact linear recovery requires rank(Z) ≥ K, using a fixed linear readout to query a single matrix state without access to original bindings. Measure recovery by cosine similarity >0.9 threshold. Experiments test learned effective rank increases with K and evaluate recovery transitions with rank caps, including self-application tests.
AI.result: Learned effective rank increases with K (Spearman ρ=1.0 at d=16). Rank caps show recovery transitions near k=K: rank 3 gives ≤0.0004 recovery vs rank 4 gives 0.97 at d=8, K=4. Most seeds retain ≥0.9996 recovery through 21-fold self-application. Learned operator approximates ideal cycle on entity subspace with rank close to K.
AI.conclusion: Yes, gradient-based training can learn the necessary rank for storing and composing associations in matrix memories, with learned rank scaling appropriately with the number of bindings and enabling reliable composition through multiple applications, though challenges remain at larger dimensions with fixed encoder width.

title: GraphEcho: Structural Redundancy and Evidence Provenance in LLM Graph Agents
summary: A large language model (LLM) agent can follow more graph paths without acquiring more independent evidence. GraphEcho tests whether agents mistake these repeated encounters for additional corroboration. The benchmark varies path counts and evidential origins while holding evidence content fixed, and evaluates both judgments and active exploration. Controlled synthetic experiments reveal model-dependent judgment shifts, but redundant supporting paths increase the share of repeated walks across all evaluated frozen agents. Provenance-aware post-training (PAPT) reduces revisits and improves synthetic accuracy, yet covers fewer distinct sources. On scientific claims, it continues to reduce repetition while accuracy declines. These findings expose a gap between efficient exploration and effective evidence use: an agent can learn to stop repeating itself while overlooking information it needs. GraphEcho provides a controlled way to evaluate both what graph agents conclude and whether their exploration reaches distinct evidential sources.

AI.tldr: LLM agents mistake repeated graph path encounters for additional evidence, even when evidence content remains the same. GraphEcho benchmark evaluates this bias and explores solutions.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand whether LLM agents incorrectly interpret repeated encounters with the same evidence through different graph paths as additional corroboration. There's a need to evaluate how agents explore and use evidence in graph-structured information environments.
AI.method: The authors create GraphEcho benchmark that varies path counts and evidential origins while keeping evidence content fixed. They conduct controlled synthetic experiments and evaluate both judgments and active exploration. They test frozen agents, introduce Provenance-aware post-training (PAPT), and apply the approach to scientific claims.
AI.result: Models show judgment shifts depending on path repetition but not evidence content. Redundant supporting paths increase repeated walks across all agents. PAPT reduces revisits and improves synthetic accuracy but covers fewer distinct sources. On scientific claims, PAPT reduces repetition but accuracy declines.
AI.conclusion: There's a gap between efficient exploration and effective evidence use: agents can learn to stop repeating themselves while missing needed information. GraphEcho provides a controlled way to evaluate both what graph agents conclude and whether their exploration reaches distinct evidential sources.

title: Prior-Free Competitive Ratios for Improving Bandits: Scale, Curvature and Horizon Are Free, but Not Jointly Under Noise
summary: In the improving multi-armed bandits problem, each of $k$ arms has an unknown nondecreasing, discretely concave reward curve $f_i$, and pulling arm $i$ for the $t$-th time yields $f_i(t)$. For sufficiently long horizons, Blum and Ravichandran (ALT 2025) proved that randomized algorithms achieve an $O(\sqrt k)$ approximation to the best single arm when the scale $m=f^*(T)$ of the optimal arm is known ($T\ge2k$), and $O(\sqrt k\log k)$ when it is not ($T>4k$), against an $Ω(\sqrt k)$ lower bound. The logarithmic factor is unnecessary: a one-page \emph{probe-and-commit} algorithm achieves competitive ratio $4\sqrt3\,\sqrt k$ for $T\ge2\lfloor\sqrt k\rfloor$, without any knowledge of the scale, and we determine the optimal ratio for every horizon, $Θ(\sqrt k+k/T)$, also for unknown horizons. Without noise, \emph{no prior is needed at all}: a random-marginal probing algorithm reading neither the scale $m$, nor the concavity-envelope exponent $β$ of Blum, Garicano, Ravichandran and Sharma (UAI 2026), nor the horizon $T$, achieves the optimal $Θ(k^{β/(1+β)}+k/T)$ simultaneously for every $β$ and every horizon. Under the multiplicative noise model of Blum and Ravichandran, probe-and-commit keeps the same all-horizon order $Θ(\sqrt k+k/T)$ without knowing the noise level (and $Θ(\sqrt k)$ on the same range), but the price of priors jumps: for any fixed noise level $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2]$, the uniform price of adaptation $φ_\varepsilon(k)$ --- the worst case over horizons $T\ge16k$ of the loss relative to $k^{β/(1+β)}$ for algorithms knowing neither $m$ nor $β$ --- is $Θ_\varepsilon(\sqrt{\log k/\log\log k})$, the lower bound asymptotic in $k$ at fixed positive $\varepsilon$ and matched by a nested random-permutation probing algorithm, whereas knowing either $m$ or $β$ alone restores a constant price.

AI.tldr: A probe-and-commit algorithm achieves optimal competitive ratio O(√k) for improving multi-armed bandits without knowing reward scale, and the paper determines optimal ratios across horizons, showing no prior knowledge needed in noise-free case, while characterizing price of priors under multiplicative noise.
AI.motivation: Previous work by Blum and Ravichandran (ALT 2025) showed randomized algorithms achieve O(√k log k) approximation without knowledge of reward scale, but the logarithmic factor was unnecessary. The paper aims to improve these bounds and understand fundamental limits of adaptation when facing unknown parameters like reward scale, concavity exponent, horizon, and noise level.
AI.method: Develops simple probe-and-commit algorithms and random-marginal probing algorithms that require no prior knowledge of parameters. Uses nested random-permutation probing for multiplicative noise setting. Analyzes optimal competitive ratios across different horizon regimes and parameter knowledge scenarios.
AI.result: Proves optimal competitive ratio of Θ(√k + k/T) for all horizons, even with unknown horizon. In noise-free case, achieves optimal Θ(k^{β/(1+β)} + k/T) without any prior knowledge. Under multiplicative noise, shows uniform price of adaptation is Θ_ε(√(log k/log log k)) for fixed noise level ε, while knowing either reward scale m or concavity exponent β restores constant price.
AI.conclusion: Simple algorithms without parameter knowledge can achieve optimal performance bounds in improving multi-armed bandits. The work characterizes fundamental trade-offs between adaptation and prior knowledge, showing when such knowledge is essential and when it can be circumvented by smart algorithm design.

title: GVD: Governed Versioning and Deduplication for Document Repositories
summary: Document repositories evolve continuously. Guidelines and policies are revised, superseded, and re-uploaded, so the same content recurs in different wording and newer versions refine or contradict earlier ones. These inconsistencies belong to the growing collection rather than to any single document, yet existing work treats versioning, duplicate detection, and contradiction detection as isolated pairwise tasks and stops once a pair is labeled. We present GVD (Governed Versioning and Deduplication), a framework that unifies cross-document version linking with rule-level conflict resolution under an auditable update policy. Incoming documents are assigned to version families through bidirectional rule alignment, and their rules are compared against the family memory to identify duplicates, contradictions, asymmetric refinements, and new knowledge, with Counterfactual Span Probing (CSP) resolving related pairs that inference misclassifies as neutral. Relation-specific policies suppress duplicates and escalate only consequential changes for review, retaining version lineage as an audit trail. The pipeline runs fully locally, with no large language model. On 120 enterprise documents processed as 140 ingestions across 59 version families, GVD reaches an F1 of 0.97 for version-family construction and 0.94 for rule-level consistency, with CSP raising rule consistency from 0.90 to 0.94.

AI.tldr: GVD is a unified framework for governed versioning and deduplication in document repositories that links documents into version families while detecting rule-level conflicts, duplicates, and refinements with an auditable update policy.
AI.motivation: Document repositories evolve continuously with guidelines/policies being revised, superseded, and re-uploaded, causing inconsistencies across versions. Existing work treats versioning, duplicate detection, and contradiction detection as isolated pairwise tasks without considering the broader collection context.
AI.method: GVD framework unifies cross-document version linking with rule-level conflict resolution using bidirectional rule alignment to assign documents to version families. It compares rules against family memory to identify duplicates, contradictions, asymmetric refinements, and new knowledge. Uses Counterfactual Span Probing (CSP) to resolve related pairs misclassified as neutral. Implements relation-specific policies that suppress duplicates and escalate only consequential changes for review. Runs fully locally without large language models.
AI.result: On 120 enterprise documents processed as 140 ingestions across 59 version families, GVD achieves F1 of 0.97 for version-family construction and 0.94 for rule-level consistency. CSP raises rule consistency from 0.90 to 0.94.
AI.conclusion: GVD successfully addresses the limitations of isolated pairwise approaches by providing a unified framework for governed versioning and deduplication that maintains audit trails, suppresses duplicates, and escalates only consequential changes while achieving high accuracy in both version-family construction and rule-level consistency detection.

title: Lecture notes on Physics Informed Neural Networks, Neural Operators, and their applications
comment: 264 pages; Lecture notes for the PhD course Physics Informed Neural Network held at the University of Bozen/Bolzano
summary:
This is the set of lecture notes for the PhD course \href{https://www.unibz.it/en/faculties/engineering/phd-computer-science/study-course-offering/2025/36967}{\textit{Physics Informed Neural Network}, held at the University of Bozen/Bolzano} in the academic year 2025/2026.
  The goal of the course was to introduce the concept of Physics Informed Deep Neural Networks (PINN) and Neural Operators (NOs), discuss their implementation from scratch in PyTorch and using advanced ad-hoc developed open-source libraries such as NVIDia PhysicsNeMo to address real-world problems in various fields (engineering, physics, petroleum reservoir). We discuss recent topics such as Mixture-of-Models, Fourier Neural Operators, Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (PIKANs) and Fourier Neural Operators.

AI.tldr: Lecture notes for a PhD course on Physics Informed Neural Networks and Neural Operators, covering implementations in PyTorch and specialized libraries like NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo.
AI.motivation: To introduce PhD students to Physics Informed Deep Neural Networks (PINNs) and Neural Operators (NOs) for solving real-world problems in engineering, physics, and petroleum reservoir simulation.
AI.method: Course-based approach with hands-on implementation from scratch in PyTorch, plus use of advanced open-source libraries like NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo. Covers recent topics including Mixture-of-Models, Fourier Neural Operators, and Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (PIKANs).
AI.result: Comprehensive lecture notes covering both foundational concepts and cutting-edge developments in physics-informed machine learning, with practical implementation examples for real-world applications.
AI.conclusion: These lecture notes provide a complete educational resource for teaching advanced physics-informed neural network methods, bridging theoretical concepts with practical implementation skills for PhD students in computational sciences.

title: NeMo Data Designer: An Extensible Framework for Multimodal Synthetic Data Generation
summary: We present NeMo Data Designer (NDD), an open-source, general-purpose framework for multi-modal synthetic data generation (SDG). Designed to be intuitive to use, NDD provides a declarative configuration format in which human and/or agent users define each dataset column, with column types spanning text, code, structured outputs, images, embeddings, and statistical samplers that are explicitly configured to steer dataset diversity. Additional column types and functionality can be introduced using the framework's flexible plugin system. NDD's configuration is an inspectable artifact, supporting workflow sharing and reproducibility. SDG is an inherently iterative process. NDD therefore builds a preview-and-revision loop into its core workflow, allowing users to generate and inspect a small number of records, refine the specification, and rerun generation at full scale. At runtime, NDD resolves dependencies, schedules calls to user-provided model endpoints, and retries failed requests. We describe NDD's architecture and programming model and present case studies spanning structured, agentic, multimodal, and domain-specialized tasks, including datasets used in Nemotron model development and in production enterprise deployments.

AI.tldr: NeMo Data Designer (NDD) is an open-source framework for multi-modal synthetic data generation that offers declarative configuration, plugin system, preview-revision loops, and dependency management for creating diverse datasets across various domains.
AI.motivation: The need for systematic, reproducible, and intuitive frameworks for synthetic data generation, especially for multi-modal datasets (text, code, images, structured outputs) used in model development and enterprise deployments. Existing approaches lack proper workflow management, inspectability, and iterative refinement capabilities.
AI.method: NDD provides a declarative configuration format where users define dataset columns with specific types (text, code, structured outputs, images, embeddings, statistical samplers). It includes a plugin system for extensibility, preview-and-revision loops for iterative refinement, dependency resolution, scheduling to model endpoints, and retry mechanisms for failed requests.
AI.result: A general-purpose framework demonstrated through case studies spanning structured, agentic, multimodal, and domain-specialized tasks. The framework supports Nemotron model development and production enterprise deployments, providing inspectable configuration artifacts for workflow sharing and reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: NDD successfully addresses the need for a comprehensive synthetic data generation framework with key features like declarative configuration, inspectable artifacts, iterative workflow, and multi-modal support, making it valuable for both research and production use cases in synthetic data creation.

title: Fathom: Per-Query Read Depth for Sparse Decoding over Offloaded KV Caches
summary: When agentic sessions run to a million tokens with many sessions resident at once, the KV cache and the index that ranks it live in host memory, and the scan that ranks all n keys for a top-k step becomes the traffic that bounds decoding. We present Fathom, a key scan in which each query decides how many bits of each key channel to read. The 4-bit K cache is stored channel-major as bit planes, so a prefix of t planes is exactly the channel's t-bit quantizer, and the query spends its bit budget by reverse water-filling over the variance-weighted importance of its channels. At one million tokens on Qwen3-8B a decode step is 1.67x faster in GPU time than with the 136-bit scans of Double Sparsity, Loki and SparQ r=32, and in the same GPU time as SparQ's 68-bit read (r=16) Fathom reads 18% fewer bytes with lower attention error on six of seven model and context settings. On RULER-style tasks every per-token scan matches exact top-k decoding, and on real coding-agent sessions Fathom reaches the step agreement of the most accurate 136-bit scan at 92 bits. The store is the 4-bit K copy a quantized serving stack already holds, and the method is not faster when the index is resident in GPU memory.

AI.tldr: Fathom is a memory-efficient key scan algorithm for large language models that uses adaptive bit reading per channel to reduce KV cache traffic, achieving faster decoding with similar accuracy compared to existing sparse attention methods.
AI.motivation: When running agentic sessions with millions of tokens and many concurrent sessions, the KV cache and ranking index reside in host memory. The scan that ranks all n keys for top-k selection becomes bandwidth-bound traffic that limits decoding speed.
AI.method: Fathom performs key scanning where each query dynamically decides how many bits to read from each key channel. The 4-bit K cache is stored channel-major as bit planes, so reading a prefix of t planes gives exactly the channel's t-bit quantizer. Queries allocate their bit budget using reverse water-filling over the variance-weighted importance of channels.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B with one million tokens, decoding is 1.67x faster in GPU time than 136-bit scans of Double Sparsity, Loki and SparQ r=32. Compared to SparQ's 68-bit read, Fathom reads 18% fewer bytes with lower attention error in 6 of 7 model/context settings. On RULER tasks, per-token scans match exact top-k decoding, and on real coding-agent sessions, Fathom achieves step agreement of most accurate 136-bit scan at just 92 bits.
AI.conclusion: Fathom provides an efficient approach for KV cache scanning in memory-bound scenarios by leveraging the 4-bit K cache already present in quantized serving stacks, achieving significant speed improvements without accuracy loss when the index resides in host memory (though it doesn't help when the index is in GPU memory).

title: A Systematic Evaluation of the COTQ Provincial Land Cover Product: Structural Consistency, Spectral Separability, and Relative Positioning Against ESA, ESRI, and Google Products
summary: High-resolution land use and land cover (LULC) products derived from Sentinel-2 imagery are widely used for environmental monitoring and land management, yet their performance can vary across regions with complex ecological gradients and heterogeneous surface conditions. In Quebec, these limitations motivated the development of a provincial 10-m land-cover product, the COTQ, designed to support annual monitoring of land occupation and soil artificialisation. This study presents a systematic evaluation of the COTQ product relative to three global 10-m LULC datasets: ESA WorldCover, ESRI LandCover, and Google DynamicWorld.
