This paper does not introduce a new mapping methodology but focuses on analysing the behaviour and consistency of the COTQ using complementary evaluation approaches. All products are harmonized under a common legend and compared using structural indicators (object-size distributions, shape complexity, Adjusted Rand Index, and Intersection over Union), spectral separability metrics derived from Sentinel-2 reflectance data, and a targeted photo-interpretation of disagreement areas. The analysis is conducted over eight Sentinel-2 tiles selected to represent the main bioclimatic domains of Québec, from temperate and boreal forests to northern tundra environments. The results show that the COTQ exhibits structural and spectral characteristics most similar to ESA WorldCover among the reference global products, while revealing systematic differences linked to class definitions and thematic priorities, particularly for urban areas, wetlands, and rocky or cryptogamic surfaces. This multi-criteria evaluation provides an objective characterization of the COTQ product and clarifies its relative positioning with respect to existing global land-cover datasets for operational land monitoring in Québec.

AI.tldr: This study systematically evaluates Quebec's provincial 10-m land-cover product (COTQ) against three global datasets (ESA WorldCover, ESRI LandCover, Google DynamicWorld) across multiple metrics to characterize its performance for regional monitoring.
AI.motivation: Existing global LULC products often underperform in regions with complex ecological gradients and heterogeneous surfaces like Quebec, necessitating a regional product (COTQ) for better land monitoring and soil artificialization tracking.
AI.method: Comparative evaluation of COTQ with three global datasets using: 1) structural indicators (object-size distributions, shape complexity, Adjusted Rand Index, IoU), 2) spectral separability metrics from Sentinel-2 reflectance, and 3) targeted photo-interpretation of disagreement areas across eight Sentinel-2 tiles representing Quebec's bioclimatic domains.
AI.result: COTQ shows closest structural and spectral similarity to ESA WorldCover among global products, but reveals systematic differences in class definitions and thematic priorities, particularly for urban areas, wetlands, and rocky/cryptogamic surfaces.
AI.conclusion: The multi-criteria evaluation provides objective characterization of COTQ's performance and clarifies its positioning relative to global datasets, demonstrating its suitability for operational land monitoring in Quebec despite differences in thematic priorities.

title: Reflect, Revise, Reuse: Training-Free Skill Evolution for GUI Agents
summary: GUI agents execute long-horizon tasks on dynamic graphical user interfaces, where pop-ups, delayed loads, and relocated widgets routinely invalidate plans fixed before execution. Recent agent-skill frameworks encapsulate reusable procedural knowledge to mitigate this, yet existing skill designs are largely developed without targeting GUI execution dynamics and treat skills as static artifacts produced before deployment rather than living procedural knowledge that improves through it. We argue that what GUI agents need is not better static skills, but skills that can be revised from execution feedback at deployment time, without additional training. We propose \textbf{EvoSkill-GUI}, a training-free framework in which each skill is a structured multi-file package containing retrieval metadata, executable plans, backup localization, failure-recovery rules, accessibility utilities, and failure cases. EvoSkill-GUI operates through a \textbf{\emph{reflect-revise-reuse}} loop: the executor performs instant in-rollout revisions, an isolated critic diagnoses failed trajectories under strict information isolation, and the executor edits specific skill files through a restricted tool interface. Across MobileWorld, AndroidWorld, and OSWorld, three mainstream GUI benchmarks spanning mobile and desktop platforms, EvoSkill-GUI consistently improves multiple base models without any training, with maximum gains of $+16.2\%$, $+6.0\%$, and $+10.5\%$ respectively, and evolved skill libraries continue to benefit related tasks rather than being rebuilt from scratch. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/EvoSkill-GUI.

AI.tldr: EvoSkill-GUI is a training-free framework that enables GUI agents to dynamically revise their skills during deployment through a reflect-revise-reuse loop, improving performance on GUI benchmarks without additional training.
AI.motivation: GUI agents face challenges with dynamic graphical user interfaces where pop-ups, delayed loads, and relocated widgets routinely invalidate pre-execution plans. Existing skill frameworks treat skills as static artifacts created before deployment rather than living procedural knowledge that can improve through execution feedback.
AI.method: EvoSkill-GUI structures each skill as a multi-file package containing retrieval metadata, executable plans, backup localization, failure-recovery rules, accessibility utilities, and failure cases. It operates through a reflect-revise-reuse loop: executor performs instant in-rollout revisions, an isolated critic diagnoses failed trajectories with strict information isolation, and executor edits specific skill files through restricted tool interface.
AI.result: Across three mainstream GUI benchmarks (MobileWorld, AndroidWorld, OSWorld) spanning mobile and desktop platforms, EvoSkill-GUI consistently improved multiple base models without any training, achieving maximum gains of +16.2%, +6.0%, and +10.5% respectively. Evolved skill libraries continue to benefit related tasks rather than requiring rebuilding from scratch.
AI.conclusion: GUI agents need dynamic skills that can be revised from execution feedback at deployment time rather than static skills. EvoSkill-GUI demonstrates that training-free skill evolution through structured revision mechanisms can significantly improve GUI agent performance across diverse platforms.

title: Imitation Learning for Autonomous Driving in CARLA
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures. Code, data samples and trained policy: https://github.com/JordyKieto/carla-imitation-learning
summary: Behavioral cloning trains a policy offline on expert demonstrations, but deployment is closed loop: each action affects the observations the policy receives next. We study how much closed-loop driving competence a compact multimodal policy can acquire from offline demonstrations in the CARLA simulator. The policy uses five-frame histories of RGB images, LiDAR, vehicle telemetry, and lane waypoints to predict throttle, brake, and steering at 20 Hz. Demonstrations were collected in three stages, ending with a systematic route-generation procedure that enumerates spawn points and feasible maneuvers and verifies completed autopilot routes. The released 1.36 million parameter policy was trained on 236,882 windows, representing about 3.3 hours of driving from 448 captures. The resulting policy drives autonomously for hours on training and held-out routes. In our runs, it did so without collisions and also transferred qualitatively to an unseen CARLA town with different road geometry. We also observed recovery from large trajectory deviations, although we do not claim systematic recovery without controlled evaluation. We report offline metrics and distinguish measured results from qualitative closed-loop observations. We release the code, trained checkpoint, ONNX model, data sample, and an evidence audit for the reported claims.

AI.tldr: A compact multimodal policy trained via behavioral cloning on offline driving demonstrations in CARLA simulator achieves hours of collision-free autonomous driving, showing recovery capabilities and transfer to unseen environments.
AI.motivation: To study how much closed-loop driving competence a compact multimodal policy can acquire from offline demonstrations alone, despite the deployment being closed-loop where actions affect future observations.
AI.method: Behavioral cloning with a 1.36M parameter policy using five-frame histories of RGB images, LiDAR, vehicle telemetry, and lane waypoints to predict throttle, brake, and steering at 20Hz. Trained on 236,882 windows from systematically collected demonstrations representing 3.3 hours of driving from 448 captures.
AI.result: The policy drives autonomously for hours on both training and held-out routes without collisions, transfers qualitatively to an unseen CARLA town with different road geometry, and shows recovery from large trajectory deviations (though not systematically evaluated).
AI.conclusion: Compact multimodal policies can acquire substantial closed-loop driving competence from offline demonstrations in simulation, enabling hours of collision-free autonomous driving with recovery capabilities and cross-environment transfer.

title: Regularized Least Squares Training of Quadratic Neural Networks with Applications to System Identification
summary: This paper proposes a least squares approach for the training of quadratic neural networks with regularization. The proposed methodology yields a lower bound on the solution of the training optimization problem for the case where the regularization coefficient is positive. Moreover, it yields closed-form expressions for the approximate solution and its sensitivity The lower bound is tight and the approximate solution is the optimal solution when the regularization coefficient is zero. Having a closed-form expression for the weights reduces considerably the computational time when compared with iterative numerical methods such as backpropagation that can get stuck in local minima. The proposed approach has three main contributions, namely, (i) it yields an analytical expression for the weights, (ii) an analytical expression for the sensitivity of the weights to errors in the data is also provided, (iii) it establishes a connection between the optimization to compute a lower bound and nuclear norm minimization. The proposed least squares training is successfully applied to a nonlinear system identification example where the proposed lower bound is compared with the optimal value.

AI.tldr: Proposes a least squares training method for quadratic neural networks with regularization that provides analytical weight solutions and sensitivity analysis, avoiding iterative optimization pitfalls.
AI.motivation: Traditional iterative methods like backpropagation for training quadratic neural networks can get stuck in local minima and are computationally expensive. There's a need for more efficient, closed-form solutions that provide analytical insights into the training process.
AI.method: A least squares approach with regularization for training quadratic neural networks. The method yields lower bounds on the solution when regularization is positive, provides closed-form expressions for approximate solutions and their sensitivity to data errors, and connects the optimization to nuclear norm minimization.
AI.result: The approach produces tight lower bounds and optimal solutions when regularization coefficient is zero. It significantly reduces computational time compared to iterative methods and provides analytical insights through closed-form weight expressions and sensitivity analysis.
AI.conclusion: The proposed least squares training method offers efficient, analytical solutions for quadratic neural networks that avoid local minima issues, provides valuable sensitivity analysis, and establishes theoretical connections to nuclear norm minimization. The method is successfully demonstrated in nonlinear system identification tasks.

title: SAGE: Governed Artifact Generation from Enterprise Guidelines
summary: Enterprise guideline documents mix narrative text, complex tables, and embedded images, and converting them into structured work artifacts still takes two to three days of manual effort each. Current language and vision-language models extract from such documents but offer no governed workflow beyond extraction: no validation, no consistency checking, no traceable artifact generation. We introduce SAGE, a governed multi-stage LLM pipeline organized around a shared versioned rule store with stable identifiers, schema-validated inter-stage contracts, and end-to-end provenance tracking. Extracted rules undergo deterministic structural validation and LLM-based semantic scoring, then a consistency module that removes duplicates, flags contradictions, and surfaces specification gaps; only uncertain or flagged items reach reviewers, while high-confidence outputs are auto-approved. On 120 documents, SAGE cuts turnaround from days to 20-100 minutes, achieving a 96% document-level success rate with 3.2% hallucination, extracting 3,896 rules and producing 812 artifacts ready for human review; without governance, hallucination rises to 15.7%.

AI.tldr: SAGE: A governed multi-stage LLM pipeline that transforms enterprise guideline documents into structured work artifacts with validation, consistency checking, and provenance tracking, reducing processing time from days to minutes.
AI.motivation: Enterprise guideline documents contain complex mixed content (narrative text, tables, images) that currently requires 2-3 days of manual effort to convert into structured work artifacts. Existing language/vision-language models only extract content without providing governed workflows for validation, consistency checking, or traceable artifact generation.
AI.method: SAGE uses a governed multi-stage LLM pipeline organized around a shared versioned rule store with stable identifiers. It features schema-validated inter-stage contracts and end-to-end provenance tracking. The system includes deterministic structural validation, LLM-based semantic scoring, and a consistency module that removes duplicates, flags contradictions, and surfaces specification gaps. Only uncertain/flagged items go to reviewers while high-confidence outputs are auto-approved.
AI.result: On 120 documents, SAGE reduced turnaround time from days to 20-100 minutes, achieving 96% document-level success rate with 3.2% hallucination. It extracted 3,896 rules and produced 812 artifacts ready for human review. Without governance, hallucination rose to 15.7%.
AI.conclusion: SAGE demonstrates that governed LLM pipelines can dramatically improve the efficiency and quality of converting complex enterprise documents into structured artifacts by providing validation, consistency checking, and provenance tracking, significantly reducing both processing time and error rates compared to ungoverned approaches.

title: DSD: Learning Diverse and Reusable Motor Skills via Diffusion Skill Discovery
summary: Humans efficiently learn new tasks by reusing a rich repertoire of motor skills across different goals and contexts. A similar strategy can also be used to enable simulated characters to efficiently perform new tasks by leveraging reusable motor skills. To support a wide range of downstream tasks, the learned repertoire should be diverse, consisting of distinct behaviors as well as spatial and temporal variation within each behavior. A commonly used method for learning diverse skills is by maximizing the mutual information between skill latents and the states produced by a policy. The marginal state entropy promotes broad behavioral coverage, while the conditional entropy encourages consistent behaviors from each latent. However, directly estimating the marginal state entropy is intractable in high-dimensional control problems. Prior methods therefore rely on indirect latent-space approximations or coarse estimators of the state distribution. These approximations may not effectively promote broad coverage of the state space, resulting in skills with limited behavioral diversity and reduced utility for downstream tasks. In this work, we propose Diffusion Skill Discovery (DSD), a skill discovery method that uses a diffusion model to approximate the entropy gradient of the policy-induced state distribution through score matching. The resulting objective encourages the discovery of skills that produce a broader range of behaviors for high-dimensional humanoid control. The learned skills are reused in two downstream control settings: hierarchical control with a task-specific high-level policy and zero-shot control through latent selection from offline trajectories. Our experiments show that DSD discovers a broader repertoire of reusable motor skills than prior skill discovery methods, leading to the emergence of complex and agile behaviors that can be reused across downstream tasks.

AI.tldr: DSD is a skill discovery method using diffusion models to approximate entropy gradients, enabling broader behavioral coverage and reusable motor skills for downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Current skill discovery methods struggle with promoting broad coverage of state space in high-dimensional control problems due to intractable marginal state entropy estimation. They rely on indirect approximations that may limit behavioral diversity and reduce utility for downstream tasks.
AI.method: Proposes Diffusion Skill Discovery (DSD) that uses a diffusion model to approximate the entropy gradient of the policy-induced state distribution through score matching, enabling more effective skill discovery in high-dimensional humanoid control.
AI.result: DSD discovers broader repertoire of reusable motor skills than prior methods, leading to emergence of complex and agile behaviors that can be successfully reused in hierarchical control with task-specific high-level policies and zero-shot control through latent selection.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion Skill Discovery effectively addresses the limitations of previous skill discovery methods by using diffusion models for entropy gradient approximation, resulting in more diverse and reusable skills that enhance performance in downstream control tasks.

title: FairCompressAgent: An Agentic Framework for Fairness-Aware Model Compression for FPGA Deployment
summary: Fairness-aware model compression requires selecting methods and configurations that balance accuracy, fairness, and deployment cost. These decisions become more difficult when compression methods are composed or the user's requirements change. In this paper, we propose FairCompressAgent (FCA), an agentic framework that integrates fairness-aware pruning, incremental quantization, and sparse low-rank factorization through a common operator interface. A language-model planner uses model profiles and measured outcomes to select compression configurations, while an execution layer performs compression, fine-tuning, evaluation, and constraint-based selection. FCA also supports requirement updates and reports the remaining violation when a request cannot be satisfied. Experiments on Fitzpatrick-17k with VGG-11 compare four search methods over 40 measured configurations. Under the accuracy-constrained request, FCA selects a compressed model with 59.54% less inference tensor storage, while validation average precision increases from 0.5141 to 0.5233 and equalized opportunity (EOpp) decreases from 0.2251 to 0.2168. It reaches the same final selection as one-shot planning with 7.33 versus 12 candidate evaluations on average, under their respective stopping policies. Repeated fine-tuning, held-out testing, and online requirement updates characterize the stability and interactive use of this compression workflow. The results demonstrate how measured feedback and explicit constraints support the selection and interactive refinement of fairness-aware compression configurations.

AI.tldr: FairCompressAgent (FCA) is an agentic framework that automates the selection and execution of fairness-aware model compression methods (pruning, quantization, sparse low-rank factorization) through constraint-based planning and measured feedback.
AI.motivation: Selecting appropriate model compression methods and configurations that balance accuracy, fairness, and deployment cost is challenging, especially when methods are composed or user requirements change. Existing approaches lack systematic frameworks for making these complex decisions.
AI.method: FCA integrates multiple compression techniques through a common operator interface, with a language-model planner that uses model profiles and measured outcomes to select configurations. An execution layer performs compression, fine-tuning, evaluation, and constraint-based selection, supporting requirement updates and reporting when requests cannot be satisfied.
AI.result: On Fitzpatrick-17k with VGG-11, FCA selected a compressed model with 59.54% less inference tensor storage while increasing validation average precision from 0.5141 to 0.5233 and decreasing equalized opportunity from 0.2251 to 0.2168 under accuracy-constrained requests. It achieved the same selection as one-shot planning with only 7.33 vs 12 candidate evaluations on average.
AI.conclusion: Measured feedback and explicit constraints effectively support the selection and interactive refinement of fairness-aware compression configurations. FCA demonstrates stability and practical utility for interactive compression workflows with changing requirements.

title: The Missing "I Don't Know": Why Three Reasoning-Reliability Findings Converge on Calibrated Abstention
comment: 12 pages, 4 tables. Accepted to AACL-IJCNLP 2026 (main conference)
summary: Three recent results describe what look like unrelated LLM reliability problems. Yin et al. (2026) show reasoning RL collapses tool-reliability representations. Suleymanov et al. (2026) show that under safety-constrained generation, large models rewrite flagged spans while small models truncate. Bastounis et al. (2024) prove any consistent-reasoning system without an implicit "I don't know" function must hallucinate infinitely often on broad problem classes. We argue these findings converge on a single intervention: calibrated abstention is what each independently identifies as the missing capability, even though the unavailability they document, a capability gap, a policy gap, and a recursion-theoretic gap, has a different source in each case. Honesty post-training has narrowed the gap in deployed models, but principled closure of the class Bastounis identifies requires a calibrated abstention function whose training signal at the leaderboard level is absent: dominant benchmarks assign zero reward to decline, so the leaderboard gradient that would select for the function does not exist. We propose four changes to evaluation: triple-scoring, abstention-rate reporting, capability-stratified evaluation, and mandatory calibration metrics. Benchmark reform is necessary, not sufficient, for closing the gap the theorem identifies.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that three seemingly unrelated LLM reliability problems all converge on the need for calibrated abstention as the missing capability, and proposes benchmark reforms to address this gap.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to identify a common solution for three distinct LLM reliability problems: reasoning RL collapse of tool-reliability representations (Yin et al., 2026), different handling of safety-constrained generation between large vs small models (Suleymanov et al., 2026), and the mathematical proof that consistent-reasoning systems without "I don't know" functions must hallucinate infinitely often (Bastounis et al., 2024). The paper argues these problems all point to the same missing capability.
AI.method: The paper uses synthesis analysis to connect three independent research findings, identifies their common thread (need for calibrated abstention), analyzes the structural problem in current evaluation systems (leaderboards rewarding zero abstention), and proposes concrete benchmark reforms.
AI.result: The analysis shows that all three reliability problems independently identify calibrated abstention as the missing capability, despite having different sources (capability gap, policy gap, and recursion-theoretic gap). The paper reveals that current benchmarking systems create perverse incentives by assigning zero reward to abstention, preventing development of calibrated abstention functions.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark reform is necessary but not sufficient to close the reliability gap. The paper proposes four specific evaluation changes: triple-scoring, abstention-rate reporting, capability-stratified evaluation, and mandatory calibration metrics to enable development of calibrated abstention capabilities in LLMs.

title: A Four-Stage Decomposition of Word-Problem Solving and Mechanistic Fragility in LLM Math Reasoning
summary: Large language models solve grade-school math word problems with high accuracy, yet a single irrelevant clause inserted into the problem can collapse it. We reconcile these observations with a mechanistic account. We show that the model's internal computation decomposes into a four-stage sequential pipeline, Schema Abstraction, Operation Planning, Operand Binding, and Computation, each stage producing a distinct intermediate representation in an identifiable band of layers. Using the same scaffold to diagnose distractor-induced failure, we localize the corruption to a single stage, Operation Planning, implemented by a set of attention heads whose causal role we validate bidirectionally. In short, we provide a mechanistic interpretation of math word problem reasoning in LLMs, and their failure when distracted.

AI.tldr: LLMs solve math word problems well but fail when irrelevant clauses are added; the paper identifies a four-stage reasoning pipeline and localizes the failure to the Operation Planning stage.
AI.motivation: Large language models achieve high accuracy on grade-school math word problems, but surprisingly collapse when a single irrelevant clause is inserted into the problem. This paradoxical observation needs mechanistic explanation to understand both successful reasoning and failure modes.
AI.method: The authors conduct mechanistic analysis showing LLMs decompose math reasoning into four sequential stages: Schema Abstraction, Operation Planning, Operand Binding, and Computation. They use diagnostic scaffolding to identify where distraction-induced failures occur, validating causal roles bidirectionally.
AI.result: The research reveals that distraction corrupts specifically the Operation Planning stage, implemented by specific attention heads. This provides a clear localization of failure, explaining why irrelevant clauses disrupt mathematical reasoning despite overall high performance.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a mechanistic interpretation of how LLMs reason about math word problems and why they fail when distracted, offering insights into the internal computational architecture and vulnerability points in complex reasoning tasks.

title: Accelerating Diffusion Sampling via Speculative Draft Trees
summary: Speculative sampling accelerates diffusion model generation by drafting inexpensive candidate states and correcting them under a coupling that preserves the target distribution exactly, reducing the number of expensive target evaluations. Existing diffusion samplers, notably those based on reflection maximal coupling, are topologically constrained: their lookahead drafts form a chain graph, a single linear sequence, which inherently limits the acceptance rate per target evaluation. We connect speculative sampling in diffusion models to relative entropy coding (REC). This perspective shows the lookahead need not be linear and motivates our central contribution, draft trees, which enrich the candidates considered per round and lower the target function evaluations. We further adopt greedy rejection sampling, an REC algorithm, as the draft-target coupling, improving acceptance while guaranteeing exact target samples. Experiments across diverse target and draft models demonstrate up to 8.3% acceleration over the reflection coupling baseline in practical settings.

AI.tldr: Speculative sampling for diffusion models is enhanced by replacing linear draft chains with tree-structured drafts using relative entropy coding principles, achieving up to 8.3% speedup over existing reflection coupling methods while maintaining exact target distribution.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion samplers use reflection maximal coupling with linear chain graphs for lookahead drafts, which inherently limits acceptance rates per target evaluation due to topological constraints. This restricts the efficiency of speculative sampling in accelerating diffusion model generation.
AI.method: The paper connects speculative sampling in diffusion models to relative entropy coding (REC), which reveals that lookahead drafts need not be linear. They propose draft trees that enrich candidate states per round and use greedy rejection sampling (an REC algorithm) as the draft-target coupling, which improves acceptance rates while guaranteeing exact target samples.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse target and draft models demonstrate up to 8.3% acceleration over the reflection coupling baseline in practical settings, showing that draft trees with greedy rejection sampling significantly reduce the number of expensive target evaluations required.
AI.conclusion: The REC perspective enables more flexible non-linear draft structures (draft trees) for speculative sampling in diffusion models, overcoming topological limitations of existing methods and achieving better acceleration while preserving exact target distribution through improved coupling algorithms.

title: Learning Heterogeneous Preferences
summary: Learning from human feedback has become a central paradigm for training modern AI systems, where models of human utility are used as reward models in policy learning. Existing methods typically assume a \emph{universal utility} function shared across a population and treat disagreement between annotators as stochastic variation. While suitable for objective tasks, this assumption breaks down in subjective domains where preferences vary systematically across individuals. We study the problem of subjective preference learning, in which observed choices arise from heterogeneous but internally consistent utility functions. Drawing upon rational choice theory, RCT \parencite{tversky1981framing}, we introduce \emph{individuated utility} functions conditioned on both the individual and their decision context, and propose a novel multi-stage architecture for estimating them from multi-modal data. We evaluate our framework on a newly collected dataset of more than $575{,}000$ pairwise aesthetic judgments from $2{,}398$ participants comparing automotive wheel designs. Our experiments show that individuated utility models substantially outperform universal utility models including foundation model baselines. Our results demonstrate that disagreement reflects meaningful preference heterogeneity rather than annotation noise. More broadly, our findings highlight the importance of collecting annotator attributes and learning individuated utility functions, enabling reward models that explicitly account for whose preferences they represent and faithfully capture human decision diversity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces individuated utility functions for subjective preference learning, moving beyond universal utility models to account for individual differences in preferences, and demonstrates superior performance on aesthetic judgment tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing human feedback learning methods assume universal utility functions shared across populations and treat disagreement between annotators as noise. This approach breaks down in subjective domains where preferences vary systematically across individuals, but current methods fail to capture this meaningful heterogeneity.
AI.method: The authors draw from rational choice theory to introduce individuated utility functions conditioned on both individuals and their decision contexts. They propose a novel multi-stage architecture for estimating these functions from multi-modal data, applied to a dataset of over 575,000 pairwise aesthetic judgments of automotive wheel designs from 2,398 participants.
AI.result: Individuated utility models substantially outperform universal utility models including foundation model baselines. The results demonstrate that disagreement reflects meaningful preference heterogeneity rather than annotation noise, showing that capturing individual differences improves performance.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of collecting annotator attributes and learning individuated utility functions, enabling reward models that explicitly account for whose preferences they represent and faithfully capture human decision diversity in subjective domains.

title: Composite-Gradient Learning for Shared Control Authority Between Deep Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Control
summary: Integrated deep reinforcement learning (DRL) and model predictive control (MPC) methods are increasingly used to control autonomous systems by combining their complementary capabilities. DRL learns control policies through interaction with the environment. MPC uses a system model to optimize control inputs while accounting for constraints. In DRL-MPC frameworks with shared control authority, both the DRL agent and the MPC controller each determine part of the control inputs. However, common learning formulations treat MPC as part of the environment and therefore do not explicitly account for MPC's contribution to control or its interaction with the DRL agent. This paper proposes a novel composite-gradient learning (CGL) method that integrates the MPC controller into the learning process by representing the DRL and MPC control inputs as a joint action and accounting for their interaction when updating the DRL agent during training. CGL is evaluated on two multi-class freeway traffic networks with different strengths of interaction between the DRL and MPC control inputs and it is compared with alternative methods that treat MPC as part of the environment or that only partially incorporate MPC into learning. The results show that CGL offers limited benefit under weak interaction, but learns higher-performing control policies than the alternative methods in a subset of training runs under strong interaction, although the average control-performance gains remain modest.

AI.tldr: A novel composite-gradient learning method integrates DRL and MPC controllers by representing their inputs as joint actions and accounting for their interaction during training, showing benefits under strong controller interactions.
AI.motivation: Current DRL-MPC frameworks with shared control authority treat MPC as part of the environment rather than explicitly accounting for MPC's contribution to control or its interaction with the DRL agent during learning, leading to suboptimal policy training.
AI.method: Proposes composite-gradient learning (CGL) method that integrates MPC controller into the learning process by representing DRL and MPC control inputs as a joint action and accounting for their interaction when updating the DRL agent during training.
AI.result: CGL offers limited benefit under weak interaction between DRL and MPC control inputs, but learns higher-performing control policies than alternative methods in a subset of training runs under strong interaction, though average control-performance gains remain modest.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly incorporating MPC's role and interactions with DRL in the learning process can improve control policy performance, particularly in scenarios with strong controller interactions, demonstrating the value of integrated learning approaches for autonomous systems.

title: SNOMED CT Concept Recommendation from Masked Clinical Context
summary: Standardizing clinical language to SNOMED CT supports interoperability, analytics, and reusable phenotyping, but concept recommendation remains difficult when relevant concepts are rare or absent from training data. We present a masked-concept recommendation benchmark using the SNOMED CT Entity Linking Challenge v1.2.1 data derived from MIMIC-IV-Note. The dataset contains 75,491 annotations across 272 discharge summaries, with 204 notes used for training and 68 for historical testing. For each unique note-concept pair, the target mention is masked from a local clinical context and the system ranks SNOMED CT concepts observed during training. We compare a popularity baseline, sparse TF-IDF concept prototypes, dense latent semantic analysis embeddings, sparse-dense fusion, retrieved-note evidence, and a retrieval-augmented hybrid. Sparse TF-IDF performs best, achieving Recall@1 of 14.81%, Recall@10 of 33.43%, MRR of 0.2114, and nDCG@10 of 0.2297. Retrieval augmentation does not improve this baseline, with Recall@10 of 31.99% and MRR of 0.1937. Performance is strongly affected by concept frequency: Recall@10 is 7.74% for concepts appearing in only one or two training notes versus 43.90% for concepts appearing in more than ten. In addition, 9.66% of test note-concept pairs contain concepts unseen during training. These findings show that local lexical context and terminology coverage are major determinants of recommendation quality in low-resource settings and provide a reproducible baseline for future ontology-grounded and biomedical-encoder retrieval systems.

AI.tldr: A benchmark for SNOMED CT concept recommendation using MIMIC-IV notes, showing sparse TF-IDF methods outperform dense embeddings and retrieval-augmented approaches, with performance heavily dependent on concept frequency and training data coverage.
AI.motivation: Standardizing clinical language to SNOMED CT supports interoperability and analytics, but concept recommendation is challenging when concepts are rare or absent from training data, necessitating better methods for low-resource settings.
AI.method: Created a masked-concept recommendation benchmark using SNOMED CT Entity Linking Challenge data from MIMIC-IV-Note with 75,491 annotations across 272 discharge summaries. Compared multiple approaches: popularity baseline, sparse TF-IDF concept prototypes, dense latent semantic analysis embeddings, sparse-dense fusion, retrieved-note evidence, and retrieval-augmented hybrid methods.
AI.result: Sparse TF-IDF performed best with Recall@1 of 14.81%, Recall@10 of 33.43%, MRR of 0.2114, and nDCG@10 of 0.2297. Retrieval augmentation did not improve performance. Performance varied dramatically by concept frequency: Recall@10 was 7.74% for concepts appearing in 1-2 training notes vs 43.90% for concepts in >10 training notes. 9.66% of test pairs contained concepts unseen during training.
AI.conclusion: Local lexical context and terminology coverage are major determinants of recommendation quality in low-resource settings. The benchmark provides a reproducible baseline for future ontology-grounded and biomedical-encoder retrieval systems, highlighting the need for better approaches for rare and unseen concepts.

title: REVERSAL-BENCH: A Reversibility Axis and Reset Oracle for Measuring the Reset-Free RL Cliff
summary: A central goal of autonomous reinforcement learning is continuous policy training without external resets. However, existing paradigms largely depend on underlying environmental reversibility, a property absent in real world manipulation, where events such as pushing objects off tables or spilling granular substances cannot be undone. We introduce REVERSAL-BENCH, a benchmark that controls reversibility via a continuous parameter $ρ\in [0, 1]$ and provides a reset oracle, a ground-truth verification mechanism to test state recoverability across eight manipulation settings in five physics engines. Evaluating a broad spectrum of policy architectures, including standard actor-critic algorithms, safe RL, and specialized reset-free frameworks, reveals a sharp reversibility cliff: reset-free agents are consistently absorbed into irrecoverable states as $ρ$ increases, whereas episodic agents maintain steady learning. We see this failure mode across autonomous reset-free baselines and constrained RL. Because reset-free agents lack external resets, any transition into an irrecoverable state results in permanent absorption, leaving the agent trapped where further learning halts. We show that this absorption phenomenon persists in full physics simulations under learned manipulation policies. By evaluating against geometrically identical reversible counterparts, we confirm that this breakdown is causally driven by irreversibility rather than obstacle complexity. We release the benchmark suite, a large multi-simulator dataset labeled with recoverability and a reset oracle. We also evaluate a safety shield that intervenes before irreversible failures occur, showing that while recoverability can be predicted accurately, active recovery primarily succeeds only when the agent can physically steer clear of the trap

AI.tldr: RL agents face absorption in irreversible states without external resets, creating a sharp performance cliff as environmental reversibility decreases, despite safety mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Real-world manipulation tasks often involve irreversible events (like pushing objects off tables or spilling substances) that cannot be undone, making autonomous reinforcement learning without external resets particularly challenging when current methods assume environmental reversibility.
AI.method: Created REVERSAL-BENCH with continuous reversibility parameter ρ ∈ [0,1] across eight manipulation settings in five physics engines; includes reset oracle for ground-truth state recoverability verification; evaluated diverse policy architectures (actor-critic, safe RL, reset-free frameworks) and safety shield interventions.
AI.result: Sharp reversibility cliff observed: reset-free agents consistently absorbed into irrecoverable states as ρ increases, while episodic agents maintain steady learning; absorption persists in full physics simulations; safety shields can predict recoverability but only succeed when agents can physically avoid traps.
AI.conclusion: Irreversibility causally drives breakdown in autonomous RL, not obstacle complexity; benchmark and labeled dataset released to study this fundamental limitation; current reset-free approaches fundamentally flawed for irreversible environments requiring new paradigms beyond safety mechanisms.

title: The Inference Engineering Pareto Atlas: Which Optimizations Dominate the Cost, Quality, and Latency Frontier?
summary: LLM inference optimizations report speedups on different models, GPUs, prompts, and quality metrics, making them hard to compare or combine. We build a cost, quality, and latency Pareto atlas to identify the best configurations for different deployment constraints. Since exhaustive testing is impractical, we measure 54 configurations of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct running on vLLM 0.12 across L4, A100, and H100 GPUs and use these anchors to calibrate a simulator. It reproduces measurements at anchored batch sizes, with cross campaign drift below 1.5 percent. A separate quality evaluation tests FP16, AWQ 4bit, FP8 weights, and FP8 KV cache on 200 GSM8K questions with five examples per prompt. Sparse attention is evaluated only in simulation. On the calibrated grid, 18 of 36 configurations reach the Pareto frontier. Combined methods reach it more often than individual methods, with 9 of 15 combinations versus 9 of 21 single methods. Quality testing changes the winners. AWQ 4bit reduces per token latency to 0.34 times baseline on L4 but loses 5.9 percent of strict GSM8K accuracy, narrowly missing the 95 percent quality floor within sampling uncertainty. Flexible answer extraction matches FP16 accuracy, suggesting the loss comes from formatting rather than arithmetic. FP8 weights retain 99.4 percent of baseline accuracy at 0.61 to 0.65 times baseline latency across all three GPUs and appear in three of four regime winners. A naive FP8 KV cache maintains normal throughput but answers none of the 200 questions correctly, showing why speed alone is insufficient. Under two prompt designs, n gram speculative decoding measures at 0.90 to 0.98 times baseline and adds no benefit on this stack. The best choice depends on the constraint and GPU: H100 wins for tight latency, while A100 wins for throughput and low cost at 0.106 dollars per million tokens.

AI.tldr: Researchers create a cost-quality-latency Pareto atlas to systematically evaluate LLM inference optimizations, using calibrated simulations and quality testing to identify best configurations for different deployment constraints across multiple GPUs.
AI.motivation: LLM inference optimizations report inconsistent speedups across different models, GPUs, prompts, and quality metrics, making them difficult to compare or combine effectively for deployment decisions.
AI.method: Build a cost-quality-latency Pareto atlas using: 1) 54 measured configurations of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on vLLM across L4, A100, H100 GPUs, 2) Calibrated simulator to extend measurements beyond tested configurations, 3) Quality evaluation testing FP16, AWQ 4bit, FP8 weights, and FP8 KV cache on 200 GSM8K questions, 4) Analysis of combined optimization methods.
AI.result: 18 of 36 configurations reach the Pareto frontier; combined methods perform better (9/15) than individual methods (9/21). AWQ 4bit reduces latency to 0.34x baseline but loses 5.9% accuracy; FP8 weights retain 99.4% accuracy at 0.61-0.65x latency. FP8 KV cache completely fails on quality despite normal throughput. Best choice depends on constraints: H100 wins for tight latency, A100 wins for throughput/cost ($0.106 per million tokens).
AI.conclusion: Systematic evaluation through Pareto analysis reveals that optimal LLM inference configurations depend on specific deployment constraints (latency, cost, quality), and that quality evaluation is critical since some optimizations significantly degrade accuracy despite speed improvements. Combined methods generally outperform single optimizations.

title: SAM-on-the-Curve: Sharpness-Aware Mode Connectivity for Robust Weight-Space Interpolation
summary: Deep neural networks that are independently trained to similar performance can be connected by low-loss parametric curves in weight space, a phenomenon known as Mode Connectivity (MC). This geometric property underpins practical techniques such as weight averaging, model ensembling, and model merging. We argue that low-loss connectivity is an incomplete geometric criterion: it controls loss only along a one-dimensional trajectory while leaving the surrounding weight-space neighborhood unconstrained, so the optimized curve may traverse sharp ridges that become fragile under distribution shift. We therefore reformulate mode connectivity as a neighborhood-robust path optimization problem, seeking a curve whose entire local neighborhood maintains low loss. We propose Sharp Mode Connectivity (SMC), which applies a first-order sharpness-aware approximation to the resulting minimax functional, enforcing flatness along the entire curve rather than only on it. We derive a practical optimization algorithm for connectivity paths under this sharpness-aware objective. Under severe blur corruptions from CIFAR-10-C, SMC achieves up to 6.09\% absolute accuracy improvement over standard MC. Remarkably, SMC produces negative loss barriers, meaning that models obtained at interior points of the optimized path can outperform the average endpoint loss. These results, validated across ResNet-18, VGG16-BN, and ViT-Tiny on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100, establish path-wise flatness as a practical principle for robust weight-space interpolation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Sharp Mode Connectivity (SMC), a novel method for finding flat, robust paths between independently trained neural network weights by optimizing for low loss across entire neighborhoods around the path, rather than just on the path itself, leading to improved robustness under distribution shift.
AI.motivation: Standard Mode Connectivity only ensures low loss along a one-dimensional path between models, but the path may traverse sharp loss regions that become fragile under distribution shift. This incomplete geometric criterion leaves surrounding weight-space neighborhoods unconstrained, making current connectivity methods vulnerable to real-world corruptions.
AI.method: Proposes Sharp Mode Connectivity (SMC) which reformulates mode connectivity as a neighborhood-robust path optimization problem. It applies a first-order sharpness-aware approximation to enforce flatness along the entire curve rather than only on it. The paper derives a practical optimization algorithm for connectivity paths under this sharpness-aware objective.
AI.result: Under severe blur corruptions from CIFAR-10-C, SMC achieves up to 6.09% absolute accuracy improvement over standard MC. Remarkably, SMC produces negative loss barriers, meaning models obtained at interior points of the optimized path can outperform the average endpoint loss. Results are validated across ResNet-18, VGG16-BN, and ViT-Tiny on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes path-wise flatness as a practical principle for robust weight-space interpolation. SMC demonstrates that optimizing for neighborhood robustness rather than just path connectivity leads to more robust connections between independently trained neural network models, with significant performance improvements under distribution shift.

title: Do Frontier Models Seek Safety Evidence Before Acting?
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures, with supplementary appendices. Code and data available at the repository linked in the paper
summary: Frontier models are often evaluated on how they respond to safety information once it is already in context. We study an earlier decision point: whether models choose to acquire safety-relevant evidence before acting. We introduce SAFE, a controlled benchmark in which models make deployment decisions with optional evidence that varies in retrieval cost, probability, severity, and presentation. Across GPT-5.5, o3, Claude Opus 4.8, and Claude Sonnet 4.6, we find distinct evidence-acquisition policies: Opus inspects nearly by default, o3 is the most skip-heavy and threshold-sensitive, and GPT-5.5 and Sonnet occupy intermediate regimes. Inspection increases strongly with severity and decreases with retrieval cost, whereas probability has much weaker behavioral influence: increasing the stated likelihood of a problem from 10% to 70% changes inspection by at most 21 percentage points. Despite these differences, Stage 1 rationales are dominated by expected-value reasoning across models. A cost-obligation decomposition further shows that avoidance is driven primarily by retrieval friction and explicit threats to the deployment payoff rather than by the remediation duties created by knowing. Counterfactual interventions reveal a further mismatch between behavior and explanation: evidence framing can strongly change decisions near the inspection boundary while going largely unmentioned, whereas probability is frequently cited despite having little causal influence. These results suggest that deployment-time safety depends not only on how models respond to known risks, but also on whether they acquire the evidence needed to know that acting is safe.

AI.tldr: Models show systematic biases in evidence acquisition for safety decisions, with inspection behavior strongly influenced by retrieval costs and severity but weakly by probability estimates, revealing misalignment between stated rationales and actual behavior.
AI.motivation: Current safety evaluations focus on how models respond to safety information already in context, but there's limited understanding of whether models proactively seek safety-relevant evidence before making deployment decisions - an earlier, crucial decision point for preventing unsafe actions.
AI.method: Developed SAFE benchmark where models make deployment decisions with optional evidence that varies across four dimensions: retrieval cost, probability, severity, and presentation. Tested frontier models (GPT-5.5, o3, Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Sonnet 4.6) and analyzed their evidence-acquisition policies, rationales, and behavioral patterns through cost-obligation decomposition and counterfactual interventions.
AI.result: Models show distinct evidence-acquisition policies: Opus inspects nearly by default, o3 is most skip-heavy and threshold-sensitive, while GPT-5.5 and Sonnet occupy intermediate positions. Inspection increases strongly with severity and decreases with retrieval cost, but probability has weak influence (10-70% change affects inspection ≤21pp). Rationales dominated by expected-value reasoning. Avoidance driven primarily by retrieval friction and explicit payoff threats rather than remediation duties. Counterfactual interventions reveal mismatch: evidence framing strongly changes decisions but goes unmentioned, while probability is frequently cited despite minimal causal influence.
AI.conclusion: Deployment-time safety depends not just on how models respond to known risks, but crucially on whether they acquire evidence needed to determine if acting is safe. Models show systematic biases in evidence-seeking behavior, with rationales often misaligned with actual decision drivers, suggesting need for better safety evaluations that capture these pre-action evidence acquisition patterns.

title: Modular Deep Learning Mechanisms for Auditable Next-Day Wildfire Spread Prediction
summary: Next-day wildfire prediction requires models whose forecasts can be evaluated alongside the assumptions and historical evidence used in their computation. Although deep learning can learn spatial patterns from remote-sensing data, predictive performance alone does not establish physical fidelity or operational trustworthiness. This study investigates three modular augmentations for next-day active-fire prediction: wind- and slope-conditioned attention biases, physics-feature retrieval-augmented output correction, and fire conditioned dual-stream gating. The attention biases expose prescribed directional preferences, while the retrieval module selects historical tiles using a nine-dimensional environmental and fire-state descriptor and applies a learned correction to a frozen model's logits. The modules are evaluated across five backbones on the Next Day Wildfire Spread benchmark, using staged ablations, directional audits, retrieval perturbations, calibration measures, and computational comparisons. The three-seed mean F1 score and area under the precision--recall curve (AUC-PR) of a SwinUNETR model with all three augmentations are 0.4216 and 0.3673. Then, a mixed ensemble (two augmented architectures and one non-augmented architecture) model achieves 0.4292 and 0.3790. Benefits vary across architectures, and retrieval-related improvements in AUC-PR do not consistently translate into higher F1. The constructed wind bias aligns closely with input wind, but its alignment with observed next-day fire displacement is much weaker, distinguishing prior inspectability from predictive physical fidelity. The study contributes a framework for exposing and evaluating selected domain-informed components within wildfire prediction models. Together, the results presented show that predictive performance, operational trustworthiness, and computational practicality need not be competing objectives.

AI.tldr: Modular augmentations for next-day wildfire prediction improve predictive performance while maintaining physical interpretability and operational trustworthiness through wind/slope attention biases, physics-feature retrieval, and dual-stream gating.
AI.motivation: Current deep learning models for wildfire prediction lack physical fidelity and operational trustworthiness despite good predictive performance. There's a need for models whose forecasts can be evaluated alongside assumptions and historical evidence used in their computation.
AI.method: Three modular augmentations: 1) wind- and slope-conditioned attention biases for directional preferences, 2) physics-feature retrieval-augmented output correction using 9D environmental/fire-state descriptors, and 3) fire-conditioned dual-stream gating. Evaluated across five backbones on Next Day Wildfire Spread benchmark with staged ablations, directional audits, retrieval perturbations, calibration measures, and computational comparisons.
AI.result: SwinUNETR model with all three augmentations achieved 0.4216 mean F1 and 0.3673 AUC-PR. A mixed ensemble (2 augmented + 1 non-augmented architectures) achieved 0.4292 F1 and 0.3790 AUC-PR. Benefits varied across architectures. Constructed wind bias aligned closely with input wind but weakly with observed fire displacement, showing distinction between inspectability and predictive physical fidelity.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a framework for exposing and evaluating domain-informed components in wildfire prediction models. Predictive performance, operational trustworthiness, and computational practicality can be achieved together through modular, interpretable augmentations that maintain physical fidelity while improving accuracy.

title: Principled Koopman Representations with Kalman Inference for Efficient Time-Series Prediction
summary: The Koopman operator has been widely used for time-series prediction in dynamical systems. However, prior work that learns latent ``Koopman spaces'' using neural networks often did not construct a valid Koopman space for forecasting, as these representations may be mathematically inconsistent with the operator-theoretic formulation and fail to capture the intrinsic low-rank structure of system dynamics. To address this issue, we introduce K$^2$SVD, a method that explicitly learns the leading singular functions of the Koopman operator by optimizing a Hilbert-Schmidt objective. This yields a well-defined low-rank approximation of the Koopman operator with an interpretable linear combination, featuring a compact latent space with less than $10\%$ of the dimensions used in previous work. In the learned Koopman space, K$^2$SVD further captures temporal evolution with a linear Gaussian state-space model and performs inference via Kalman filtering, mitigating noise accumulation during multi-step prediction. Empirical results show that K$^2$SVD outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple datasets, with significantly faster prediction speeds and lower computational cost than previous efficiency-focused models. This highlights the benefits of principled low-rank Koopman representations and opens up broader potential for applications.

AI.tldr: K²SVD is a novel method that learns low-rank Koopman operator approximations by optimizing a Hilbert-Schmidt objective, creating interpretable linear representations for efficient and accurate time-series prediction.
AI.motivation: Previous neural network approaches for learning Koopman representations often fail to construct mathematically valid Koopman spaces for forecasting, lacking consistency with operator-theoretic formulations and missing the intrinsic low-rank structure of system dynamics.
AI.method: K²SVD explicitly learns the leading singular functions of the Koopman operator by optimizing a Hilbert-Schmidt objective, creating a well-defined low-rank approximation with interpretable linear combination. It then uses a linear Gaussian state-space model with Kalman filtering for temporal evolution and noise mitigation during multi-step prediction.
AI.result: The method achieves significantly more compact latent spaces (less than 10% of previous dimensions), outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple datasets, with faster prediction speeds and lower computational costs than previous efficiency-focused models.
AI.conclusion: K²SVD demonstrates the benefits of principled low-rank Koopman representations, highlighting their potential for broader applications through improved mathematical consistency, interpretability, and computational efficiency.

title: OBC-Prune: Outcome-Based Calibration for Large Reasoning Model Pruning
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) generate long chain-of-thought traces before answering, creating significant inference overhead. Pruning can reduce this cost, but its effectiveness depends on the calibration data used to estimate parameter importance. Recent work calibrates on the model's own rollouts instead of generic dataset, but treats all reasoning tokens uniformly, regardless of whether they contribute to successful reasoning. As a result, pruning protects weights by statistical salience rather than by their contribution to correct reasoning, so weights behind erroneous computation survive as readily as those behind correct computation. These erroneous patterns then get carried into the pruned model, degrading reasoning quality, producing both lower accuracy and longer reasoning traces. We propose Outcome-Based Calibration for Large Reasoning Model Pruning (OBC-Prune) to close this gap. OBC first constructs difficulty-matched pairs of correct and incorrect rollouts from problems the model answers inconsistently. It then estimates the causal importance of each reasoning sentence through intervention-based analysis, quantifying how removing its influence affects subsequent predictions. These causal importance scores are converted into per-token weights that rescale the calibration activations used by one-shot pruning methods (SparseGPT, Wanda, ALPS), without modifying the underlying pruning algorithms. Experiments on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, and 14B models at 40\% and 50\% sparsity demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art calibration baselines across most model sizes and sparsity levels on MATH500, LiveCodeBench, and AIME 2025. These results indicate that preserving causally important reasoning circuits is a substantially more effective pruning objective than uniformly preserving observed activations.

AI.tldr: OBC-Prune is a novel calibration method for pruning large reasoning models that uses causal intervention analysis to weight reasoning tokens by their contribution to correct answers, improving accuracy over uniform calibration methods.
AI.motivation: Current pruning methods for large reasoning models use uniform calibration on model rollouts, treating all reasoning tokens equally regardless of whether they contribute to correct reasoning. This leads to protecting weights behind erroneous computations, degrading reasoning quality and producing lower accuracy with longer reasoning traces.
AI.method: OBC-Prune first constructs difficulty-matched pairs of correct and incorrect rollouts from problems the model answers inconsistently. It then estimates causal importance of each reasoning sentence through intervention-based analysis, quantifying how removing its influence affects subsequent predictions. These scores are converted into per-token weights that rescale calibration activations used by one-shot pruning methods like SparseGPT, Wanda, and ALPS, without modifying the underlying pruning algorithms.
AI.result: Experiments on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, and 14B models at 40% and 50% sparsity show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art calibration baselines across most model sizes and sparsity levels on MATH500, LiveCodeBench, and AIME 2025 benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Preserving causally important reasoning circuits is a substantially more effective pruning objective than uniformly preserving observed activations, demonstrating the value of outcome-based calibration for large reasoning model pruning.

title: The Free Inference Dimension: Complexity Measure for Zero-Collision Navigation under Hypothesis Mixtures
summary:
Solomonoff induction frames prediction as a mixture over computable hypotheses, typically leading to identification of the true environment. In a finite meta-reinforcement learning setting with nested constraint families, in our previous work, we observe a different regime: a value-mixture (VM) agent achieves near-optimal, zero-collision navigation without identifying the true environment, a phenomenon we call Free Inference. This regime persists up to a sharp density threshold, beyond which performance degrades and posterior-mode selection (PMS) becomes preferable.
  We formalize this behavior via the Free Inference dimension dFI(S,N), a combinatorial measure of the environmental complexity a VM agent can handle while preserving trajectory coherence. We prove dFI is strictly smaller than the VC-dimension and relates to the Natarajan dimension up to a path-length factor, capturing the cost of non-decomposable loss. A PAC-style relaxation yields generalization bounds driven by dFI^(epsilon,delta). We also define a complementary PMS identification dimension and show that a hybrid strategy---averaging until the first collision, then switching to selection---is optimal, with links to Littlestone-type dimensions supported by grid-world experiments.

AI.tldr: VM agents achieve optimal performance without identifying true environments up to a density threshold, formalized via Free Inference dimension dFI, with hybrid VM/PMS strategies proven optimal.
AI.motivation: Understanding why and when value-mixture (VM) agents in meta-RL can achieve near-optimal performance without environment identification (Free Inference), contrary to Solomonoff induction where prediction typically requires identifying the true environment.
AI.method: Introduce Free Inference dimension dFI(S,N) as combinatorial measure of environmental complexity VM agents can handle while preserving trajectory coherence. Prove relations to VC/Natarajan dimensions. Define complementary PMS identification dimension. Prove optimality of hybrid strategy (VM averaging until first collision, then switching to PMS selection). Validate with grid-world experiments.
AI.result: dFI is strictly smaller than VC-dimension and relates to Natarajan dimension with path-length factor. PAC-style relaxation yields generalization bounds via dFI^(epsilon,delta). Hybrid VM/PMS strategy is optimal, with connections to Littlestone-type dimensions supported experimentally.
AI.conclusion: Free Inference represents a distinct regime from Solomonoff induction where optimal behavior doesn't require environment identification. The dFI dimension formalizes this capacity, and hybrid strategies leveraging both VM and PMS approaches are optimal for finite meta-RL with nested constraint families.

title: Collaborative Memory for Multi-Agent VLM Systems
summary: Vision-language model (VLM) agents combine specialized perception, tools, and reasoning to address complex visual tasks. In multi-agent settings, different agents inspect different image regions, video frames, or visual representations, so collaboration extends beyond distributed reasoning to distributed perception. This makes shared visual context a central problem in VLM agent collaboration. In this paper, we frame memory hierarchy, cross-agent sharing, and consistency mechanisms around the need to reconcile interpretations and update dependent reasoning. Effective collaboration requires agents to build on contributions from other agents, recover missing visual context, and reconcile differing interpretations as new evidence emerges. Shared visual memory preserves not only images or textual summaries but also the dependencies among observations, agent interpretations, and subsequent reasoning. Together, these design considerations shape how information flows and evolves across VLM agents. The proposed framework provides a foundation for building reliable and resource-efficient agent teams.

AI.tldr: A framework for VLM agent collaboration addressing distributed perception and shared visual context through memory hierarchy, cross-agent sharing, and consistency mechanisms.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent VLM settings, different agents inspect different visual regions/frames/representations, creating challenges for distributed perception beyond just distributed reasoning. Shared visual context becomes a central problem when agents need to build on each other's contributions and reconcile differing interpretations.
AI.method: Proposes a framework with memory hierarchy, cross-agent sharing mechanisms, and consistency mechanisms to reconcile interpretations and update dependent reasoning. Shared visual memory preserves not only images/textual summaries but also dependencies among observations, agent interpretations, and subsequent reasoning.
AI.result: The framework addresses how information flows and evolves across VLM agents, enabling effective collaboration where agents can build on each other's contributions, recover missing visual context, and reconcile differing interpretations as new evidence emerges.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a foundation for building reliable and resource-efficient agent teams by solving the shared visual context problem in VLM agent collaboration through systematic design of memory and consistency mechanisms.

title: NObSP: Functional Decomposition of Neural Networks via Oblique Subspace Projections
comment: 24 pages, including 6 pages of supplementary material. Code available at https://github.com/santialferez/nobsp_lib
summary: Understanding how deep neural networks make decisions remains a fundamental challenge. We present NObSP (Nonlinear Oblique Subspace Projections), a framework that decomposes predictions into explicit per feature contribution functions and an interaction residual. NObSP exploits the linear final layer of a trained network and uses oblique projections in sample space to reduce double counting when learned feature subspaces overlap, thereby supporting both local explanations and global functional analysis. We establish connections to functional ANOVA and the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem and derive an efficient partial regression algorithm for out of sample evaluation. For convolutional networks, NObSP-CAM produces class activation maps without backward passes after a one time calibration. Experiments on tabular and vision benchmarks show faithfulness comparable to established attribution methods. On a synthetic benchmark with known component functions, NObSP obtains a Function Reproduction Score of 0.989, compared with 0.966 for KernelSHAP and 0.922 for Integrated Gradients. On TinyImageNet, contribution vector embeddings improve mean nearest neighbor class purity from 0.654 for raw activations to 0.713 and reduce mean neighbor distance by more than half. These results indicate that NObSP complements scalar attribution methods by recovering functional contribution profiles with separable positive and negative evidence.

AI.tldr: NObSP is a framework that decomposes neural network predictions into per-feature contribution functions and interaction residuals using oblique subspace projections, enabling both local explanations and global functional analysis without backward passes for convolutional networks.
AI.motivation: Understanding how deep neural networks make decisions remains a fundamental challenge. Existing methods often provide scalar attributions but lack explicit functional decomposition of predictions into per-feature contributions and interaction terms.
AI.method: NObSP exploits the linear final layer of trained networks and uses oblique projections in sample space to reduce double counting when learned feature subspaces overlap. It establishes connections to functional ANOVA and the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, and derives an efficient partial regression algorithm for out-of-sample evaluation. For CNNs, NObSP-CAM produces class activation maps without backward passes after one-time calibration.
AI.result: On synthetic benchmarks with known component functions, NObSP achieves Function Reproduction Score of 0.989 vs. 0.966 for KernelSHAP and 0.922 for Integrated Gradients. On TinyImageNet, contribution vector embeddings improve mean nearest neighbor class purity from 0.654 to 0.713 and reduce mean neighbor distance by more than half. Faithfulness comparable to established attribution methods on tabular and vision benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: NObSP complements scalar attribution methods by recovering functional contribution profiles with separable positive and negative evidence, enabling better understanding of neural network decisions through explicit per-feature contribution functions and interaction residuals.

title: Measuring AI Leadership: Development and Validation of a Multidimensional Measure for AI-Native Organizations
summary: AI is changing what leaders must judge, explain, learn, and coordinate, yet existing measures do not capture these behaviors at the level needed to study leadership in AI-enabled work. We develop the AI Leadership Battery, which organizes 36 behaviorally specific subdimensions into 11 theory-specified content families. Following established scale-development procedures, the research used deductive item generation; content validation of definitional correspondence and definitional distinctiveness; exploratory factor analysis and item reduction; confirmatory factor analysis in independent samples; and tests of internal consistency reliability, convergent validity, discriminant validity, and criterion-related and incremental validity. Across the development and validation studies, the analyses provided evidence for the Battery's content, multidimensional structure, reliability, and distinction from selected orbiting constructs. The Battery also contributed additional information beyond orbiting constructs across organizational growth, decision speed, customer/stakeholder response capability, AI-enabled team performance, AI-enabled work experience, AI security and risk management, and AI adoption and integration. The resulting measure provides researchers with a behavioral framework for examining how leaders in AI-enabled work regulate judgment, learning, adaptation, transparency, and accountability.

AI.tldr: Researchers developed the AI Leadership Battery, a comprehensive measurement tool with 36 subdimensions across 11 content areas to assess leadership behaviors in AI-enabled work environments.
AI.motivation: Existing leadership measures don't capture the specific behaviors needed for AI-enabled work, where leaders must judge, explain, learn, and coordinate differently due to AI integration.
AI.method: Used established scale-development procedures including deductive item generation, content validation (definitional correspondence and distinctiveness), exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis across multiple samples, and extensive psychometric testing for reliability and validity.
AI.result: The AI Leadership Battery demonstrated strong content validity, multidimensional structure, reliability, and distinction from related constructs. It showed incremental predictive validity across multiple organizational outcomes including growth, decision speed, team performance, AI security, and adoption.
AI.conclusion: The AI Leadership Battery provides researchers with a behavioral framework to examine how leaders regulate judgment, learning, adaptation, transparency, and accountability in AI-enabled work environments.

title: Procedural Pretraining for Molecular Property Prediction
summary: Molecular property prediction is often limited by the small size of labeled downstream datasets, motivating pretraining on large corpora of unlabeled molecules. In this work, we ask whether useful inductive biases can instead be learned from abstract, procedurally generated data before a model sees any molecular data. We introduce a three-stage training pipeline consisting of procedural pretraining, molecular pretraining on SMILES, and downstream fine-tuning, and evaluate several procedural tasks spanning sequence structure, cellular automata, and graph reasoning. We find that procedural pretraining can improve molecular property prediction even after subsequent molecular pretraining: on Lipophilicity, \textsc{Reverse} reduces test error by 4.8\%. For context, the magnitude of this improvement is roughly 90\% of the performance difference between our 250K-molecule baseline and the publicly released MoLFormer checkpoint pretrained on approximately 100M molecules. Our analysis shows that the benefit is strongest under downstream data scarcity, depends on the structure of the procedural data rather than only surface-level statistics, and does not increase monotonically with additional procedural training. Instead, transfer typically peaks at an intermediate procedural budget and deteriorates as the model approaches convergence on the procedural task. We further find that, for several tasks, much of the transferable information is localized in the attention layers, while feed-forward layers can contribute to over-specialization. These results show that procedural data can provide transferable structure for molecular learning and offer a complementary route to improving performance when labeled molecular data are limited.

AI.tldr: Procedural pretraining on abstract generated data improves molecular property prediction, especially under data scarcity, with benefits peaking at intermediate training levels.
AI.motivation: Molecular property prediction is limited by small labeled datasets. The paper explores whether inductive biases can be learned from abstract procedural data before seeing any molecular data, as an alternative to pretraining on large unlabeled molecule corpora.
AI.method: Three-stage training: (1) procedural pretraining on abstract tasks (sequence structure, cellular automata, graph reasoning), (2) molecular pretraining on SMILES representations, and (3) downstream fine-tuning on molecular property prediction tasks.
AI.result: Procedural pretraining improves molecular prediction (4.8% error reduction on Lipophilicity). Benefits are strongest with scarce downstream data, depend on procedural data structure (not just surface statistics), peak at intermediate training budgets, and are localized in attention layers (feed-forward layers cause over-specialization).
AI.conclusion: Procedural data provides transferable structure for molecular learning and offers a complementary approach to improve performance when labeled molecular data are limited.

title: Memory Has Geometry: Non-Uniform Geometric Memory for Long-Horizon Personalized AI
comment: Accepted to the IEEE ICDM 2026 (BlueSky). 6 pages, 2 figures, and 2 tables
summary: Long-term memory is becoming a core substrate for personalized AI, yet most systems still represent personalization as discrete records in a largely static latent space, accessed under one global similarity notion. For data mining, this creates a mismatch: the evidence is a temporal event stream, while the dominant abstraction is a searchable record set. We argue that long-horizon personalization should instead model memory as a user-specific dynamical state space with locally heterogeneous geometry. Geometry here is a computational language, not a literal claim about cognition: it captures stable versus volatile regions, variable-rate drift, heterogeneous neighborhoods, and uncertainty about current user state. Profiles and isolated events remain useful as points, but interaction, feedback, and elapsed time induce trajectories. Memory access then becomes trajectory-conditioned reconstruction of the relevant user state, not only nearest-neighbor lookup.

AI.tldr: The paper argues for rethinking long-term memory in AI personalization from static record sets to dynamic state spaces with heterogeneous geometry to better model temporal user behavior.
