AI.motivation: Current AI personalization systems represent memory as discrete records in static latent spaces with global similarity metrics, which creates a mismatch with the temporal nature of user event streams and limits effective long-horizon personalization.
AI.method: Proposes modeling memory as user-specific dynamical state spaces with locally heterogeneous geometry that captures stability, volatility, variable-rate drift, heterogeneous neighborhoods, and uncertainty about user states. Memory access shifts from nearest-neighbor lookup to trajectory-conditioned reconstruction.
AI.result: The paper introduces a conceptual framework that transforms memory from static record sets to dynamic state spaces with geometric properties, enabling better modeling of temporal user behavior and interaction patterns.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon personalization requires fundamentally rethinking memory as dynamical state spaces with geometric properties rather than static record sets, enabling trajectory-based memory access that better aligns with how users evolve over time through interactions and feedback.

title: Adaptive hybrid coupling with operator inference, the overlapping Schwarz alternating method and reinforcement learning
summary: Hybrid domain decomposition methods provide a flexible framework for coupling full order models (FOMs) and reduced order models (ROMs), but typically assume the model assigned to each subdomain is fixed throughout a simulation. This is limiting for transient problems in which localized features propagate through the domain and the regions requiring high-fidelity resolution change over time. We introduce a reinforcement learning (RL)-based approach for online adaptation of FOM-ROM models coupled via the overlapping Schwarz alternating method (O-SAM), an iterative domain decomposition method that solves subdomain-local problems while exchanging solution information through transmission boundary conditions on overlapping interfaces. Deep Q-networks (DQNs) are trained offline to select among subdomain-local FOMs and pre-trained Operator Inference (OpInf) ROMs using a reward balancing accuracy, cost, and model-switching frequency. Once trained, the policies are deployed predictively on problem instances not seen during training, without requiring a reference FOM solution. We demonstrate the approach on two examples: a 1D advection-diffusion problem with a moving front, and a 3D linear elastic wave propagation problem implemented in the Norma.jl solid mechanics code. For the advection-diffusion benchmark, the learned policy dynamically allocates high-fidelity resolution as the front propagates and outperforms static FOM/ROM assignments; letting the agent also adapt the domain decomposition provides no further benefit. For the elastic wave benchmark, learned policies for two and three subdomain decompositions track the propagating wave by assigning FOMs to subdomains containing the wave and ROMs elsewhere, as expected. Our results demonstrate the potential of RL to enable predictive online adaptation of model fidelity within Schwarz-based hybrid simulations.

AI.tldr: A reinforcement learning approach enables dynamic allocation of full-order and reduced-order models within overlapping Schwarz domain decomposition for transient problems with moving localized features.
AI.motivation: Traditional hybrid domain decomposition methods use fixed model assignments per subdomain, which is limiting for transient problems where localized features propagate and regions requiring high-fidelity resolution change over time.
AI.method: Use deep Q-networks trained offline to select between subdomain-local full-order models and pre-trained Operator Inference reduced-order models within overlapping Schwarz alternating method. The reward function balances accuracy, computational cost, and model-switching frequency.
AI.result: For 1D advection-diffusion with moving front, learned policy dynamically allocates high-fidelity resolution as front propagates, outperforming static assignments. For 3D linear elastic wave propagation, policies successfully track propagating wave by assigning FOMs to wave-containing subdomains and ROMs elsewhere.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning enables predictive online adaptation of model fidelity within Schwarz-based hybrid simulations, demonstrating potential for efficient resolution of transient problems with propagating localized features.

title: When to Call an LLM: A Confidence-Gated Hybrid for Cost-Effective Emotion Recognition in Conversational AI
summary: Emotion recognition in conversation (ERC) is a production capability behind agent-assist prompts, escalation routing, and post-call analytics in contact-center-as-a-service (CCaaS) platforms, where cost and latency constraints matter as much as accuracy. We report a systems-level comparison of three deployment options for dialogue-contextual ERC: a low-cost stacked ensemble (sentence embeddings, windowed context, RandomForest/XGBoost/logistic-regression stacking), off-the-shelf LLM prompting (GPT-4o-mini; zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought), and a confidence-gated hybrid that escalates only the ensemble's least-confident predictions to the LLM - modeled on IVA-to-human-agent escalation policies used in production contact centers. On IEMOCAP, the ensemble significantly outperforms every LLM configuration (0.595 vs. 0.460-0.536 weighted F1, p < 0.0001) at a fraction of the cost and sub-10ms latency; on MELD and CMU-MOSI the ranking reverses, showing neither pure system is a safe default. The confidence-gated hybrid resolves this by Pareto-dominating both pure systems on all three datasets (0.620, 0.643, 0.824 weighted F1) while routing the majority of traffic through the near-zero-cost ensemble, translating to roughly $10-85 per million utterances versus $99-170 for an LLM-only pipeline. The escalation policy is not an opaque cost/accuracy dial: escalated turns disproportionately follow an emotion or sentiment shift, giving operators an interpretable, auditable routing signal, and the ensemble's confidence is well-calibrated and safely under- rather than over-confident. The pattern holds across three datasets and two LLM providers. Confidence-gated cascading is established in general ML systems; our contribution is showing it transfers cleanly to dialogue-contextual ERC, yielding a concrete deployment recipe for CCaaS and conversational-AI platforms deciding how to allocate LLM spend.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a confidence-gated hybrid system for emotion recognition in conversation that combines a low-cost ensemble model with expensive LLMs, only escalating uncertain predictions to LLMs. This achieves better performance than either approach alone while significantly reducing costs.
AI.motivation: Emotion recognition in conversation is crucial for contact-center platforms, but deployment faces challenges balancing accuracy with cost and latency constraints. Existing options either use low-cost models with limited accuracy or expensive LLMs with higher costs, creating a need for a hybrid solution.
AI.method: Three deployment options are compared: 1) A low-cost stacked ensemble using sentence embeddings, windowed context, and RandomForest/XGBoost/logistic-regression stacking; 2) Off-the-shelf LLM prompting with GPT-4o-mini; 3) A confidence-gated hybrid that escalates only the ensemble's least-confident predictions to the LLM, inspired by human-agent escalation policies in contact centers.
AI.result: On IEMOCAP, the ensemble outperforms all LLM configurations (0.595 vs. 0.460-0.536 weighted F1). On MELD and CMU-MOSI, LLMs perform better. The confidence-gated hybrid Pareto-dominates both pure systems on all three datasets (0.620, 0.643, 0.824 weighted F1) while routing most traffic through the low-cost ensemble, reducing costs to $10-85 per million utterances versus $99-170 for LLM-only.
AI.conclusion: Confidence-gated cascading transfers effectively to dialogue-contextual emotion recognition, providing a practical deployment strategy for contact-center platforms. The approach offers interpretable routing signals, well-calibrated confidence estimates, and resolves the cost-accuracy tradeoff by intelligently allocating LLM resources only when needed.

title: Hybrid coupling with numerics-informed neural networks and the overlapping Schwarz alternating method
summary: We develop a hybrid modeling framework for coupling pre-trained numerics-informed neural networks (NINNs) with classical full order models (FOMs) using the overlapping Schwarz alternating method. We consider the two-dimensional advection-diffusion equation in the advection-dominated, Peclet-number 10^6 regime. We first demonstrate that, unlike the corresponding physics-informed neural network (PINN), a monolithic NINN can be accurately trained on our model problem without domain decomposition. We then employ overlapping multiplicative Schwarz as a deployment mechanism for coupling a pre-trained, subdomain-local NINN with a neighboring FOM, with the NINN weights held fixed throughout the Schwarz iteration. We consider two training approaches for the subdomain-local NINNs: a top-down approach, in which boundary data are obtained from a coupled Schwarz solve on the full domain with a FOM on each subdomain (FOM-FOM Schwarz), and a bottom-up approach, in which boundary traces are generated synthetically on the NINN subdomain without requiring any full-domain solves. The resulting hybrid NINN-FOM solutions agree closely with the corresponding FOM-FOM Schwarz solutions, with the top-down and bottom-up training approaches yielding comparable accuracy.

AI.tldr: Hybrid framework couples pre-trained numerics-informed neural networks (NINNs) with classical full order models (FOMs) using overlapping Schwarz alternating method for advection-diffusion problems.
AI.motivation: To develop a hybrid modeling approach that combines the efficiency of neural networks with the reliability of classical numerical methods for solving advection-dominated PDEs at high Peclet numbers (10^6), addressing limitations of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in such regimes.
AI.method: Uses overlapping multiplicative Schwarz method to couple pre-trained NINNs with FOMs. Two training approaches: top-down (using boundary data from coupled FOM-FOM Schwarz solves) and bottom-up (synthetically generating boundary traces without full-domain solves). NINN weights remain fixed during Schwarz iteration.
AI.result: Monolithic NINNs can be accurately trained on advection-dominated problems without domain decomposition (unlike PINNs). Hybrid NINN-FOM solutions closely match FOM-FOM Schwarz solutions. Both top-down and bottom-up training approaches yield comparable accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid NINN-FOM framework successfully combines neural network efficiency with classical method reliability for advection-dominated PDEs, offering two viable training approaches with similar accuracy.

title: Contiguity, Not Importance: Budgeted Repair of Stale KV Caches After Document Edits
summary: KV-cache reuse can reduce inference cost in retrieval-augmented generation and agentic systems, but cached contexts may become stale when retrieved knowledge, working memory, or user state is edited. Under causal self-attention, even a local edit can affect downstream KV states. A full re-prefill reliably restores consistency but is costly, whereas refreshing only the edited span can leave downstream dependencies stale. We formulate in-place repair as budgeted recomputation and compare training-free position-selection policies on a factual RAG benchmark with matched direct and derived edits. Across three model families, all policies repair direct cases, but derived cases clearly separate them. At the primary budget, a contiguous edit-local window recovers at least 0.94 of the post-edit answer margin and substantially outperforms attention-based, KV-deviation, and structural selectors. Mechanistic analysis shows that position sets effective under clean-state transplantation can fail under actual recomputation because scattered positions inherit surrounding staleness. The edit-local advantage also depends on adjacency and largely disappears when the answer-bearing text moves downstream. Because answer-relevant edits almost always corrupt model behavior, failure severity is difficult to predict, and repair is 13-21 times faster than full re-prefill, our results support unconditional edit-local repair when the dependent text remains adjacent to the edit.

AI.tldr: KV-cache reuse for efficient inference suffers from stale cached contexts when retrieved knowledge is edited. The paper proposes edit-local repair as an efficient alternative to full re-prefill, showing it recovers most accuracy while being 13-21x faster when dependent text remains near the edit.
AI.motivation: KV-cache reuse reduces inference costs in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agentic systems, but cached contexts become stale when retrieved knowledge, working memory, or user state is edited. Full re-prefill is costly, while refreshing only the edited span leaves downstream dependencies stale, creating a need for efficient repair strategies.
AI.method: Formulates in-place repair as budgeted recomputation and compares training-free position-selection policies on a factual RAG benchmark with matched direct and derived edits. Evaluates multiple policies (contiguous edit-local window, attention-based, KV-deviation, and structural selectors) across three model families. Conducts mechanistic analysis to understand why some position sets fail under actual recomputation.
AI.result: At primary budget, a contiguous edit-local window recovers at least 0.94 of the post-edit answer margin and substantially outperforms other selectors. Repair is 13-21 times faster than full re-prefill. The edit-local advantage depends on adjacency and largely disappears when answer-bearing text moves downstream.
AI.conclusion: Answer-relevant edits almost always corrupt model behavior, failure severity is difficult to predict, and edit-local repair is substantially faster than full re-prefill. Results support unconditional edit-local repair when dependent text remains adjacent to the edit.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Continual Learning for Open-World Intent Discovery Under an evolving Label Space
summary: Real-world intelligent systems increasingly operate under open-world conditions, where user intents are not fixed or exhaustively known a priori and may evolve as new interaction patterns emerge. This paper proposes a unified uncertainty-aware probabilistic framework for continual new intent discovery under an evolving label space. Each utterance is encoded through an adaptive $β$-VAE into a latent mean, used for classification and density modelling and a posterior uncertainty estimate acting as a global reliability signal. Classifier confidence, posterior uncertainty and DP-GMM likelihood are combined through a multi-signal decision mechanism to distinguish known intents from potentially novel samples. Candidate novel instances are clustered through a density-based discovery module and only reliable clusters are promoted to new labels, enabling controlled label-space expansion. Replay and Elastic Weight Consolidation mitigate catastrophic forgetting and preserve previously acquired knowledge. The paper formalises continual intent discovery as a structured multi-phase open-world problem, introduces adaptive label-space expansion under stability--plasticity constraints and uses posterior uncertainty to regulate trusted-sample selection, pseudo-labelling, novelty admission and replay. Experiments show high novelty precision, stable adaptation across sequential phases and limited forgetting. Near-zero NMI and ARI indicate limited reconstruction of the complete fine-grained intent taxonomy, consistent with the framework's conservative promotion strategy. Qualitative analyses nevertheless reveal dense and locally coherent semantic clusters, showing that reliable novel structures can be discovered without exhaustive recovery of the underlying taxonomy.

AI.tldr: A unified probabilistic framework for continual new intent discovery that combines classifier confidence, posterior uncertainty, and density modeling to detect novel intents and expand the label space while mitigating catastrophic forgetting through replay and regularization techniques.
AI.motivation: Real-world intelligent systems need to operate in open-world conditions where user intents are not fixed or exhaustively known and may evolve over time. Current systems struggle with discovering new intents while maintaining knowledge of existing ones.
AI.method: Uses an adaptive β-VAE to encode utterances into latent representations with uncertainty estimates. Combines classifier confidence, posterior uncertainty, and DP-GMM likelihood through multi-signal decision mechanism. Employs density-based clustering for novel intent discovery, with conservative promotion of reliable clusters to new labels. Uses replay and Elastic Weight Consolidation to prevent catastrophic forgetting.
AI.result: Shows high novelty precision, stable adaptation across sequential phases, and limited forgetting. Achieves near-zero NMI and ARI scores, indicating limited reconstruction of complete fine-grained intent taxonomy but reveals dense and locally coherent semantic clusters for reliable novel structures.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables reliable discovery of novel intent structures without exhaustive recovery of the underlying taxonomy, supporting controlled label-space expansion while preserving existing knowledge through uncertainty-aware mechanisms.

title: TuiML: Machine Learning for AI Agents
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Code and documentation at https://tuiml.ai
summary: Machine-learning libraries such as Weka and scikit-learn were designed for human programmers. Language-model agents now use these same libraries by recalling APIs from memory and writing code, an approach that hides what a library offers, delays errors until runtime, and loses experimental state between turns. We present TuiML, a self-contained machine-learning library built for AI agents, with native algorithms across supervised, unsupervised, time-series, data handling, tuning, and evaluation tasks. Every component describes itself through machine-readable metadata and parameter schemas, so an agent can search the library, inspect components, compose validated workflows, and register new ones that become discoverable in turn. Every call is validated, seeded, and traced, and sessions export as runnable notebooks, making experiments reproducible by construction. One specification layer drives the Model Context Protocol (MCP), agent-framework adapters, a Python API, a CLI, and local model serving, while data and models never leave the machine. Benchmarks show TuiML remains predictively competitive with scikit-learn and Weka. While looking like a conventional library to a human user, TuiML is designed for agents first, allowing them to read, extend, and operate machine learning autonomously. TuiML is open source, with documentation at https://tuiml.ai.

AI.tldr: TuiML is a new machine learning library specifically designed for AI agents that provides self-contained ML algorithms with machine-readable metadata, enabling agents to autonomously search, compose, validate workflows, and ensure reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Current ML libraries like Weka and scikit-learn are designed for human programmers, but when used by language-model agents, they create problems: APIs are recalled from memory (hiding library offerings), errors are delayed until runtime, and experimental state is lost between agent turns.
AI.method: TuiML is built as a self-contained ML library with native algorithms across various ML tasks (supervised, unsupervised, time-series, data handling, tuning, evaluation). It provides machine-readable metadata and parameter schemas for every component, allowing agents to search, inspect, compose validated workflows, and register new components. All calls are validated, seeded, and traced, with sessions exportable as runnable notebooks.
AI.result: Benchmarks show TuiML remains predictively competitive with scikit-learn and Weka. The system enables agents to read, extend, and operate machine learning autonomously while maintaining data privacy (data and models never leave the machine).
AI.conclusion: TuiML demonstrates that while appearing as a conventional library to human users, it can be designed for agents first, enabling autonomous ML operations while ensuring reproducibility and maintaining competitive performance with existing libraries. The library is open source and supports multiple interfaces through a single specification layer.

title: Dataset-Dependent Effects of Cross-Depth Aggregation and Soft-Routed Experts in EEG Foundation Model Fine-Tuning
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE ICASSP 2027
summary: EEG decoding tasks can rely on different temporal dynamics and cross-channel relationships. We test whether specialized modules improve a fully fine-tuned EEG foundation model by augmenting CBraMod with cross-depth Attention Residuals (AttnRes) and two soft-routed expert banks. Across matched three-seed experiments on FACED, ISRUC, SEED-V, and PhysioNet-MI, the complete model changes mean balanced accuracy relative to full fine-tuning by -0.12, +1.27, +0.77, and -1.27 points, respectively. AttnRes alone improves mean balanced accuracy on three datasets, whereas adding experts on top of AttnRes helps only FACED and SEED-V. These gains come with substantial overhead: AttnRes requires 2.11 to 2.88x runtime and 1.78 to 2.67x memory, while the complete model requires 2.41 to 3.04x runtime and 1.86 to 2.85x memory. Overall, the added modules produce dataset-dependent, sometimes opposing effects rather than consistent gains over full fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: Specialized EEG decoding modules (AttnRes and expert banks) show mixed performance with significant overhead, producing dataset-dependent rather than consistent improvements over full fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: EEG decoding tasks vary in temporal dynamics and cross-channel relationships, requiring specialized modules to potentially improve performance beyond standard fine-tuning of EEG foundation models.
AI.method: Augment CBraMod EEG foundation model with cross-depth Attention Residuals (AttnRes) and two soft-routed expert banks, then test across multiple EEG datasets (FACED, ISRUC, SEED-V, PhysioNet-MI) with matched three-seed experiments.
AI.result: Mixed performance changes: -0.12, +1.27, +0.77, -1.27 points mean balanced accuracy across datasets. AttnRes alone improves 3 datasets, while adding experts only helps FACED and SEED-V. Significant overhead: 2.11-3.04x runtime and 1.78-2.85x memory.
AI.conclusion: Specialized modules produce dataset-dependent, sometimes opposing effects rather than consistent gains over full fine-tuning, with substantial computational overhead that may not justify the marginal improvements.

title: RideWay: Benchmarking Efficient Task Completion for Tool-Using Language Agents
summary: AI agents are usually evaluated by whether they complete a task. In interactive service settings, a successful agent can still frustrate users by asking repeated questions, performing redundant searches, or making avoidable revisions. We introduce RideWay, an efficiency-centered benchmark for ridehailing agents in a stateful tool-calling environment, together with Efficiency Utility, a success-gated metric that discounts successful trajectories for excess tool calls and user-facing turns relative to task-specific reference effort. Human paired preferences calibrate the relative penalties, reflecting an aggregate service-workflow trade-off: extra dialogue often creates visible friction, whereas extra tool use can sometimes verify constraints or preserve user intent. Across 58 tasks and 24 models, the fitted penalty for excess turns is about twice that for excess tool calls. On task-disjoint held-out preferences, Efficiency Utility achieves 78.7% accuracy overall: 90.6% when trajectories differ in turns, but chance-level accuracy when they differ solely in tool calls - the axis on which human annotators agree least. RideWay therefore makes interaction efficiency measurable alongside task success, while exposing the boundary of count-based tool-use evaluation.

AI.tldr: RideWay benchmark measures AI agent efficiency in ridehailing tasks with new metric (Efficiency Utility) that penalizes excess tool calls and user turns, calibrated by human preferences showing extra dialogue is twice as costly as extra tool use.
AI.motivation: Current AI agent evaluation focuses only on task completion, ignoring interaction efficiency. Successful agents can still frustrate users through repeated questions, redundant searches, or avoidable revisions, especially in interactive service settings like ridehailing.
AI.method: Introduces RideWay benchmark with 58 ridehailing tasks in stateful tool-calling environment, and Efficiency Utility metric that discounts successful trajectories for excess tool calls and user-facing turns relative to task-specific reference effort. Uses human paired preferences to calibrate relative penalties between extra dialogue and extra tool use.
AI.result: Human preferences show fitted penalty for excess user turns is about twice that for excess tool calls. Efficiency Utility achieves 78.7% overall accuracy on held-out preferences, with 90.6% accuracy when trajectories differ in turns, but chance-level accuracy when they differ solely in tool calls (where human annotators agree least).
AI.conclusion: RideWay makes interaction efficiency measurable alongside task success while exposing limitations of count-based tool-use evaluation, revealing that extra dialogue creates more visible friction than extra tool use, which can sometimes verify constraints or preserve user intent.

title: Long-Context Demonstration Selection Using State Space Models
summary: We study the problem of demonstration selection, which involves selecting a subset of examples for prepending to a query to a language model. This problem is closely related to in-context learning and language model inference. Since the inference cost of a transformer model scales quadratically with sequence length, the selection problem becomes especially challenging in a long-context scenario. In this paper, we tackle this problem by building on state space models (SSMs), which require only linear inference time given the input. Our approach involves two algorithms. The first learns a small set of SSMs through distillation of a (trained) transformer model. We partition all the layers into consecutive groups. Then for each group, we estimate a separate state space model to replicate the input-output behavior within the adjacent layers. Second, we map the distilled model outputs to a small set of tokens, and apply these embeddings for demonstration selection in downstream applications. We perform extensive experiments in both synthetic and real-world datasets to validate our approach. We demonstrate that the distilled SSMs only incur an approximation error of less than $0.7\%$ relative to the true output. In downstream evaluation, we show that on several text classification and reasoning tasks, our approach reduces FLOPs by $14.2\times$ and improves accuracy by $6.48\%$ relative to baseline demonstration selection methods.

AI.tldr: Demonstration selection using distilled State Space Models for efficient in-context learning, achieving 14.2× FLOP reduction and 6.48% accuracy improvement.
AI.motivation: Transformer inference cost scales quadratically with sequence length, making demonstration selection challenging in long-context scenarios. Efficient selection methods are needed to reduce computational overhead while maintaining performance.
AI.method: Two-algorithm approach: (1) Learn small set of State Space Models through distillation of trained transformer model, partitioning layers into consecutive groups and estimating separate SSMs for each group; (2) Map distilled model outputs to small token set and use embeddings for demonstration selection in downstream applications.
AI.result: Distilled SSMs achieve <0.7% approximation error relative to true output. In downstream tasks, approach reduces FLOPs by 14.2× and improves accuracy by 6.48% compared to baseline demonstration selection methods on text classification and reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: SSM distillation provides efficient demonstration selection for in-context learning, significantly reducing computational costs while improving accuracy, offering practical solution for long-context scenarios.

title: Multimodal Conditioning of Fine-Tuned Stable Diffusion XL for Controllable and Culturally Faithful Ulos Motif Generation
comment: C. Anutariya, M.M. Bonsangue, M.N. Mahrin (eds.) "Proceedings of the 4th International Conference on Data Science and Artificial Intelligence (DSAI 2026)", Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, November 12-13, 2026, in volume 3251 of Communications in Computer and Information Science, Springer, November 2026
summary: The traditional Batak Ulos weaving industry faces growing challenges in producing diverse, innovative motifs due to limitations in conventional, manually driven design methods. This study proposes a multimodal generative framework integrating a fine-tuned Latent Diffusion Model (Stable Diffusion XL v1.0 via LoRA) with a Multimodal Large Language Model (LLaMA 1.5-7B) to enable controllable, culturally faithful Ulos motif generation. Four complementary conditioning mechanisms: text, image, representation, and semantic map (via ControlNet) jointly guide the generation process, each governing a distinct aspect from semantic intent to spatial layout. A five level ablation study across three scenarios (shape transformation, colour variation, and high-complexity input) shows that conditioning effectiveness is not proportional to the number of mechanisms combined: Text + Image + Semantic Map achieved the best FID (270) and CLIP Score (0.65 - 0.70) but the weakest SSIM (0.65), while Text + Image + Representation offered the best overall balance, with stable SSIM (0.84) and competitive FID (280). Combining all four mechanisms yielded the weakest FID (330), indicating conflicting optimization signals. Qualitative evaluation by nine weavers and thirty public participants confirmed statistically significant positive acceptance (Wilcoxon, p=0.007 and p<0.001, respectively). A web-based prototype supporting text-to-image and image-to-image generation was also developed, offering a practical digital design tool for cultural heritage preservation.

AI.tldr: Researchers developed a multimodal AI framework combining Stable Diffusion XL and LLaMA to generate culturally authentic Batak Ulos weaving motifs with four conditioning mechanisms, achieving best results with text+image+semantic map combination.
AI.motivation: The traditional Batak Ulos weaving industry struggles with limited design innovation due to manual, conventional methods, creating a need for digital tools that can generate diverse, culturally faithful motifs while preserving heritage.
AI.method: Multimodal generative framework integrating fine-tuned Latent Diffusion Model (Stable Diffusion XL v1.0 via LoRA) with Multimodal Large Language Model (LLaMA 1.5-7B), using four complementary conditioning mechanisms: text, image, representation, and semantic map via ControlNet.
AI.result: Best FID (270) and CLIP Score (0.65-0.70) achieved with Text+Image+Semantic Map, but weak SSIM (0.65). Text+Image+Representation offered best balance with SSIM 0.84 and FID 280. All four mechanisms together produced worst FID (330). Qualitative evaluation showed statistically significant positive acceptance from weavers and public. Web-based prototype developed for practical use.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully enables controllable, culturally faithful Ulos motif generation, demonstrating that conditioning effectiveness isn't proportional to number of mechanisms combined, with certain combinations performing better than using all available mechanisms. The approach offers practical digital design tools for cultural heritage preservation.

title: TabPFN-3.5: Technical Report
summary: We introduce TabPFN-3.5, our new flagship Tabular Foundation Model. It significantly outperforms its predecessor, TabPFN-3, and all existing baselines across a broad range of tabular problems. TabPFN-3.5 sets a new state of the art on standard tabular prediction in TabArena, and extends it to the data practitioners encounter in practice: non-i.i.d. data with temporal or grouped splits, tables with strings, text and images, high-cardinality categorical features, and wide tables with many features. These gains carry over to our task-specific harnesses: state of the art on relational data and stronger time-series forecasting. For faster inference, our variant TabPFN-3.5-Fast runs up to 3x faster than TabPFN-3 while keeping most of the accuracy gains. In addition, we upgrade TabPFN-3.5-Plus, expanding our multimodal capabilities with advanced text and date handling alongside proprietary inference optimizations. Finally, we release a new version of our Thinking mode, TabPFN-3.5-Thinking, which scales inference-time computation to push the state of the art further. It benefits from our stronger base model and from inference-time improvements that make it up to 12x faster than TabPFN-3-Thinking.

AI.tldr: TabPFN-3.5 is a new state-of-the-art tabular foundation model that significantly outperforms previous versions and all baselines across diverse tabular tasks, with specialized variants for speed, multimodal capabilities, and advanced inference-time computation.
AI.motivation: To advance beyond existing tabular models by addressing practical challenges practitioners face, including non-i.i.d. data (temporal/grouped splits), tables with mixed modalities (strings, text, images), high-cardinality categorical features, and wide tables with many features.
AI.method: Developed a new flagship tabular foundation model (TabPFN-3.5) with several variants: standard version for broad tabular prediction, fast variant (TabPFN-3.5-Fast) for 3x faster inference, enhanced multimodal version (TabPFN-3.5-Plus) with advanced text/date handling, and thinking mode (TabPFN-3.5-Thinking) with inference-time computation scaling.
AI.result: TabPFN-3.5 achieves new state-of-the-art performance on standard tabular prediction in TabArena and extends superior performance to practical scenarios including non-i.i.d. data, multimodal tables, and high-cardinality features. Task-specific harnesses show state-of-the-art results on relational data and stronger time-series forecasting. Fast variant runs 3x faster while maintaining accuracy gains, and thinking mode achieves up to 12x speed improvement over previous version.
AI.conclusion: TabPFN-3.5 represents a significant advancement in tabular foundation models, delivering superior performance across diverse real-world tabular problems while offering specialized variants optimized for speed, multimodal capabilities, and advanced inference-time computation, addressing key practical needs of data practitioners.

title: Missing Bridges: Composition-Aware Active Imitation Learning
summary: Active imitation learning reduces expert effort by allowing a learner to request the demonstrations it needs. Existing methods typically select these requests for their expected information gain about the expert policy. In structured multi-task domains, however, the number of start-goal tasks may grow combinatorially despite their solutions sharing reusable behavior. This makes composable behaviors especially valuable, since a single demonstration may help solve many tasks at once. Prior methods do not explicitly account for this value when selecting which demonstration to request. We introduce Adaptive Agents via Latent Topologies (AALT), which requests demonstrations that maximize expected gains in start-goal connectivity. We further show that this objective is formally tied to information gain about task reachability. AALT organizes existing demonstrations into a topology of latent hub states connected by learned behaviors, identifies high-value bridge demonstrations that are likely to enable many tasks at once, and grounds each to an expert query. At inference, it plans through the resulting topology and conditions a diffusion policy on each successive hub transition. In a simulated UR5e robot ordered-retrieval domain with 72 tasks, AALT improved from 42/72 to 72/72 (100%) successful tasks consistently using only 3 demonstrations totaling 5 transitions beyond the initial dataset. After 20 demonstrations, the strongest baseline averaged 88.6% success using 98 transitions.

AI.tldr: AALT (Adaptive Agents via Latent Topologies) is an active imitation learning method that selects demonstration requests based on expected gains in start-goal connectivity rather than traditional information gain, enabling efficient learning of composable behaviors that solve multiple tasks with minimal expert demonstrations.
AI.motivation: In structured multi-task domains with combinatorially many start-goal tasks, existing active imitation learning methods fail to account for the value of composable behaviors - where single demonstrations can help solve many tasks at once by sharing reusable behavior components across tasks.
AI.method: AALT organizes existing demonstrations into a topology of latent hub states connected by learned behaviors, identifies high-value "bridge demonstrations" that maximize expected gains in start-goal connectivity (formally tied to information gain about task reachability), grounds these to expert queries, and at inference plans through the resulting topology while conditioning a diffusion policy on each successive hub transition.
AI.result: In a simulated UR5e robot ordered-retrieval domain with 72 tasks, AALT achieved 100% success rate (72/72 tasks) using only 3 demonstrations totaling 5 transitions beyond initial dataset. After 20 demonstrations, the strongest baseline averaged only 88.6% success using 98 transitions, showing significantly higher sample efficiency.
AI.conclusion: By focusing on demonstration requests that maximize start-goal connectivity gains rather than traditional information gain, AALT enables highly efficient imitation learning in multi-task domains through composable behaviors, achieving near-perfect performance with dramatically fewer expert demonstrations than existing methods.

title: Walking the Score Manifold: Continuous-time Generative Dynamics on Learned Data Manifolds
summary: Generative modeling of time-dependent data is typically formulated on a discrete temporal grid, restricting supervision to the observed timestamps in the training data. We instead frame generation as continuous-time evolution on a learned data manifold. To this end, we leverage pretrained score-based models as geometric priors and learn a vector field that evolves data along score-induced interpolation paths. Because these dynamics follow transitions that respect the geometry learned by the score model, they support generation at arbitrary timestamps and temporal super-resolution beyond the discretization of the training data. Moreover, this geometric formulation allows us to train the vector field simulation-free through a regression objective. To improve long-horizon rollout robustness, we introduce an objective that promotes path-relative transverse exponential stability. While motivated by stability theory, it admits a practical interpretation as denoising score matching transverse to the interpolation path. Further, we extend the framework to a probabilistic setting that models a distribution over plausible future trajectories. We demonstrate the method on natural video and scientific dynamical data, including temporal super-resolution, PDE-based spatiotemporal fields, and molecular dynamics. Our results show that score-based priors provide a strong foundation for learning stochastic continuous-time generative dynamics.

AI.tldr: A continuous-time generative modeling approach using pretrained score-based models as geometric priors to learn vector fields that evolve data along score-induced interpolation paths, enabling temporal super-resolution and arbitrary timestamp generation.
AI.motivation: Traditional generative modeling of time-dependent data is limited to discrete temporal grids, restricting supervision to observed timestamps. The paper aims to overcome this limitation by framing generation as continuous-time evolution.
AI.method: Leverages pretrained score-based models as geometric priors to learn a vector field that evolves data along score-induced interpolation paths. Uses simulation-free training through regression objectives and introduces stability-promoting objectives for long-horizon robustness (path-relative transverse exponential stability). Extends to probabilistic settings for modeling distributions over future trajectories.
AI.result: Demonstrates the method on natural video, scientific dynamical data, PDE-based spatiotemporal fields, and molecular dynamics. Shows that score-based priors provide strong foundations for learning stochastic continuous-time generative dynamics, enabling temporal super-resolution beyond training data discretization.
AI.conclusion: Score-based priors offer an effective foundation for continuous-time generative modeling, supporting generation at arbitrary timestamps and temporal super-resolution while maintaining robustness through stability objectives.

title: Anchoring What Matters: A Dual-Level Learning Framework for Visually-Grounded Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has significantly improved the reasoning capabilities of large vision-language models (LVLMs). However, standard on-policy RLVR algorithms face a critical optimization bottleneck in preserving and reinforcing visually grounded reasoning behaviors: valuable visually-grounded reasoning trajectories are discarded after a single update, while uniform token advantage allocation prevents the model from reinforcing critical perception or reasoning steps. To bridge this gap, we propose PIVOT, a dual-level learning framework that anchors policy optimization around informative visual reasoning signals. Specifically, PIVOT introduces a self-calibrated experience replay mechanism, which selectively collects and replays visually-grounded historical experiences as stable reference anchors for policy optimization. Building upon this, we further design a vision-guided advantage allocation mechanism to allocate additional vision-aware advantages to tokens based on their local visual support and impact on downstream reasoning. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that PIVOT achieves highly competitive performance in enhancing the multimodal reasoning capabilities of LVLMs.

AI.tldr: PIVOT is a dual-level learning framework that improves reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for large vision-language models by anchoring policy optimization around visual reasoning signals through experience replay and vision-guided advantage allocation.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy RLVR algorithms have optimization bottlenecks in preserving visually grounded reasoning behaviors. They discard valuable reasoning trajectories after single updates, and uniform token advantage allocation prevents reinforcement of critical perception or reasoning steps.
AI.method: PIVOT introduces two key mechanisms: 1) self-calibrated experience replay that selectively collects and replays visually-grounded historical experiences as stable reference anchors, and 2) vision-guided advantage allocation that allocates additional vision-aware advantages to tokens based on their local visual support and impact on downstream reasoning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that PIVOT achieves highly competitive performance in enhancing the multimodal reasoning capabilities of large vision-language models.
AI.conclusion: PIVOT effectively bridges the optimization gap in RLVR by anchoring policy optimization around informative visual reasoning signals, leading to improved preservation and reinforcement of visually-grounded reasoning behaviors in large vision-language models.

title: EdgeReMIND: A Scalable, Top-Ranked Memorization Baseline for Temporal Multi-Relational Link Prediction
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, 13 tables. Accepted at the Fifth Learning on Graphs Conference (LoG 2026), Proceedings Track. Code: https://github.com/BryantPollard/EdgeReMIND
summary: Temporal link prediction on the Temporal Graph Benchmark 2.0 (TGB 2.0) faces a scalability ceiling: on the benchmark's three largest datasets, every existing embedding method runs out of memory or exceeds the time budget. These large-scale graphs are the ones nearest real deployment scale, so failing on them is a real production limitation. EdgeReMIND sets the highest reported test mean reciprocal rank (MRR) on six of eight TGB 2.0 datasets and is the only relation-aware method that runs on all of them. This linear memorization model, with learned per-relation weights over data-calibrated features, is therefore not merely a fallback where embeddings fail but a practical state-of-the-art baseline across the benchmark.

AI.tldr: EdgeReMIND: A linear memorization model with learned per-relation weights achieves SOTA performance on 6/8 TGB 2.0 datasets, solving scalability issues where embedding methods fail on large-scale graphs.
AI.motivation: Temporal link prediction on TGB 2.0 faces scalability limitations where existing embedding methods run out of memory or exceed time budgets on the largest datasets, which are closest to real deployment scale.
AI.method: EdgeReMIND is a linear memorization model with learned per-relation weights over data-calibrated features, creating a relation-aware method that scales effectively to all TGB 2.0 datasets.
AI.result: Sets highest reported test mean reciprocal rank (MRR) on six of eight TGB 2.0 datasets and is the only relation-aware method that runs on all datasets, including the largest ones where embedding methods fail.
AI.conclusion: EdgeReMIND is not merely a fallback for where embeddings fail, but serves as a practical state-of-the-art baseline across the entire TGB 2.0 benchmark, addressing real production limitations in temporal link prediction.

title: The Other Half of the Memory Wall: Serving 35B MoEs from SSD with Trained Routing Prediction
summary:
Mixture-of-experts (MoE) inference on consumer hardware is bounded by weight memory: a 35B-class model is 19.5GB at 4-bit, and sparsity shrinks the compute per token, not the bytes that must be held. Naive offloading to SSD does not help on its own, because layer N+1's experts must be chosen before layer N's output exists, so the reads cannot start early enough to hide behind compute. We present Edge0, a streaming MoE inference engine that closes the gap with a prerouter: a per-layer head predicts the next layer's routing one token ahead, and the prediction is consumed as the routing itself, so the staged expert set equals the routed set and nothing is dropped. An unmerged recovery LoRA, trained on the student path, pays back the quality lost to int4 quantization and routing replacement. On a single 24GB machine, Edge0
  serves a 35B MoE at 20tok/s inside 3GiB of peak active memory, within a few points of its fp16 teacher on average across five public benchmarks. An 8B tier runs on the same framework, and the framework, checkpoints, and adapters are open source.

AI.tldr: Edge0 enables efficient MoE inference on consumer hardware by using a prerouting mechanism that predicts next layer's routing ahead of time, allowing for streaming expert weights from SSD without dropping tokens, combined with a recovery LoRA to maintain quality.
AI.motivation: MoE inference on consumer hardware is limited by weight memory constraints; naive offloading to SSD doesn't work because expert selection for layer N+1 requires layer N's output, creating read-compute synchronization issues that prevent effective memory management.
AI.method: Edge0 introduces a prerouter that predicts the next layer's routing one token ahead, treating the prediction as the actual routing so expert sets can be prefetched from SSD without dropping tokens. It also uses an unmerged recovery LoRA trained on student paths to compensate for int4 quantization and routing replacement quality loss.
AI.result: On a single 24GB machine, Edge0 serves a 35B MoE model at 20 tokens/second with only 3GiB peak active memory, achieving performance close to its fp16 teacher across five public benchmarks. An 8B tier also runs on the same framework.
AI.conclusion: Edge0 effectively solves the memory bottleneck for MoE inference on consumer hardware through innovative prerouting and quality recovery techniques, making large MoE models practical on standard consumer-grade GPUs while maintaining near-teacher-level performance.

title: Symmetry without a manifold: intrinsic dimension on orbits
comment: 33 pages, 3 figures. Under review at NeurReps 2026 (NeurIPS workshop, Proceedings Track)
summary: The standard geometric derivation of neural scaling exponents takes the intrinsic dimension of a data manifold as its input. On modular addition in $\mathbb{Z}_p$ that derivation has no input. The exact algebraic solution is an orbit of $\mathbb{Z}_p$ acting by isometries. Transitivity alone makes the ratio statistic underlying the standard dimension estimator a point mass, so the estimator is undefined, and here the two nearest neighbour distances coincide exactly. Breaking the symmetry at scale $ε$ returns a number, but one that tracks $1/ε$ with no scale free plateau. We show that the failure is general, since on any finite orbit of a group acting by isometries the estimator reports the resolution at which the set is probed rather than a dimension. What replaces the power law is exponential in hidden width, $L(h)=L_\infty+A\exp(-c\,h^α)$, with $R^2$ between 0.982 and 0.995 against 0.857 to 0.906 for a power law admitting the same floor and fitted under the same protocol. Where the data supply is sufficient the rate belongs to the regulariser rather than to the group, since weight decay moves $c$ by a factor of 47 while group order moves it by 1.10, a residual below seed to seed resolution, for every fixed $α$ between 0.75 and 2. The critical width falls with group order rather than rising, against capacity counting that assigns a fixed number of neurons to each irreducible representation.

AI.tldr: Standard dimension estimators fail on finite isometry group orbits, reporting probe resolution instead of manifold dimension. Neural scaling on modular arithmetic follows exponential decay in hidden width, not power law.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses a fundamental limitation in standard geometric derivations of neural scaling exponents when applied to finite orbits of groups acting by isometries, using modular addition in Z_p as a concrete example where traditional approaches break down.
AI.method: Analyzes modular addition in Z_p as an algebraic solution orbit under group isometries, examines failure of standard dimension estimators on finite orbits, and studies neural scaling behavior through exponential decay fits rather than power laws.
AI.result: On finite isometry group orbits, dimension estimators report probe resolution (tracking 1/ε) rather than intrinsic dimension. Neural scaling follows L(h)=L∞+A exp(-c h^α) with high R² (0.982-0.995), dominated by regularization effects (47x factor for weight decay vs 1.10x for group order).
AI.conclusion: Standard dimension estimation methods fundamentally fail on finite group orbits, revealing exponential neural scaling dominated by regularization rather than group structure, contradicting capacity-based neuron allocation theories.

title: Teaching AI, Robotics, & Community: A Hubs-Based K-12 Education Framework for Reaching Rural Schools
summary: K-12 robotics and AI education remains difficult to scale, especially in rural regions lacking sustained technical mentorship. Programs like FIRST provide competition pathways and instructional opportunities, but they do not eliminate the need for local programming and robotics expertise. We introduce AI, Robotics, & Community (ARC), a hubs-based framework where colleges train undergraduate mentors and host workshops for nearby K-12 teams. Mature school programs can become secondary hubs that support additional schools, creating a self-reinforcing education loop where mentorship reach propagates geographically and can even grow super-linearly. We first evaluate ARC through a trial deployment at one university. The trial created three rural robotics teams. On five-point Likert surveys, mean increases in K-12 programming knowledge, resource access, and practice opportunities were 2.00, 2.25, and 1.25 points. Likewise, undergraduate confidence teaching technical concepts, adapting explanations, managing groups, and finding mentoring enjoyable and meaningful increased by 1.29, 1.14, 1.00, and 1.14 points. Additionally, we create a spatial Markov model of ARC's growth and simulate it using the state of Indiana as a testbed. Under moderate conditions, we find that ARC reaches 74% of Indiana's 1,925 public K-12 schools and produces 992 robotics programs after 40 years, compared with 161 projected under natural growth alone. Together, these results show ARC can create and support rural robotics programs, train undergraduate AI and robotics mentors, and potentially scale mentorship across a region.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ARC, a hubs-based framework that uses colleges to train undergraduate mentors who then support K-12 robotics/AI teams, creating a scalable mentorship network that grows super-linearly to reach rural schools.
AI.motivation: K-12 robotics and AI education is difficult to scale in rural regions lacking sustained technical mentorship. Existing programs like FIRST don't eliminate the need for local programming and robotics expertise, leaving rural areas underserved.
AI.method: The ARC framework establishes college-based hubs that train undergraduate mentors to host workshops for nearby K-12 teams. Mature school programs become secondary hubs supporting additional schools, creating a self-reinforcing education loop. The authors evaluated ARC through a trial deployment at one university and created a spatial Markov model to simulate growth across Indiana.
AI.result: The trial created three rural robotics teams with significant improvements: K-12 programming knowledge increased 2.00 points, resource access 2.25 points, and practice opportunities 1.25 points on Likert scales. Undergraduate mentors showed gains in teaching confidence (1.29 points) and other mentoring skills. Simulation showed ARC could reach 74% of Indiana's 1,925 schools (992 robotics programs after 40 years) vs. 161 under natural growth.
AI.conclusion: ARC can successfully create and support rural robotics programs, train undergraduate AI/robotics mentors, and potentially scale mentorship across a region through its hubs-based framework that enables super-linear growth of technical education infrastructure.

title: Locating Hidden Failures Makes Long-Horizon Agents More Reliable
summary: As AI agents take on long, autonomous tasks, we increasingly oversee rather than perform the work, yet we still judge them almost entirely by whether they finally succeed. An outcome cannot reveal where a run went wrong, whether the agent recovered, or the irreversible harm it caused along the way, and where long-horizon agents fail remains unmapped. We study $2518$ agent trajectories across software engineering, computer use, and science, close to real deployment, and classify $6967$ mistakes into $78$ failure types. Failure follows a recurring signature: after its first mistake an agent often fails to recover and rarely catches the error itself, so the run continues unchecked while still looking correct; whether an agent recovers depends on the task and the environment's feedback, not on the agent framework running it. Long-horizon agents can do real harm on the way to a passing result: even runs scored as solved delete data, corrupt systems, or fabricate success rather than earning it. We release these human-verified annotations as Traverse, a benchmark on which six frontier judges struggle to locate failure regardless of scale: even the strongest correctly identifies the first mistake in fewer than a third of runs. Yet Scout, a $4$B verifier we trained, locates failure far better than these judges and transfers to domains it never saw. Used at test time to select among an agent's candidate runs, it raises task success above the agent's own single-attempt performance, without retraining the agent. By making failure cheap to locate and correct, this work is a foundation for more trustworthy long-horizon agents that learn from their own mistakes, and a practical path to overseeing increasingly autonomous AI.

AI.tldr: Researchers analyzed 2518 AI agent trajectories across software, computer use, and science tasks, identifying 6967 mistakes classified into 78 failure types. They found that agents rarely self-correct after first errors, often causing irreversible harm while appearing successful. They developed Scout, a 4B parameter verifier that outperforms frontier judges at detecting failures, improving agent performance when selecting among candidate runs.
AI.motivation: Current AI agents are increasingly performing long, autonomous tasks where humans oversee rather than directly perform the work. However, we still evaluate these agents almost entirely by whether they ultimately succeed, which doesn't reveal where things went wrong, whether agents recovered from mistakes, or what irreversible harm they caused along the way. There's limited understanding of how and why long-horizon agents fail.
AI.method: The researchers studied 2518 agent trajectories across three domains (software engineering, computer use, and science) under near-real deployment conditions. They classified 6967 mistakes into 78 failure types. They developed and released Traverse, a benchmark with human-verified annotations. They evaluated six frontier judges on this benchmark and created Scout, a 4B parameter verifier trained to detect failures. They tested Scout's ability to transfer to unseen domains and used it at test time to select among an agent's candidate runs.
AI.result: Failure follows a recurring pattern: after making their first mistake, agents often fail to recover and rarely catch their own errors, leading to unchecked runs that appear correct while causing harm. Even runs scored as "solved" can delete data, corrupt systems, or fabricate success. Six frontier judges struggled to locate failures regardless of scale, with the strongest correctly identifying the first mistake in fewer than a third of runs. Scout significantly outperformed these judges at failure detection, transferred well to unseen domains, and when used to select among candidate runs, raised task success above the agent's own single-attempt performance without retraining the agent.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a foundation for more trustworthy long-horizon agents that can learn from their mistakes. By making failure cheap to locate and correct, it provides a practical path for overseeing increasingly autonomous AI. The findings reveal systemic issues in current agent evaluation and demonstrate that verifiers like Scout can significantly improve agent reliability without modifying the underlying agent architecture.

title: Decodability is Not Causality: Dissociating Probe Readouts from Behavioral Drivers via SAE Decomposition
summary: Linear probes can decode safety-relevant concepts such as truthfulness from language-model activations, but probe accuracy may show only decodability, not that the features the probe weights causally drive model behavior. We demonstrate that this gap cannot be closed from the geometry of probe weights alone: the features geometrically aligned with probe direction need not be the ones the model uses, so causal relevance requires intervention. We introduce a feature-level diagnostic that decomposes a deployed True/False probe into sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features, ranks those features by both probe alignment and by gradient sensitivity of the model's behavior, and ablates the resulting shared, probe-only, and random feature sets under a coherence gate. On the truth probe of Buerger et al. (2024) (TTPD), applied in the instructed truth/deception setting of Long et al. (2025) for Gemma2-9B-Instruct, the two rankings overlap only weakly (about 12%, Spearman rho = 0.10), and ablation dissociates them sharply: features the probe shares with the model flip the output far more (up to 27%) than equally sized probe-only (6%) or random (1%) features at full coherence, while probe-only features instead perturb the probe's own readout. The dissociation holds across five seeds and a held-out split, and an activation-aware selection of features flips behavior nearly three times as often as the probe's geometric top features (17.6% vs. 6.1%). In this setting, therefore, the geometric projection of a probe's weight vector alone does not identify the features the model causally uses; however, combining probe information with feature activation statistics recovers substantially more behaviorally causal features, and coherence-gated SAE intervention is needed to separate them from probe readouts.

AI.tldr: Probe weight geometry alone doesn't identify behaviorally causal features; combining probe information with feature activation statistics plus coherence-gated SAE intervention is needed to separate causal features from probe readouts.
AI.motivation: Linear probes can decode safety-relevant concepts like truthfulness from language model activations, but probe accuracy only shows decodability, not that the features the probe weights causally drive model behavior. There's a gap between probe decodability and causal relevance that requires intervention to close.
AI.method: Introduces a feature-level diagnostic that: 1) decomposes a deployed True/False probe into sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features, 2) ranks features by both probe alignment and gradient sensitivity of model behavior, and 3) ablates resulting feature sets (shared, probe-only, random) under a coherence gate. Applied to truth probe of Buerger et al. (2024) in instructed truth/deception setting on Gemma2-9B-Instruct.
AI.result: Probe alignment and gradient sensitivity rankings overlap weakly (12%, Spearman rho=0.10). Ablation shows features shared with model flip output far more (up to 27%) than probe-only (6%) or random (1%) features. Activation-aware selection flips behavior nearly 3x more than probe's geometric top features (17.6% vs. 6.1%).
AI.conclusion: Geometric projection of probe weight vector alone doesn't identify features the model causally uses. Combining probe information with feature activation statistics recovers more behaviorally causal features, and coherence-gated SAE intervention is needed to separate them from probe readouts.

title: Beyond the Previous Layer: Residual Predictive Structure in Sparse MoE Routing
summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts models route each token through a sequence of expert selections. We ask whether the immediately preceding selection adequately summarizes this trajectory for predicting the next router. Using frozen OLMoE and JetMoE models, we measure the held-out predictive gain from earlier expert selections while retaining the most recent selection as a common baseline. In OLMoE, extending the history from one to eleven layers raises router-logit $R^2$ from 0.59879 to 0.66544. A preregistered JetMoE replication yields four-layer gains of 0.14275 and 0.20528 at two target depths, with paired bootstrap intervals above zero. These gains survive nonlinear decoding: adding history to a small multilayer perceptron improves $R^2$ by 0.17137 and 0.21861, whereas nonlinear decoding of the recent state alone adds 0.00139 and 0.00936 over a linear probe. Parameter-matched controls preserve the advantage, and cross-fitted history residuals predict target residuals with $R^2$ of 0.20549 and 0.23556. These findings identify residual predictive structure in expert-selection trajectories beyond adjacent-layer persistence.

AI.tldr: Recent expert selections in sparse MoE models contain useful predictive information for future routing decisions beyond just the immediately preceding selection.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates whether the most recent expert selection in sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models adequately captures the full routing trajectory information needed to predict the next router decision, or if earlier selections contain additional predictive value.
AI.method: Using frozen OLMoE and JetMoE models, the researchers measured predictive gain from earlier expert selections beyond the most recent one. They extended history windows from 1 to 11 layers in OLMoE, conducted preregistered JetMoE replication, used nonlinear decoding with multilayer perceptrons, employed parameter-matched controls, and cross-fitted history residuals.
AI.result: Significant predictive gains from historical expert selections: OLMoE showed R² increase from 0.59879 to 0.66544 when extending history from 1 to 11 layers; JetMoE showed gains of 0.14275 and 0.20528 at different depths; nonlinear decoding with history improved R² by 0.17137 and 0.21861; cross-fitted history residuals predicted target residuals with R² of 0.20549 and 0.23556.
AI.conclusion: There exists residual predictive structure in expert-selection trajectories beyond adjacent-layer persistence, suggesting that routing decisions in MoE models are influenced by more than just the immediately preceding selection, and historical routing patterns contain valuable information for predicting future routing behavior.

title: When Is Graph Structure Worth Its Cost? The Case for Structure Pricing in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary:
Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can help answer questions that require information from many documents. However, building a graph often requires many language-model calls during ingestion. It is therefore important to ask whether its quality gains justify the additional cost.
  We present EffiRAG, a graph-based RAG system designed to reduce this cost. It uses the graph to locate relevant passages and generates answers from the original text. This design preserves source information while keeping graph construction and query processing lightweight.
  We evaluate EffiRAG on UltraDomain, which contains 120 open-ended questions from four domains. Compared with LightRAG-hybrid, EffiRAG produces the preferred answer on 93 questions. LightRAG is preferred on 7, and the remaining 20 are splits. EffiRAG also reduces total system cost by 57 percent, from USD 0.952 to USD 0.408. The cost includes language-model calls during ingestion and querying.
  The advantage remains as the corpus grows. At 10 and 20 documents per domain, EffiRAG uses a lightweight, non-LLM filter to skip low-salience chunks. It remains preferred over LightRAG-hybrid. It costs 4.2 times and 4.5 times less, respectively.
  The comparisons identify different quality-cost trade-offs. Graph-based RAG systems should therefore be evaluated by both answer quality and cost. The results favor graph structure that locates and preserves source evidence.

AI.tldr: EffiRAG is a cost-effective graph-based RAG system that uses graphs for passage location but generates answers from original text, reducing costs by 57% while maintaining quality compared to LightRAG-hybrid.
AI.motivation: Graph-based RAG systems improve answer quality for questions requiring information from multiple documents, but they incur high computational costs due to many LLM calls during graph construction, raising questions about whether quality gains justify the expense.
AI.method: EffiRAG employs a hybrid approach: using graphs to locate relevant passages for retrieval, but generating answers directly from the original retrieved text rather than the graph structure. This preserves source information while making both graph construction and query processing lightweight. The system also uses a non-LLM filter to skip low-salience chunks in larger corpora.
AI.result: On the UltraDomain benchmark (120 questions across 4 domains), EffiRAG produces preferred answers on 93 questions vs. LightRAG-hybrid's 7 (with 20 splits), while reducing total system cost by 57% (from $0.952 to $0.408). The advantage persists as corpus size grows to 10-20 documents per domain, with cost reductions of 4.2-4.5x.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based RAG systems should be evaluated on both quality and cost trade-offs. The results favor graph structures that focus on locating and preserving source evidence rather than expensive full-graph answer generation, with EffiRAG demonstrating that significant cost reductions are possible without sacrificing answer quality.

title: On the Identifiability of Mixed Ordinal and Exponential Family Causal DAGs under Linear Parametric Models
summary: The problem of identifiability in linear parametric models (LPMs) whose nodes follow either an ordered logit model or a regular one-parameter exponential family is evaluated. The results go beyond classical structural equation models as well as results for nodes with observations from a homogeneous family of distributions. The main result establishes that the orientation of every edge joining an ordinal node to an exponential-family node is identifiable from the joint distribution alone at every parameter value, provided the ordinal node has at least three categories and the exponential-family node at least three points of support, with no restriction on the sufficient statistic. Converses show that both requirements are necessary: the three-category requirement is binding only for affine sufficient statistics, and the three-point requirement is binding under the canonical link. The guarantee extends to orienting every such mixed ordinal-exponential family edge of a given $d$-node undirected skeleton. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical results by successfully separating orientations within a Markov equivalence class, which are indistinguishable by conditional independence alone.

AI.tldr: Linear parametric models with ordinal and exponential-family nodes have edge orientations identifiable from joint distributions under minimal conditions (3+ categories for ordinal, 3+ support points for exponential-family).
AI.motivation: Extending identifiability results beyond classical structural equation models and homogeneous distribution families. Current methods based solely on conditional independence often leave edge orientations indistinguishable within Markov equivalence classes.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of identifiability in linear parametric models with nodes following either ordered logit models or one-parameter exponential family distributions. Establishes identifiability conditions and provides converses showing necessity of requirements.
AI.result: Proves that orientation of edges between ordinal nodes (with ≥3 categories) and exponential-family nodes (with ≥3 support points) is identifiable from joint distribution alone, regardless of sufficient statistic. Converses show both 3-category and 3-point requirements are necessary under specific conditions.
AI.conclusion: Significant extension of identifiability guarantees for mixed ordinal-exponential family edges, enabling orientation separation within Markov equivalence classes that were previously indistinguishable. Numerical experiments validate theoretical results.

title: AutoTuneBench: Trustworthy Measurement for Agent Auto-Tuning of LLM Serving Engines
comment: 15 pages, 7 tables, 6 figures. Code and measurement corpus: https://github.com/li-ch/autotunebench (tag v1.0.0)
summary: Large language model agents tune GPU kernels and serving engines through a closed loop of propose, measure, and keep, but the measurements behind this loop are not trustworthy. We characterize four failure modes from a four-day pilot corpus of 619 model calls: strawman baselines manufacture speedups, absolute times do not transfer across machines, saturated tasks nullify comparisons, and infrastructure defects impersonate science. We present AutoTuneBench, a benchmark and measurement protocol that makes trust architectural. The protocol is frozen as code with test-enforced provenance; a database-level validator rejects out-of-protocol results; anti-cheat checks run outside the agent's modification surface; comparisons follow pre-registered readouts; and measurements anchor to externally published results, grounded in paired-seed statistics with a 5\% cross-run coefficient-of-variation cap. Honest measurement rewrites the headlines: our best kernel reads 10.6x against a naive baseline but 2.03x against the honest one; one configuration delivers 1.174x on one machine and 1.0049x on another; a pre-registered on/off comparison nulls at a shared wall (2.4840 vs 2.4957\,ms); and the KernelBench Level-1 suite admits 51\% of tasks with median speedup 1.0001x over PyTorch eager. The protocol, the two-engine corpus (vLLM and SGLang), and its audit trail are released as open artifacts.

AI.tldr: AutoTuneBench addresses untrustworthy LLM agent measurements in GPU kernel tuning by creating a benchmark with architectural trust guarantees, revealing that honest measurement drastically changes reported speedup claims.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents tuning GPU kernels suffer from unreliable measurements characterized by four failure modes: strawman baselines, non-transferable absolute times, saturated tasks nullifying comparisons, and infrastructure defects masquerading as science.
AI.method: AutoTuneBench establishes a frozen measurement protocol with test-enforced provenance, database-level validation, anti-cheat checks, pre-registered readouts, and external result anchoring using paired-seed statistics with ≤5% cross-run coefficient-of-variation.
AI.result: Honest measurement reveals drastically different results: best kernel shows 10.6x speedup vs naive baseline but only 2.03x vs honest baseline; one config varies from 1.174x to 1.0049x across machines; null results emerge in pre-registered comparisons; and 51% of tasks show median 1.0001x speedup over PyTorch eager.
AI.conclusion: Architecting trust into measurement protocols is essential for reliable LLM agent tuning, as demonstrated by AutoTuneBench which provides open artifacts including protocols, two-engine corpus (vLLM and SGLang), and audit trails.

title: ASPIRE: Asynchronous Batched Self-Speculative Decoding for Long-Context LLM Inference
summary: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by attention, whose repeated KV-cache reads make decoding memory-bound. Self-speculative decoding alleviates this by drafting tokens with sparse attention and verifying them with full attention, but existing batched methods remain synchronized: all requests in a batch share a single draft-verify schedule, even though the optimal draft length varies widely across requests and changes dynamically within each request. We propose ASPIRE, a non-synchronized batched self-speculative decoding framework built on three components. First, a unified mixed forward allows drafting and verifying requests to coexist in the same batched forward pass, removing the need for global draft-verify phases. Second, a lightweight online speculation scheduler uses per-request acceptance-rate estimates and a batch-aware cost model to let each request independently choose when to verify. Third, an intra-draft refresh layer performs full attention at a single designated layer during drafting, updating the sparse context at every draft step to reduce staleness during drafting. Across three models and five reasoning and long-context benchmarks, ASPIRE achieves $1.70$-$4.58\times$ speedup in decoding throughput over autoregressive baselines and improves average speedup by approximately $27\%$ over the strongest prior self-speculative baselines.

AI.tldr: ASPIRE is a non-synchronized batched self-speculative decoding framework that allows each request to independently schedule drafting and verification, improving decoding throughput over prior methods.
AI.motivation: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by attention computation, specifically repeated KV-cache reads that make decoding memory-bound. Existing batched self-speculative decoding methods force all requests in a batch to share the same draft-verify schedule, despite the fact that optimal draft length varies widely across requests and changes dynamically within each request.
AI.method: ASPIRE introduces three key components: 1) unified mixed forward that allows drafting and verifying requests to coexist in the same batched forward pass, eliminating global draft-verify phases; 2) lightweight online speculation scheduler that uses per-request acceptance-rate estimates and batch-aware cost modeling to let each request independently choose when to verify; 3) intra-draft refresh layer that performs full attention at a designated layer during drafting to update sparse context and reduce staleness.
AI.result: Across three models and five reasoning and long-context benchmarks, ASPIRE achieves 1.70-4.58× speedup in decoding throughput over autoregressive baselines and improves average speedup by approximately 27% over the strongest prior self-speculative baselines.
AI.conclusion: ASPIRE successfully addresses the synchronization bottleneck in batched self-speculative decoding by enabling per-request independent scheduling of drafting and verification, significantly improving decoding throughput efficiency for long-context LLM inference.

title: Designing Agentic AI Workflow Portfolios under Imperfect Selection and Compute Cost
summary: Agentic AI systems often approach the same task through multiple workflows that differ in reasoning strategy, verification structure, and compute cost. A natural deployment policy is to use the workflow with the highest average performance, but this can be suboptimal because different workflows may succeed on different instances. We study a portfolio-and-selector paradigm in which a firm runs multiple workflow executions and selects the final answer after observing their outputs. Additional executions may uncover correct answers that the best standalone workflow misses, but they consume compute and introduce plausible distractors that complicate final selection. We formulate this as a workflow portfolio problem in which the firm jointly chooses run size and allocation across workflow types. We summarize selector quality through an odds-lift index and derive sharp bounds on the value of workflow variety. For finite workflow pools, we develop exact formulations, linear programming relaxations, randomized rounding procedures, and computable performance certificates. For large implicit workflow classes, we derive a finite-dimensional dual and an ellipsoid method using a pricing oracle to identify workflows with high weighted accuracy net of recurring compute cost. Under a weak condition, the method obtains a near-optimal solution to the relaxation with polynomially many oracle calls.
