We evaluate the framework on three datasets: ABCD, Schema-Guided Dialogue, and HotpotQA. Relative to the best standalone workflow, portfolio optimization improves held-out selector accuracy by 3.1, 7.5, and 0.9 percentage points, respectively. Dual-guided workflow generation adds 3.5 points on ABCD and 24.1 on HotpotQA, with no additional gain on Schema-Guided Dialogue.

AI.tldr: Portfolio optimization of AI workflows improves task performance by running multiple workflows and selecting the best output, outperforming single best workflow approaches.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems use different workflows for the same task, but using only the best average workflow is suboptimal because workflows succeed on different instances. A portfolio approach could uncover correct answers that single workflows miss.
AI.method: Formulate workflow portfolio problem to jointly choose run size and allocation across workflow types. Develop exact formulations, linear programming relaxations, randomized rounding, and performance certificates for finite workflow pools. For large workflow classes, derive finite-dimensional dual and ellipsoid method with pricing oracle to identify high-performing workflows.
AI.result: Portfolio optimization improved held-out selector accuracy by 3.1 percentage points on ABCD, 7.5 on Schema-Guided Dialogue, and 0.9 on HotpotQA compared to best standalone workflow. Dual-guided workflow generation added 3.5 points on ABCD and 24.1 on HotpotQA.
AI.conclusion: Portfolio-and-selector paradigm with workflow optimization provides significant performance gains over single-workflow approaches, with theoretical guarantees and practical implementations that scale to large workflow classes.

title: Maximum Strong Independent Sets in Hypergraphs: Reductions, Bounds, and Greedy Certificates
summary: We study the maximum strong independent set problem in a finite hypergraph: find the largest vertex set that intersects every hyperedge in at most one vertex. This objective arises whenever each observed block is a local incompatibility constraint but transitive closure across overlapping blocks is not justified. A motivating example is multi-band LSH-MinHash deduplication, where each collision bucket gives local evidence, while connected-component contraction can impose spurious global equivalences. The paper develops an incidence-structural toolkit for this problem. We prove exact reductions for dominance, incidence twins, and weight-1 blocks; derive closed-form and low-weight upper bounds; introduce puncturing and covering certificates that sharpen those bounds; and analyze a layered greedy clustering algorithm driven by block weights and residual incidence. The algorithmic analysis includes feasibility, maximality, conditional optimality, a layered witness-matching upper bound, and incidence-local complexity bounds. The results give correctness, termination, fixed-point, and optimality certificates for broad incidence families, together with examples showing when different certificates separate or coincide.

AI.tldr: The paper develops mathematical and algorithmic tools for finding maximum strong independent sets in hypergraphs, with applications to deduplication problems where local evidence shouldn't be extended globally through transitive closure.
AI.motivation: The problem arises when dealing with local incompatibility constraints (like collision buckets in deduplication) where transitive closure across overlapping blocks creates spurious equivalences. The goal is to find largest vertex sets that intersect each hyperedge in at most one vertex, avoiding forced global connections.
AI.method: Develops incidence-structural toolkit with exact reductions (dominance, incidence twins, weight-1 blocks), closed-form upper bounds, puncturing/covering certificates, and a layered greedy clustering algorithm driven by block weights and residual incidence.
AI.result: Provides correctness, termination, fixed-point, and optimality certificates for broad incidence families. Includes feasibility, maximality, conditional optimality analyses, layered witness-matching upper bounds, and incidence-local complexity bounds.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a comprehensive theoretical framework for maximum strong independent set problems, showing when different certificates separate or coincide, with applications to practical deduplication scenarios where local evidence shouldn't be globally extended.

title: Symbolic Temporal Supervision of LLM Agents Using Contracts
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents augmented by tools can automate complex, multi-step tasks, such as web navigation, code generation, and workflow orchestration, by acting on external systems through tool calls. However, hallucinations, distributional instability, and adversarial manipulations in LLMs, and the irreversible consequences of certain tool calls can lead to harmful outcomes. Existing safeguards either grade recorded trajectories post hoc with stochastic LLM judges or block unsafe actions one call at a time, and no single deterministic artifact supports both roles. We present ContrAgent, a contract-based framework for symbolic temporal supervision of LLM agents. ContrAgent captures an agent's behavior as a sequence of tool calls and formalizes it as a trace over a fixed set of checkable predicates. It then specifies required behaviors using assume-guarantee contracts in linear temporal logic over finite traces (LTLf). Each contract is compiled to a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that serves two roles: gating agent actions online and evaluating recorded traces offline. A contract library, acting as a reusable knowledge base, is maintained independently of the agent's model and can be applied across different agents within the same task domain. We show the effectiveness of our approach on four benchmarks spanning both roles, where ContrAgent matches state-of-the-art LLM-judge and rule-based guardrail baselines while producing deterministic, reproducible verdicts and, in the online mode, orders-of-magnitude lower per-call latency.

AI.tldr: ContrAgent is a contract-based framework using symbolic temporal logic to supervise LLM agents, enabling both online action gating and offline trajectory evaluation with deterministic, low-latency safeguards.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent safeguards are inadequate - they either use stochastic LLM judges post-hoc or block unsafe actions one at a time, lacking deterministic artifacts that support both online and offline supervision roles while addressing hallucinations, instability, and irreversible consequences of tool calls.
AI.method: Formalizes agent behavior as traces over checkable predicates, specifies required behaviors using assume-guarantee contracts in linear temporal logic over finite traces (LTLf), compiles each contract to deterministic finite automaton (DFA) for dual roles, and maintains a reusable contract library independent of agent models.
AI.result: Matches state-of-the-art LLM-judge and rule-based guardrail baselines on four benchmarks while providing deterministic, reproducible verdicts and orders-of-magnitude lower per-call latency in online mode.
AI.conclusion: ContrAgent provides an effective symbolic temporal supervision framework that addresses the limitations of existing LLM agent safeguards through formal contracts, enabling deterministic, efficient, and reusable safety mechanisms across different agents in the same task domain.

title: QuanText: Protecting Dataset-Level Secrets in Textual Data Sharing
summary: Natural-language datasets support many downstream applications and research studies, but releasing text can reveal sensitive global properties of the underlying data source, such as the proportion of records associated with a particular gender, diagnosis, or political stance. Existing work has largely focused on property inference attacks that recover such global properties, while defenses for protecting these dataset-level secrets remain limited. Differential privacy, although effective for protecting individual records, provides only weak protection for aggregate properties. We propose Randomized Quantization for Text (QuanText), a training-free and large-language-model-agnostic data release mechanism that protects global secrets in textual datasets while preserving data utility. Given a dataset-level secret, such as the proportion of records with a particular diagnosis, and attributes whose utility should be preserved, such as topic and sentiment, QuanText perturbs both the secret distribution and the distributions of correlated attributes. It does so by constructing candidate release distributions over secret and non-secret attributes, randomly selecting a candidate sufficiently close to the private empirical distribution, and rewriting each private text sample to match the selected distribution using attribute-related snippets from the original text. QuanText is inspired by the Statistic Maximal Leakage (SML) framework, which bounds leakage about a secret function of a data distribution. Under idealized conditions, we show that QuanText satisfies an SML guarantee. Since these conditions may not hold exactly in practice, we also evaluate QuanText empirically on real-world datasets. Our results show that QuanText achieves a better empirical privacy-utility trade-off than competing data generation baselines.

AI.tldr: QuanText is a privacy-preserving text data release mechanism that protects dataset-level secrets (like demographic proportions) while maintaining utility for non-sensitive attributes, achieving better privacy-utility trade-offs than existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing privacy protections for text data focus on individual records through differential privacy, but provide weak protection for aggregate properties (dataset-level secrets) like gender proportions or political stance distributions. There's a need for mechanisms that specifically protect these global secrets while preserving data utility for downstream applications.
AI.method: QuanText is a training-free, LLM-agnostic method that: 1) Identifies dataset-level secrets and utility attributes, 2) Constructs candidate release distributions over both secret and correlated non-secret attributes, 3) Randomly selects a candidate distribution close to the private empirical distribution, 4) Rewrites each text sample using attribute-related snippets from the original text to match the selected distribution.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on real-world datasets shows QuanText achieves better privacy-utility trade-offs than competing data generation baselines. Under idealized conditions, the method satisfies a Statistic Maximal Leakage guarantee for bounding secret function leakage.
AI.conclusion: QuanText provides an effective solution for protecting dataset-level secrets in text data releases while maintaining utility, addressing a gap in existing privacy protections that focus primarily on individual record privacy rather than aggregate property protection.

title: Time-Aligned Evolving Concept Graphs for Scientific Relation Forecasting
summary: Forecasting scientific relations can guide discovery by identifying promising connections before they emerge. Existing approaches often model concept semantics and graph structure separately or summarize semantics over coarse historical snapshots, leaving semantic representations potentially misaligned with rapidly evolving graph evidence. We propose a time-aligned evolving concept graph framework that jointly models semantic and structural evolution. Its core idea is to treat dated papers as shared update events, reconstructing semantic and structural states from the same publication history through each prediction time. Pair-level fusion combines these states to forecast first co-occurrence, relation formation, and conditional relation type. Holding architecture and training fixed, refreshing context alongside graph updates improves mean relation AUPRC by 16.6% over frozen context. On a graph built from 187,848 papers with 270,687 concepts and 7.45 million co-occurrence links, the complete framework improves mean relation AUROC from 0.9290 for the strongest evaluated baseline to 0.9722, with mean population-weighted AUPRC 0.005778.

AI.tldr: Proposes a time-aligned evolving concept graph framework that jointly models semantic and structural evolution to forecast scientific relations by treating papers as shared update events.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches model concept semantics and graph structure separately or use coarse historical snapshots, leading to potential misalignment between semantic representations and rapidly evolving graph evidence.
AI.method: Time-aligned evolving concept graph framework reconstructs semantic and structural states from the same publication history through each prediction time. Uses pair-level fusion to combine these states for forecasting first co-occurrence, relation formation, and conditional relation type.
AI.result: Improves mean relation AUPRC by 16.6% over frozen context. On graph with 187,848 papers, 270,687 concepts, 7.45M co-occurrence links, improves mean relation AUROC from 0.9290 to 0.9722, with mean population-weighted AUPRC of 0.005778.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modeling semantic and structural evolution through time-aligned updates significantly improves forecasting of scientific relations by better aligning representations with evolving graph evidence.

title: The Attention Within: Consensus Dynamics in Selective State Space Models
summary:
Selective state space models (SSMs) have recently emerged as a compelling alternative to transformers, combining competitive performance with substantially improved inference efficiency. At each SSM layer, a sequence of hidden states are propagated by a recurrence, mixing information of different tokens. Despite using a different mechanism, this mixing plays a role analogous to attention in transformers. In fact, recent works have shown that the two architectures may be closer than they first appear, as this recurrence admits a formulation akin to linear attention. In transformers, attention is known to drive the tokens to cluster, i.e., to reach consensus, collapsing in the limit to a single direction. Thus, we ask: does the recurrence at the core of SSMs drive the tokens to consensus, as attention does in transformers?
  To answer this question, we take a dynamical systems perspective on SSMs, modeling the evolution of tokens across layers as an ordinary differential equation. By exploiting input-to-state stability arguments, we establish local exponential stability of the consensus equilibria and characterize their domain of attraction for time-varying weight matrices, a setting not addressed by previous results. We thereby show that the resemblance between SSMs and transformers does run deeper: the recurrence at the core of SSMs aggregates tokens just as attention does. Numerical experiments on a pretrained Mamba-2 model point to the output gate as the component that regulates the extent of this consensus, preventing the tokens from reaching it in full.

AI.tldr: SSMs drive tokens to consensus like attention in transformers, with output gates regulating this effect to prevent full collapse.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the recurrence mechanism in Selective State Space Models (SSMs) drives tokens to consensus similar to how attention causes tokens to cluster in transformers, given recent findings that SSMs and transformers may be more similar than they appear.
AI.method: Uses dynamical systems perspective to model token evolution across SSM layers as ordinary differential equations. Employs input-to-state stability arguments to establish local exponential stability of consensus equilibria and characterize their domain of attraction for time-varying weight matrices. Conducts numerical experiments on a pretrained Mamba-2 model.
AI.result: Shows that SSMs do drive tokens to consensus like attention in transformers. The output gate is identified as the component that regulates the extent of this consensus, preventing tokens from reaching full consensus in practice.
AI.conclusion: The resemblance between SSMs and transformers runs deeper than previously thought - both architectures aggregate tokens toward consensus, though SSMs regulate this effect through their output gates to maintain useful representations.

title: WFM: Wiki Foundation Model for Complex Agentic Reasoning
summary: Real-world agents fundamentally require persistent non-parametric knowledge for dynamic reasoning, i.e., long-term memory and retrieval-augmented generation. While graphs have shown reliable advantages in providing structured evidence, the sparse graph representations naturally restrict machine readability and semantic density required for complex agentic workflows. Driven by this limitation, the entire industry is witnessing a paradigm shift from traditional sparse graphs to LLM Wiki, an agent-native knowledge representation that couples dense document contexts with markdown files containing multi-layered topological linkages. However, parameterizing such rich semantics is challenging to encode dense textual contexts using traditional sparse graph embeddings. Moreover, learning LLM Wiki with existing graph encoders could overwhelm distributed system overheads that hinder deployment in large-scale commercial scenarios. To this end, we propose a novel paradigm Wiki Foundation Model, i.e., WFM, tailored for scalable, agent-native representation and retrieval. Specifically, (i) we formalize a Wiki Graph schema that seamlessly bridges fine-grained structures with dense contexts, maintaining explicit topologies alongside continuous semantics; (ii) A query-conditioned attentive aggregation is tailored for rich wiki message passing and explicit attention variance regularization; (iii) We engineer an infrastructural NCCL boundary exchange protocol that hoists static partition indices and leverages fixed-shape GPU-to-GPU collectives, bypassing CPU serialization and memory copy overheads. Extensive evaluations across five long-term agent memory and multi-hop reasoning benchmarks demonstrate the remarkable performance of WFM, while achieving a 10.5 times training acceleration on distributed clusters.

AI.tldr: WFM is a new foundation model for agent-native knowledge representation that combines dense document contexts with topological linkages in wiki-like structures, enabling scalable and efficient retrieval for dynamic reasoning.
AI.motivation: Traditional sparse graph representations restrict machine readability and semantic density needed for complex agentic workflows, while existing graph encoders struggle with the rich semantics of wiki-like structures and face scalability issues in distributed systems.
AI.method: Three main components: (1) Formalized Wiki Graph schema bridging fine-grained structures with dense contexts, (2) Query-conditioned attentive aggregation with attention variance regularization for wiki message passing, (3) Infrastructure-level NCCL boundary exchange protocol for efficient distributed training.
AI.result: WFM demonstrates remarkable performance across five long-term agent memory and multi-hop reasoning benchmarks while achieving 10.5× training acceleration on distributed clusters compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: WFM provides a scalable, agent-native solution for persistent non-parametric knowledge representation that effectively combines the structured advantages of graphs with the semantic density required for complex agentic workflows.

title: Structural Inference under Hidden Agents
summary: Recovering latent interaction structures from multi-agent dynamics is important for understanding and predicting interacting systems. Trajectory-based structural inference has achieved promising performance, but conventional formulations assume that the trajectories of all modeled agents are available. In practice, agents may become unobserved at deployment because of limited sensing, occlusion, or communication failure. Existing studies have considered unseen-node estimation, structural inference under partial observations, and missing-value imputation, yet the joint recovery of hidden-agent trajectories and their interactions remains underexplored. We formulate this problem as structural inference under hidden agents. Its key difficulty is a circular dependency: recovering interactions involving a hidden agent requires an estimate of its trajectory, while trajectory reconstruction can itself benefit from structural information. To address this challenge, we propose Structural Inference under Hidden Agents (SIHA), which combines structure-agnostic initialization with structure-guided iterative refinement. SIHA reconstructs hidden trajectories from visible observations, infers interactions using Neural Relational Inference, and feeds the estimated structure back into hidden-state reconstruction through multi-strength structural attention and iterative state--structure updates. Experiments on three benchmark dynamical systems demonstrate consistent improvements in visible-to-visible structural inference, while also showing benefits in hidden-state reconstruction and future prediction. Motion-capture experiments with simulated whole-limb occlusion further demonstrate its effectiveness in realistic hidden-agent settings.

AI.tldr: SIHA is a method that jointly recovers hidden-agent trajectories and their interaction structures from partially observable multi-agent systems by combining trajectory reconstruction with structural inference in an iterative refinement process.
AI.motivation: Current structural inference methods assume full observation of all agents, but in real-world scenarios agents may become unobserved due to sensing limitations, occlusion, or communication failures. The joint recovery of hidden-agent trajectories and their interactions remains underexplored despite its practical importance.
AI.method: SIHA uses a structure-agnostic initialization followed by structure-guided iterative refinement. It reconstructs hidden trajectories from visible observations, infers interactions using Neural Relational Inference, then feeds the estimated structure back into hidden-state reconstruction through multi-strength structural attention and iterative state-structure updates.
AI.result: Experiments on three benchmark dynamical systems show consistent improvements in visible-to-visible structural inference, while also demonstrating benefits in hidden-state reconstruction and future prediction. Motion-capture experiments with simulated whole-limb occlusion further validate effectiveness in realistic hidden-agent settings.
AI.conclusion: SIHA successfully addresses the circular dependency problem in structural inference with hidden agents through iterative refinement, enabling practical application in partially observable multi-agent systems and demonstrating improved performance across multiple metrics.

title: Re2A: Situated Conversational Recommendation via Rubric-based Preference Reasoning and Alignment
summary: Real-world recommendation scenarios are commonly grounded in shared physical environments during user-recommender interactions. This motivates situated conversational recommendation (SCR), a complex task requiring recommender assistants to jointly reason over dialogue history, co-observed scenes, and in-scene item attributes. However, current approaches struggle with this setting due to two intertwined challenges: accurately understanding situated user preferences throughout the conversation and generating responses that simultaneously satisfy user needs and grounded situations. To this end, we propose Re2A, a framework that formulates SCR as a structured reason-then-align process. We introduce rubric-based preference reasoning, which uses automated rubrics to guide the model toward producing explicit preference states. Based on these states, we propose a preference-conditioned optimization to align response generation with dual objectives: user preference satisfaction and situation consistency. Extensive experiments on two SCR datasets demonstrate that Re2A consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, delivering more precise, context-aware conversational recommendations. Our code is available at https://github.com/DongdingLin/Re2A.

AI.tldr: Re2A framework improves situated conversational recommendation by structuring it as a reason-then-align process with rubric-based preference reasoning and preference-conditioned optimization.
AI.motivation: Real-world recommendation scenarios often occur in shared physical environments, requiring systems to jointly reason over dialogue history, co-observed scenes, and in-scene item attributes. Current approaches struggle with accurately understanding situated user preferences throughout conversations and generating responses that satisfy both user needs and grounded situations.
AI.method: Propose Re2A framework that formulates Situated Conversational Recommendation (SCR) as a structured reason-then-align process. Introduces rubric-based preference reasoning using automated rubrics to guide the model toward producing explicit preference states, followed by preference-conditioned optimization to align response generation with dual objectives: user preference satisfaction and situation consistency.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on two SCR datasets demonstrate that Re2A consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, delivering more precise, context-aware conversational recommendations.
AI.conclusion: The Re2A framework effectively addresses the challenges in situated conversational recommendation by separating reasoning and alignment, resulting in superior performance for context-aware recommendation systems operating in physical environments.

title: Regional Explanations via Causal Sufficiency and Necessity
summary: Model explainability is essential for understanding and trusting machine learning models. Existing explainable AI methods often explain predictions through feature importance, counterfactual explanations, or rules. However, a region-level characterization of when and only when a prediction behavior arises remains less explored. This paper proposes Causal Sufficient and Necessary Regional Explanations (SNRE), a framework that learns an input region $A$ and output region $B$ such that membership in $A$ is both sufficient and necessary for the model output to fall in $B$. Motivated by the classical Probability of Necessity and Sufficiency (PNS), we formulate a region-level PNS measure through stochastic interventions and derive a differentiable finite-sample estimator for optimization. SNRE parameterizes the input-output region pair with explicit and interpretable algebraic region families, together with a learnable feature mask, balancing expressiveness and interpretability. Experiments demonstrate that SNRE learns region pairs with strong sufficiency-necessity performance, robust explanation behavior, and practical utility for model analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SNRE, a new explainable AI framework that learns input-output region pairs where input region membership is both sufficient and necessary for model output behavior, providing stronger causal explanations than feature importance alone.
AI.motivation: Current explainable AI methods (feature importance, counterfactuals, rules) lack region-level characterization of when and only when prediction behaviors arise. There's a need for explanations that establish both sufficiency and necessity conditions for model predictions.
AI.method: Proposes Causal Sufficient and Necessary Regional Explanations (SNRE) framework that learns input region A and output region B with sufficiency-necessity relationship. Formulates region-level Probability of Necessity and Sufficiency measure through stochastic interventions with differentiable finite-sample estimator. Parameterizes regions with interpretable algebraic families and learnable feature mask.
AI.result: Experiments show SNRE learns region pairs with strong sufficiency-necessity performance, robust explanation behavior, and practical utility for model analysis. The method balances expressiveness and interpretability.
AI.conclusion: SNRE provides a novel causal explanation framework that goes beyond existing methods by establishing both sufficient and necessary conditions for model predictions at the region level, offering more comprehensive model understanding and trust.

title: REPAIR: Resolving Long-Tail Confusion in Scientific Retrievers via Fact-Verified Iterative Refinement
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). 30 pages, 5 figures, 20 tables. Code: https://github.com/yerimoh/REPAIR
summary: Precise retrieval of scientific information is fundamentally constrained by long-tailed concepts and high fact-sensitivity of scientific corpora. These challenges often limit the effectiveness of dense retrievers and hallucination-prone LLM augmentation. To address this, we present REPAIR, a self-evolving data augmentation framework for scientific dense retrievers. REPAIR iteratively synthesizes training data to address knowledge gaps by cycling through diagnosis of long-tail concepts, API-guided evidence expansion, and differentiation via hard negative mining. This process effectively grounds retrieval in factual reality to resolve fine-grained distinctions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that REPAIR significantly outperforms 19 strong baselines on nine materials science and biomedical benchmarks. Our work highlights that diagnosing and factually augmenting data to long-tail deficits is essential for robust scientific retrieval.

AI.tldr: REPAIR is a self-evolving data augmentation framework that improves scientific dense retrieval by iteratively synthesizing training data to address long-tail knowledge gaps through diagnosis, evidence expansion, and hard negative mining.
AI.motivation: Scientific information retrieval is fundamentally constrained by long-tailed concepts and high fact-sensitivity of scientific corpora, which limit the effectiveness of dense retrievers and hallucination-prone LLM augmentation.
AI.method: REPAIR uses a self-evolving framework that cycles through: 1) diagnosis of long-tail concepts, 2) API-guided evidence expansion, and 3) differentiation via hard negative mining to iteratively synthesize training data addressing knowledge gaps.
AI.result: REPAIR significantly outperforms 19 strong baselines on nine materials science and biomedical benchmarks, demonstrating superior performance in scientific retrieval tasks.
AI.conclusion: Diagnosing and factually augmenting data to address long-tail deficits is essential for robust scientific retrieval, and REPAIR provides an effective framework for achieving this through self-evolving data augmentation.

title: Beyond Embedding Transfer: Component Roles in Grokking Transfer and Stability
summary: Warm-start transfer can make algorithmic tasks generalize rapidly, yet it is unclear which model components provide the gain and whether that gain remains stable under continued optimization. We study cross-operator transfer on modular arithmetic and separate efficacy (early velocity) from stability (post-reach drawdown). In a scale-matched 108-run battery across 12 seed blocks (96-run 2^3 factorial plus 12-run scale control), transferring internal attention/MLP weights (B) alongside token embeddings and readout (E+U) improves early accuracy by 5.46 pp (Holm p=0.0039) and cuts confirmation latency by 558 steps (Holm p=0.0088). While readout plus internal-block transfer satisfies the pre-specified +/-500-step latency equivalence criterion in 1-layer models (TOST p=0.0011, though Full is faster in 11/12 paired seeds), a prospective 2-layer replication confirms the internal-block advantage (12/12 seeds, +704.67 integral units, p=4.88x10^-4) while revealing an architectural boundary: omitting donor embeddings falls 4475.6 units below Full, outside the +/-250-unit margin. Continued target training frequently triggers severe post-grokking relapse. Freezing transferred representation carriers (E, U) nearly eliminates offline relapse (19.40% -> 0.07%, Holm p=0.005859). Online validation-triggered gating slashes True Max Drawdown from 22.06% to 0.60% on 2a+b (p=0.000488), with prospective confirmations extending protection across affine, nonlinear quadratic, and 2-layer targets (10.94-23.47 pp reductions), distinguishing continual stabilization from static early stopping. In non-abelian S_5, unshielded transfer surges transiently (95.4% peak), but a prospective shielding cohort yields no confirmed benefit (+0.15 +/- 1.14 pp). These results establish a component-level dissociation between transfer acceleration and trajectory stability, and expose the empirical boundaries of parameter shielding.

AI.tldr: Transferring internal attention/MLP weights with embeddings improves early learning but causes relapse; freezing representations prevents relapse, revealing separation between transfer acceleration and stability.
AI.motivation: While warm-start transfer helps generalization, it's unclear which model components contribute most to gains and whether those gains remain stable during continued optimization after transfer.
AI.method: Used cross-operator transfer on modular arithmetic tasks with 108-run factorial design across 12 seed blocks. Tested component-level transfers (embeddings, attention/MLP weights, readout) and measured both early velocity and post-reach stability. Used TOST tests for equivalence and prospective replications across architectures.
AI.result: Transferring internal attention/MLP weights with embeddings improved early accuracy by 5.46pp and reduced confirmation latency by 558 steps. However, continued training often caused severe relapse. Freezing transferred representations reduced relapse from 19.40% to 0.07%. Validation-triggered gating reduced drawdown from 22.06% to 0.60%. Non-abelian S_5 tasks showed only transient benefits without long-term gains.
AI.conclusion: There's a clear dissociation between transfer acceleration (benefits from internal components) and trajectory stability (requires representation freezing or gating). Parameter shielding has empirical boundaries, and effective transfer requires different strategies for initial speed versus long-term stability.

title: BENCHCOMPASS: From Scores to Signals for Training and Harness Decisions in Payment-Domain LLMs
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
summary: Payment operations are a critical financial infrastructure, but the value of large language models in this domain remains unclear because payment rules change quickly, evidence is fragmented, and decisions depend on transaction state, participant role, region, and payment rail. Existing benchmarks do not isolate whether failures come from missing payment-rule knowledge, poor use of supplied evidence, or brittleness under imperfect harness inputs. We introduce BENCHCOMPASS, a payment-domain benchmark whose construction pipeline builds scenario-grounded tasks from typed evidence packs, applies LLM-based quality checks, creates task-input attack variants, and reserves final item admission for domain experts. The release contains an expert-reviewed Pro benchmark covering payment knowledge, context-grounded scenario reasoning, and Attacked Open robustness, plus a lower-assurance Normal pool for inspection and future curation. Across 16 model variants, BENCHCOMPASS shows qualitatively different failure modes: missing parametric payment knowledge, incomplete reasoning over supplied rules, and failure to reject plausible but invalid workflows. The benchmark remains unsaturated: the best frontier model reaches 89.6% on Open Context-Grounded Reasoning and 81.7% under attacked inputs, while a representative 32B open-weight model reaches 69.8% and 42.6%. Benchmark data and code are available at https://github.com/ant-intl/BenchCompass.

AI.tldr: BENCHCOMPASS is a new payment-domain benchmark that isolates specific failure modes in LLMs for payment operations by creating scenario-grounded tasks with typed evidence packs, quality checks, and expert review.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks fail to isolate why LLMs fail in payment operations - whether due to missing payment-rule knowledge, poor use of supplied evidence, or brittleness under imperfect inputs. Payment operations are critical infrastructure with rapidly changing rules, fragmented evidence, and complex dependencies on transaction state, participant roles, regions, and payment rails.
AI.method: Created a benchmark construction pipeline that: 1) builds scenario-grounded tasks from typed evidence packs, 2) applies LLM-based quality checks, 3) creates task-input attack variants to test robustness, and 4) reserves final item admission for domain experts. Includes an expert-reviewed Pro benchmark and a Normal pool for inspection.
AI.result: Across 16 model variants, BENCHCOMPASS revealed three distinct failure modes: missing parametric payment knowledge, incomplete reasoning over supplied rules, and failure to reject plausible but invalid workflows. Benchmark remains unsaturated - best frontier model achieves 89.6% on Open Context-Grounded Reasoning and 81.7% under attacked inputs, while a 32B open-weight model achieves 69.8% and 42.6% respectively.
AI.conclusion: BENCHCOMPASS successfully isolates specific LLM failure modes in payment operations and shows current models still have significant room for improvement, with the benchmark remaining unsaturated. The benchmark enables better evaluation of LLMs for critical payment infrastructure applications.

title: FedPGT: Progressive Gradient Transmission for Vehicular Federated Learning over Time-Varying Channels
summary: Vehicular federated learning (VFL) enables privacy-preserving collaborative model training for intelligent transportation systems, where communication resource allocation and gradient sparsification techniques have been explored to reduce communication overhead. However, vehicle mobility leads to rapidly varying channel conditions and transmission capacity, rendering predetermined resource allocation and sparsification decisions ineffective. In this paper, we propose FedPGT, a progressive gradient transmission scheme for VFL over time-varying channels, where vehicles progressively transmit high-magnitude gradient entries in response to instantaneous channel conditions. We establish a convergence bound that characterizes the impact of transmitted gradient entries and reveals diminishing-return behavior governed by a power-law decay. Motivated by this result, we formulate a stochastic optimization problem for online decision-making, where the main challenge lies in a cumulatively coupled, non-separable objective. To handle this challenge, we introduce per-slot surrogate transmission variables to decouple the long-term dependence across time slots and convert the original objective into an additive per-slot optimization problem, enabling a Lyapunov drift-plus-penalty approach for online scheduling. We further develop a low-complexity resource allocation algorithm for efficient online implementation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves a 3.65% accuracy improvement on the CIFAR-10 image classification task and a 12.66% reduction in average displacement error on the Argoverse trajectory prediction task compared with state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating its applicability to diverse learning tasks under highly dynamic vehicular environments.

AI.tldr: FedPGT is a progressive gradient transmission scheme for vehicular federated learning that dynamically transmits high-magnitude gradients based on instantaneous channel conditions, achieving better performance than existing methods under highly mobile vehicular environments.
AI.motivation: Traditional communication resource allocation and gradient sparsification techniques for VFL become ineffective due to vehicle mobility causing rapidly varying channel conditions and transmission capacity, requiring adaptive solutions.
AI.method: FedPGT employs progressive gradient transmission where vehicles transmit high-magnitude gradient entries progressively based on instantaneous channel conditions. It uses per-slot surrogate variables to decouple long-term dependencies, enabling Lyapunov drift-plus-penalty approach for online scheduling with low-complexity resource allocation.
AI.result: Experimental results show 3.65% accuracy improvement on CIFAR-10 classification and 12.66% reduction in average displacement error on Argoverse trajectory prediction compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: FedPGT effectively addresses the challenges of time-varying channels in VFL through adaptive progressive gradient transmission, demonstrating superior performance across diverse learning tasks in dynamic vehicular environments.

title: Who Audits Whom, on What Substrate, with What Evidence? An Independence-Graded Audit Protocol for Agentic AI
summary: Agentic AI systems plan, invoke tools and act with limited supervision; they are now both the subject of audits and, increasingly, the auditor. Independence, the foundation of assurance,is still applied to them as a binary. We argue that it must be graded along three orthogonal axes: principal independence (who controls the auditor), substrate independence (an auditor sharing the auditee's foundation-model family, toolchain or guardrails fails with it) and evidence independence (whether evidence is attestable rather than self-reported). Each axis has precedent; the contribution is to grade all three on a single audit, aggregate them by the weakest link, and apply the same rubric when the auditor is itself an agent. We give the model a formal basis by transplanting the beta-factor model of common-cause failure from reliability engineering, a seven-step protocol whose outputs a third party can verify, a structural detectability analysis of a procurement-controls agent audited at three grades, and a Monte Carlo study of the model in which a conventional internal audit of an agent-a real audit team, a second agent, provider logsp-surfaces 5.9% of the faults it could in principle see and none at all in half the fault classes. We map the triple to the EU AI Act as amended, ISO/IEC 42006, UK public-sector risk-management guidance and audit-regulator practice.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework for grading AI auditor independence across three axes (principal, substrate, evidence) and applies reliability engineering models to show that conventional audits miss most faults in AI systems.
AI.motivation: Current approaches treat AI auditor independence as binary, but as AI agents increasingly audit other AI systems, a more nuanced graded approach is needed to properly assess assurance quality and identify limitations in conventional audit methods.
AI.method: Proposes grading independence along three orthogonal axes (principal, substrate, evidence), transplants beta-factor model from reliability engineering, develops a 7-step verifiable protocol, conducts structural detectability analysis of procurement-controls agent audits, and performs Monte Carlo simulation comparing conventional vs. graded approaches.
AI.result: Conventional internal audits of AI agents surface only 5.9% of potentially detectable faults and miss entire fault classes in half the cases, demonstrating the inadequacy of binary independence assessments compared to the proposed graded framework.
AI.conclusion: AI auditor independence must be graded across three axes rather than treated as binary, with weakest-link aggregation; this framework is applicable when auditors themselves are AI agents and aligns with emerging regulatory standards like the EU AI Act and ISO/IEC 42006.

title: Agora: Git as Shared Memory for Collective AutoResearch
summary: Autonomous research loops such as AutoResearch show that one coding agent can improve a training setup unattended. Run several of them and each session starts from scratch, so more agents tend to mean more duplicated search rather than more discovery. Agora is a shared memory for such agents: research is recorded as an append-only directed acyclic graph (DAG) stored in Git, so that every claim is a commit anyone can check out and rerun. Each result, insight, hypothesis, verification, and report is an immutable commit whose parent edges say what it builds on; a derived index exposes the frontier, the neglected branches, and the verification status of each claim, and a diversity-aware selection rule keeps the community from collapsing onto one leader. We describe the system and report its first sustained use: a run of nearly 12 days in which 13 language-model workers, with no assigned tasks and no central planner, worked on a weight-transfer problem. Given 141 pretrained donor models and a frozen 119.6M-parameter attention-SSM hybrid whose dimensions match no donor, the workers had to initialize the target without training data or gradient updates. They published 1,703 contributions and drove the evaluator from 3.39 to 1.899 bits per byte, closing 62% of the gap to a trained GPT-2 124M. The winning recipe compresses donor next-token statistics into the target's embedding and output head, then adds a short-range context signal through sparse edits to attention, feed-forward, and state-space blocks. Its 145-commit ancestry spans 15 accounts, and 165 independent reproductions were posted, none of which failed. We describe the single mid-run human intervention that pulled the community out of a monoculture, what the trace does and does not establish, and the controlled comparison that would settle whether shared research state improves discovery per unit of compute.

AI.tldr: Agora: A shared memory system for AI research agents using Git-based DAGs to prevent duplicate work and promote collaborative discovery across multiple autonomous agents.
AI.motivation: Current autonomous research systems like AutoResearch have agents working independently from scratch, leading to duplicated effort rather than collaborative discovery. There's a need for shared research state to prevent redundant work and enable collective progress.
AI.method: Agora uses Git-based append-only directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) where each research contribution is an immutable commit with parent edges showing dependencies. Features include derived index for frontier tracking, diversity-aware selection to prevent monoculture, and enabling independent verification through checkable commits.
AI.result: In a 12-day experiment with 13 language-model agents, they improved a weight-transfer problem from 3.39 to 1.899 bits per byte (closing 62% of gap to trained GPT-2). Produced 1,703 contributions, winning solution spanned 145 commits across 15 accounts, with 165 independent reproductions (none failed). Diversity intervention rescued system from monoculture.
AI.conclusion: Shared research state through Agora enables collaborative discovery without duplication, demonstrated by autonomous agents collectively solving complex problems with reproducible results. System prevents monoculture through diversity mechanisms and enables verification through immutable commits.

title: Building Trust in Artificial Intelligence: A Necessity for Railway Applications
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is currently only applied to non-safety critical applications due to the strict standards and regulations for railway industries. We propose to review the three main fields necessary to increase trust in data science and AI algorithms and reach compliance: robustness, Operational Design Domain (ODD), and explainability. Robustness is the ability of an AI system to maintain its level of performance under any circumstances (ISO24029). ODDs allow the explicit definition of operating conditions under which a system is intended to operate, according to the recently published DIN DKE SPEC 99004. Explainability is the property of an AI system to express important factors influencing the AI system results in a way that humans can understand. Those 3 domains of research are already well investigated by nonrailway actors, with algorithms and methods ready to use for railway applications. A system view is necessary to ensure all trustworthy requirements interact continuously in a safe MLOps environment thereby fostering acceptance from regulators, operators and the public. Beyond safeguarding safety-critical applications, we aim to show that fostering deep trust in AI, as now required by regulatory frameworks worldwide, will unlock its full potential and transform the pace of adoption across mission-critical domains.

AI.tldr: Three key AI trust domains - robustness, Operational Design Domain (ODD), and explainability - need to be addressed for railway safety-critical applications to meet industry standards and unlock AI's full potential.
AI.motivation: AI is currently restricted to non-safety critical railway applications due to strict industry standards and regulations. There's a need to build trust in AI algorithms to achieve compliance and enable their use in safety-critical railway systems.
AI.method: Proposes reviewing three established research domains: robustness (AI performance stability under all circumstances per ISO24029), ODD (explicit definition of operating conditions per DIN DKE SPEC 99004), and explainability (human-understandable expression of factors influencing AI results). These domains are well-investigated outside railways with ready-to-use algorithms.
AI.result: A system view integrating all three trust domains in a safe MLOps environment is necessary to ensure continuous interaction of trustworthy requirements, fostering acceptance from regulators, operators, and the public.
AI.conclusion: Building deep trust in AI through addressing robustness, ODD, and explainability will not only enable safety-critical railway applications but also unlock AI's full potential and accelerate adoption across mission-critical domains worldwide.

title: iMINDBench: iEEG Multi-Institution Neural Decoding Benchmark
summary: Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) is widely used to record electrical activity directly from electrodes inside the human brain, making it an attractive modality for neural decoding. However, progress in iEEG decoding, especially toward general-purpose foundation models, remains difficult to measure reliably: datasets are task- or institution-specific, limiting evidence of generalization across tasks and recording environments, and preprocessing choices can strongly influence performance, making model improvements difficult to distinguish from preprocessing gains. Thus, we introduce iMINDBench, an iEEG Multi-Institution Neural Decoding Benchmark that evaluates models on a shared suite of fifteen decoding tasks across three naturalistic movie-watching datasets. The benchmark additionally defines standardized preprocessing tracks and fixed evaluation splits to support consistent model comparisons. Using iMINDBench, we find that the evaluated pretrained systems generally outperform baselines within their respective preprocessing tracks, while strong spectral baselines remain competitive across institutional datasets. In our scaling study, adding up to 25 times more supervised data from other subjects or institutions yields only small or task-dependent gains over within-session training. Together, these findings highlight the need for iEEG models that improve on strong preprocessing baselines and make more effective use of data across subjects and institutions. Project website: https://imindbench.github.io/

AI.tldr: iMINDBench is a standardized benchmark for iEEG decoding models that evaluates performance across 15 tasks from 3 movie-watching datasets, with fixed preprocessing tracks and evaluation splits to enable reliable model comparison.
AI.motivation: Current iEEG decoding research faces challenges in measuring progress reliably due to: 1) task- or institution-specific datasets that limit evidence of generalization across different tasks and recording environments, and 2) preprocessing choices that strongly influence performance, making it difficult to distinguish genuine model improvements from preprocessing gains.
AI.method: The authors introduce iMINDBench, which includes: 1) 15 decoding tasks across three naturalistic movie-watching iEEG datasets, 2) standardized preprocessing tracks with fixed evaluation splits, 3) systematic evaluation of existing pretrained systems against baselines, and 4) a scaling study examining the effect of adding supervised data from other subjects or institutions (up to 25x more data).
AI.result: 1) Pretrained systems generally outperform baselines within their respective preprocessing tracks. 2) Strong spectral baselines remain competitive across institutional datasets. 3) Adding up to 25 times more supervised data from other subjects or institutions yields only small or task-dependent gains over within-session training.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark reveals that current iEEG models need to: 1) demonstrate improvements beyond strong preprocessing baselines, and 2) make more effective use of data across subjects and institutions. The findings highlight the need for better general-purpose foundation models for iEEG decoding.

title: FoundAna: A GNN-assisted Foundation Model for Graph Anomaly Detection
summary: Graph anomaly detection aims to identify graph structures (e.g., nodes, edges, or subgraphs) that deviate significantly from expected patterns, which supports critical applications in fraud detection, spam identification, network intrusion, etc. Despite the growing methods in the field, existing approaches follow a one-model-per-dataset paradigm, limiting their transferability across diverse real-world scenarios due to task heterogeneity, label scarcity, and domain variability. In this work, we introduce FoundAna, a GNN-assisted Foundation Model for Graph Anomaly Detection - the first foundation model framework designated for generalizable, cross-graph anomaly detection by combining GNNs and transformers. FoundAna integrates an anomaly detection-specific GNN component with a standard transformer encoder augmented by four complementary positional encodings, which enable the model to capture both local and global structural information. Specifically, the positional encoding enriched node representations are passed through attribute and adjacency decoders, and the reconstruction errors serve as the anomaly score. Extensive experiments on nine benchmark datasets spanning financial, social, and citation network domains demonstrate that FoundAna consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The code implementation and Supplementary materials are here: https://github.com/FoundAna331/FoundAna.

AI.tldr: FoundAna is the first foundation model framework for graph anomaly detection that combines GNNs and transformers to achieve cross-graph generalization across diverse domains.
AI.motivation: Existing graph anomaly detection methods follow a one-model-per-dataset paradigm, limiting transferability due to task heterogeneity, label scarcity, and domain variability across different real-world scenarios.
AI.method: FoundAna integrates an anomaly detection-specific GNN component with a standard transformer encoder augmented by four complementary positional encodings to capture both local and global structural information. Positional encoding enriched node representations are passed through attribute and adjacency decoders, and reconstruction errors serve as anomaly scores.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on nine benchmark datasets spanning financial, social, and citation network domains demonstrate that FoundAna consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: FoundAna represents a significant advancement in graph anomaly detection by providing a generalizable foundation model that overcomes the limitations of single-dataset approaches and enables effective cross-domain anomaly detection.

title: What Counts as Strategic Reasoning? A Systematic Mapping of Chess Research on Humans, Engines, and Language Models
comment: Under review; replication package available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22695754
summary:
Chess has long served as a model domain for studying search, expertise, decision-making, and artificial intelligence. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has renewed the relevance of chess as a controlled environment for investigating strategic reasoning and comparing human and artificial decision-making. We present a systematic mapping study of recent research spanning human players, classical chess engines, neural and reinforcement-learning systems, LLMs, and hybrid approaches. The final map comprises 84 core study families, classified according to agent type, strategic-reasoning stages, and evaluation dimensions.
  The map reveals a literature strongly concentrated on situation assessment, evaluation, and action selection, while explicit planning, explanation, metacognition, and human--AI collaboration remain less explored. LLM research places particular emphasis on state representation and generalization, whereas grounded explanation appears more frequently in hybrid approaches combining language models with engines, expert knowledge, or other external structures. Two distinctions emerge that the map aggregates rather than resolves: hybrid systems differ in where and when heterogeneous capabilities combine, and evaluations that show improved human performance do not thereby establish human--AI synergy. We propose both as extensions of the mapping framework.
  We argue that chess provides a useful bridge between cognitive and computational perspectives on strategic reasoning, and identify explicit planning, grounded and faithful explanation, metacognitive calibration, and human--AI complementarity as directions for future research.

AI.tldr: Systematic mapping study of chess research across human players, classical engines, neural systems, LLMs, and hybrid approaches reveals concentration on situation assessment/evaluation/action selection, with gaps in planning, explanation, metacognition, and human-AI collaboration.
AI.motivation: Chess serves as a model domain for studying search, expertise, decision-making, and AI. The emergence of LLMs renewed chess's relevance as a controlled environment for investigating strategic reasoning and comparing human vs. artificial decision-making.
AI.method: Conducted a systematic mapping study of recent research covering human players, classical chess engines, neural/reinforcement-learning systems, LLMs, and hybrid approaches. Analyzed 84 core study families classified by agent type, strategic-reasoning stages, and evaluation dimensions.
AI.result: The map shows literature strongly concentrated on situation assessment, evaluation, and action selection, while explicit planning, explanation, metacognition, and human-AI collaboration remain less explored. LLM research emphasizes state representation and generalization; grounded explanation appears more in hybrid approaches. Key distinctions: hybrid systems differ in where/when heterogeneous capabilities combine, and evaluations showing improved human performance don't necessarily establish human-AI synergy.
AI.conclusion: Chess provides a useful bridge between cognitive and computational perspectives on strategic reasoning. Future research should focus on explicit planning, grounded and faithful explanation, metacognitive calibration, and human-AI complementarity. The mapping framework can be extended to better capture hybrid system architectures and human-AI synergy evaluations.

title: Learning Fractional-Order Dynamics from a Single Trajectory
summary: Many real-world processes exhibit long-range dependence, where the current state depends on a slowly decaying trace of past states rather than on the most recent state alone. This paper studies system identification for discrete-time fractional-order linear time-invariant systems from a single observed trajectory of length $t$, a setting that captures such non-Markovian dynamics through the Grünwald--Letnikov difference operator. Unlike Markovian systems, fractional-order systems couple estimation across the entire history, making both statistical analysis and practical identification more challenging. We propose \emph{Fractional-Order Ordinary-Least-Squares Grid-Search (FO-GS)}, a simple two-stage estimator that exploits the diagonal structure of the fractional-difference operator to decouple the identification problem row-wise. Under the stability assumption, we establish high-probability, non-asymptotic error bounds for estimating both the fractional order and the system matrix in the heterogeneous setting, with both estimation errors scaling as \(\mathcal{O}(t^{-1/2})\). Through experiments, we show that \emph{FO-GS} outperforms existing baselines in recovering both the fractional order and the underlying system dynamics.

AI.tldr: A simple two-stage estimator (FO-GS) for identifying discrete-time fractional-order linear systems achieves optimal 1/√t estimation rates for both fractional order and system matrix, outperforming existing methods.
AI.motivation: Many real-world processes exhibit long-range dependence/non-Markovian dynamics where current state depends on slowly decaying past states, not just recent ones. Fractional-order systems capture this but make identification challenging due to coupling across entire history.
AI.method: Proposes Fractional-Order Ordinary-Least-Squares Grid-Search (FO-GS), a two-stage estimator exploiting diagonal structure of fractional-difference operator to decouple identification row-wise. First estimates fractional order, then system matrix.
AI.result: Under stability assumptions, establishes high-probability non-asymptotic error bounds with both fractional order and system matrix estimation errors scaling as O(1/√t). Experimental results show FO-GS outperforms existing baselines in recovering both parameters.
AI.conclusion: FO-GS provides an effective, theoretically-grounded approach to fractional-order system identification with optimal convergence rates, addressing the challenges of non-Markovian dynamics estimation.

title: Visual Compliance via Executable Safety Rule Entailment
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026. 36 pages, 20 figures, 24 tables
summary: Recent advances in LLMs and VLMs have enabled safety systems to reason beyond simple risk patterns toward more contextual and semantic safety concerns. However, as risk patterns continue to evolve and safety rules become more complex, existing training-based end-to-end safeguards face persistent challenges in adaptability and explainable reasoning over complex safety rules. To address these challenges, we propose GuardEn (Guarding by Safety Rule Entailment), an executable safeguard framework that decomposes safety policies into atomic propositions through Safety-Rule Compilation, modeling their composition as executable code. At test time, Scene-Grounded Execution instantiates these atomic propositions with contextual visual information derived from scene graphs, enabling rule-grounded and interpretable safety reasoning. Experiments on SafetyVisionBench demonstrate the effectiveness of programmable safeguard for complex visual safety assessment, achieving an average improvement of 9.8 F1 points over the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: GuardEn is an executable safeguard framework that decomposes complex safety policies into atomic propositions and uses scene-grounded execution for interpretable safety reasoning in visual contexts, significantly outperforming existing baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing training-based end-to-end safety systems struggle with adaptability and explainable reasoning over evolving complex safety rules, especially as risk patterns become more sophisticated and context-dependent in vision-language models.
AI.method: Proposes GuardEn with two main components: 1) Safety-Rule Compilation that decomposes safety policies into atomic propositions modeled as executable code, and 2) Scene-Grounded Execution that instantiates these propositions with contextual visual information from scene graphs for rule-grounded safety reasoning.
AI.result: Experiments on SafetyVisionBench show GuardEn achieves an average improvement of 9.8 F1 points over the strongest baseline, demonstrating effectiveness for complex visual safety assessment through programmable safeguards.
AI.conclusion: GuardEn provides an executable, interpretable framework for safety reasoning that addresses adaptability and explainability limitations of existing end-to-end approaches, enabling better handling of complex, evolving safety rules in visual contexts.

title: Colla-Q: Toward Collaborative Experts in MoE Quantization via Minimax Precision Balancing
comment: Accepted by the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP) 2026
summary: In this paper, we present a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) quantization method based on activation entropy. Although quantization reduces memory and computational costs, it can substantially degrade performance. In particular, performance decline is pronounced in quantized MoE models, where individual experts have a small number of parameters that are sensitive to low-bit representation. Considering that MoE operates as an ensemble model with collaborative contributions from routed experts, a significant performance decline of a particular expert due to quantization can harm model performance. Therefore, we propose Colla-Q, a bit-allocation framework to maintain balanced performance across experts through an activation-entropy-based bit-width allocation algorithm. This approach encourages each expert to operate collaboratively in the quantized model, thereby 1) improving the overall MoE performance and 2) reducing the dependence on the calibration dataset. Since uniformly adjusting each expert's performance facilitates robustness and stability of the MoE model, the proposed MoE quantization method can generalize more consistently across different calibration datasets. Our code is available at: https://github.com/mmai-laboratory/Colla_Q

AI.tldr: Colla-Q: A Mixture-of-Experts quantization method that uses activation-entropy-based bit-width allocation to maintain balanced performance across experts, improving overall MoE performance while reducing calibration dataset dependence.
AI.motivation: Quantization reduces memory/computational costs but degrades performance, especially in MoE models where individual experts have few parameters sensitive to low-bit representation. Performance decline in any single expert can harm overall MoE performance since it operates as an ensemble with collaborative contributions from routed experts.
AI.method: Proposes Colla-Q, a bit-allocation framework using an activation-entropy-based bit-width allocation algorithm. This approach maintains balanced performance across experts in the quantized model by allocating different bit-widths based on each expert's activation entropy rather than uniform quantization.
AI.result: The method improves overall MoE performance and reduces dependence on calibration datasets. By ensuring uniform performance across experts, it enhances the quantized model's robustness and stability, leading to more consistent generalization across different calibration datasets.
AI.conclusion: Colla-Q successfully addresses the MoE quantization challenge by proposing an entropy-based bit-allocation strategy that maintains expert collaboration in quantized models, achieving better performance with less calibration data dependency while improving generalization consistency.

title: Faithful yet Collusive: Why Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Cannot Detect Collusion in LLM Pricing Agents under Oligopolistic Competition
comment: 20 pages, Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: Large language models (LLM) deployed as autonomous pricing agents may sustain supracompetitive prices through tacit coordination. We develop a causal graph divergence framework that separately measures structural faithfulness and intent faithfulness of LLM pricing agents in Bertrand competition. Across nine LLMs under duopoly and triopoly conditions, collusive behavior and chain-of-thought (CoT) faithfulness dissociate along both dimensions: the most collusive model accurately reports cooperative intent yet reasons structurally unfaithfully, while the most structurally faithful model sustains supra-Nash pricing under both market structures. These findings establish that CoT monitoring alone cannot serve as a standalone safeguard against algorithmic collusion.

AI.tldr: LLM pricing agents can achieve supracompetitive prices through tacit coordination, and Chain-of-Thought monitoring alone doesn't prevent algorithmic collusion.
AI.motivation: Large language models deployed as autonomous pricing agents may sustain supracompetitive prices through tacit coordination, raising concerns about algorithmic collusion in markets.
AI.method: Developed a causal graph divergence framework to separately measure structural faithfulness and intent faithfulness of LLM pricing agents in Bertrand competition, tested across nine LLMs under duopoly and triopoly conditions.
AI.result: Found dissociation between collusive behavior and chain-of-thought faithfulness: the most collusive model accurately reports cooperative intent but reasons structurally unfaithfully, while the most structurally faithful model sustains supra-Nash pricing in both market structures.
AI.conclusion: Chain-of-thought monitoring alone cannot serve as a standalone safeguard against algorithmic collusion by LLM pricing agents.

title: Rethinking How We Evaluate Methodological Progress in Health AI
summary: Methodological progress in artificial intelligence (AI) for electronic health records (EHRs) depends on our ability to determine which algorithms work better, and under which conditions. However, such progress is thought to be hindered by difficulties in reproducibility and in defining clinically meaningful evaluation tasks. We empirically study these barriers by re-implementing 12 historical and recent algorithms within a shared evaluation framework and evaluating them on two clinical datasets, MIMIC-IV and NWICU. We compare two complementary task families: expert-authored clinically meaningful tasks and generated tasks defined from randomly sampled event codes and prediction horizons. We ask whether relative algorithms comparisons transfer across task families and datasets, whether residual task heterogeneity contains useful methodological structure, and what a controlled comparison reveals about progress over the last decade. We find that aggregate pairwise comparisons transfer strongly across evaluation settings, including from randomly generated tasks to clinically meaningful tasks and across datasets. At the same time, clinically meaningful tasks exhibit greater task-method interaction, providing preliminary evidence that task properties can help explain when particular modeling choices are advantageous. Finally, newer algorithms do not consistently outperform earlier approaches: gradient-boosted trees remain highly competitive when paired with a modern, wide and sparse representation of the EHR. Together, these results suggest that useful methodological knowledge may require less task engineering than commonly assumed, while highlighting the importance of understanding the structured heterogeneity that remains across tasks and methods.

AI.tldr: A systematic evaluation of 12 AI algorithms for EHR data finds that relative algorithm performance transfers well across different task types (clinical vs. random) and datasets, with gradient-boosted trees remaining competitive with newer methods when using modern representations.
AI.motivation: Methodological progress in AI for EHRs is hindered by reproducibility issues and difficulty defining clinically meaningful evaluation tasks, making it hard to determine which algorithms work better under which conditions.
AI.method: Re-implemented 12 historical and recent algorithms within a shared evaluation framework, evaluated on two clinical datasets (MIMIC-IV and NWICU), comparing two task families: expert-authored clinically meaningful tasks and randomly generated tasks from event codes and prediction horizons.
AI.result: Aggregate pairwise algorithm comparisons transfer strongly across evaluation settings (including from random to clinical tasks and across datasets). Clinically meaningful tasks show greater task-method interaction, revealing when specific modeling choices are advantageous. Newer algorithms don't consistently outperform older approaches - gradient-boosted trees remain competitive with modern EHR representations.
AI.conclusion: Useful methodological knowledge may require less task engineering than commonly assumed, but understanding the structured heterogeneity across tasks and methods remains important for advancing AI in EHR applications.

title: Market Signal Injection: Adversarial Context Manipulation of LLM Pricing Agents
comment: 30 pages, Accepted to FinNLP 2026 Workshop @ EMNLP 2026
summary: Large language model (LLM) pricing agents may respond to how market data is presented, even when its numerical values remain unchanged. We introduce market signal injection (MSI), an attack that manipulates numerical formatting, competitor ordering, or qualitative market commentary without issuing explicit instructions. We evaluate nine open-weight models in simulated Bertrand duopoly and triopoly markets and three proprietary models in duopoly markets. Sentiment-based attacks produce the largest behavioral shifts, which propagate to other firms and alter profits and consumer surplus. Susceptibility varies across model families, and larger models are not consistently more robust. Matched neutral-text controls and a rule-based agent support a framing-based account of these shifts under the fixed demand parameters of our simulation. Episode-held-out probes distinguish baseline from attacked activations in all eleven re-evaluated model--condition pairs: linear AUC is 1.00 and MLP AUC ranges from 0.93 to 0.99. This separability does not by itself identify harmful pricing decisions. Input canonicalization removes the tested sentiment attacks, while decision boundary anchoring, which combines prompt constraints with output projection, provides partial mitigation under the tested adaptive attacks. These results identify data presentation as an attack surface for LLM pricing agents and motivate defenses that account for interactions among agents.

AI.tldr: Market signal injection (MSI) attacks manipulate how market data is presented (formatting, ordering, commentary) to influence LLM pricing agents without changing numerical values, causing significant behavioral shifts that affect profits and consumer surplus.
AI.motivation: LLM pricing agents may be vulnerable to how market data is presented, not just the numerical values. This creates a new attack surface where subtle manipulations of data formatting and presentation could influence pricing decisions without explicit malicious instructions.
AI.method: The researchers introduced market signal injection (MSI) attacks that manipulate numerical formatting, competitor ordering, or qualitative market commentary. They evaluated nine open-weight models in simulated Bertrand duopoly/triopoly markets and three proprietary models in duopolies. Used matched neutral-text controls, rule-based agents, episode-held-out probes for activation analysis, and tested defenses like input canonicalization and decision boundary anchoring.
AI.result: Sentiment-based attacks produced the largest behavioral shifts that propagated to other firms, altering profits and consumer surplus. Susceptibility varied across model families, with larger models not consistently more robust. Linear AUC for distinguishing attacked vs baseline activations was 1.00, MLP AUC ranged 0.93-0.99. Input canonicalization removed tested sentiment attacks, while decision boundary anchoring provided partial mitigation.
AI.conclusion: Data presentation represents a novel attack surface for LLM pricing agents, motivating defenses that account for agent interactions. The research demonstrates that formatting manipulations can significantly influence LLM behavior even when numerical data remains unchanged, highlighting security vulnerabilities in automated pricing systems.

title: Reaching Every Position Without Searching: Rotating Sparse Wiring on the Hypercube as a Substitute for Attention
summary: Attention pays, at every layer and for every input, the cost of searching for whom to connect. We ask how far one can get with wiring that is fixed, sparse, and simply rotated from layer to layer. Treating the $n$ positions of a sequence as the vertices of a $\log_2 n$-dimensional hypercube and connecting each position, at layer $\ell$, to its neighbour along dimension $\ell \bmod \log_2 n$, information from every position reaches every other in $\log_2 n$ layers with $2n$ links per layer instead of $n^2$. On a synthetic task that is unsolvable unless all positions are reached, this rotation matches all-to-all wiring at $1/32$ of the links, while the same sparse pattern held fixed across layers fails; what matters is that every dimension is touched, not the order. On character-level language modelling of a public corpus (the first $12$M characters of enwik8), a hybrid that keeps two attention layers among sixteen sparse ones reaches $0.06$ bits-per-character lower held-out loss than a fully attentive model of the same width at the same step budget (three seeds each, no overlap), with $1/7$ of the links, $42\%$ fewer parameters, and $2.4\times$ less wall-clock time; the purely rotated schedule is level with the hybrid. The same ordering holds on a second corpus of mixed Japanese, English and code, where the gap widens to $0.16$. The usable learning-rate window is four to eight times wider than attention's on both. We also report what did not work - learned coordinates, and a "dynamics" variant whose apparent gains turned out to be an artefact of a saturated kernel - and the measurement discipline (frozen corpus, full-coverage evaluation, seed spread as the bar for ranking) that we found necessary to say anything at all at this scale.

AI.tldr: Sparse, fixed wiring rotated across layers matches performance of full attention with far fewer connections in transformer models.
AI.motivation: Standard attention mechanisms have quadratic computational cost for pairwise connections. The authors explore whether fixed, sparse wiring patterns rotated across layers can achieve similar performance with dramatically reduced computational cost.
AI.method: Treat sequence positions as vertices of a log₂ n-dimensional hypercube. At each layer ℓ, connect each position to its neighbor along dimension ℓ mod log₂ n. This creates sparse connectivity with only 2n links per layer instead of n², allowing information to propagate between all positions in log₂ n layers.
AI.result: On synthetic tasks requiring all-to-all connectivity, rotation matches all-to-all wiring with 1/32 of links, while fixed patterns fail. On enwik8 character-level modeling, hybrid models (2 attention layers + 14 sparse) beat fully attentive models with 1/7 links, 42% fewer parameters, and 2.4× faster training.
