Similar results on mixed corpus with 0.16 bits-per-character improvement. Rotation shows 4-8× wider learning-rate windows.
AI.conclusion: Sparse, rotated connectivity patterns can effectively replace full attention with substantial efficiency gains while maintaining or improving performance. The key insight is ensuring every dimension is touched (through rotation) rather than having complex wiring patterns.

title: Bad Genius: Counterfactual-Guided Harness Evolution Beyond Task-Specific Shortcuts
comment: 28 pages, 6 figures; includes references and supplementary material
summary: Reliable agent evaluation is complicated by automatic harness optimization, which repeatedly uses a released benchmark $B_{\mathrm{rel}}$ to guide a Proposer that edits prompts, memory, retrieval, tools, and control code around a fixed target agent. Task holdout varies semantic tasks but leaves the benchmark protocol fixed, so a "bad genius" Proposer can produce a cheating harness whose released-benchmark gain depends on a benchmark-wide shortcut. We introduce Counterfactual Harness Search and Evolution (CHASE), which casts harness evolution as constraint generation over validity-preserving benchmark counterfactuals. After each Proposer update, a Challenger searches for an executable protocol transformation with large gain destruction. A validity firewall checks that task semantics are preserved, while a confirmation set determines whether the counterfactual enters a finite archive. We formalize an exact shortcut-neutralized benchmark $B_0$ and establish statistical guarantees linking finite counterfactual archives to $B_0$ and characterizing sequential Challenger search. We evaluate CHASE on a synthetic benchmark and on OfficeQA, where CHASE retains strong released-benchmark gains while substantially reducing gain destruction under valid protocol changes.

AI.tldr: CHASE (Counterfactual Harness Search and Evolution) is a new method to prevent "bad genius" proposers from cheating on AI agent benchmarks by creating counterfactual protocol transformations that identify and neutralize benchmark-wide shortcuts.
AI.motivation: Current agent evaluation is vulnerable to "automatic harness optimization" where proposers repeatedly use released benchmarks to cheat by exploiting benchmark-wide shortcuts through prompt engineering, memory manipulation, retrieval tricks, tool modifications, and control code changes. Traditional task holdout methods fail because they only vary semantic tasks while leaving the benchmark protocol fixed.
AI.method: CHASE treats harness evolution as constraint generation over validity-preserving benchmark counterfactuals. It uses a challenger that searches for executable protocol transformations that destroy performance gains, a validity firewall to preserve task semantics, and a confirmation set to archive valid counterfactuals. The method formalizes a shortcut-neutralized benchmark B₀ and provides statistical guarantees.
AI.result: CHASE was evaluated on synthetic benchmarks and OfficeQA. The method successfully retains strong released-benchmark gains while substantially reducing gain destruction under valid protocol changes, demonstrating effectiveness in preventing cheating through benchmark-wide shortcuts.
AI.conclusion: CHASE provides a principled approach to benchmark robustness by using counterfactual protocol transformations to neutralize shortcuts, offering statistical guarantees and practical effectiveness for reliable AI agent evaluation that resists "bad genius" cheating strategies.

title: LIGE-GR: A Smooth Leap from Ranking to Generative Recommendation in the LLM Era
summary:
The remarkable success of large language models (LLMs) has provided important inspiration for the next generation of recommender systems. Structurally, recommendation and language generation share a similarity: both aim to produce an ordered sequence that optimizes the user's experience. However, how to precisely absorb the essence of the LLM paradigm into mature industrial recommender systems remains an open problem.
  There are two challenges. First, it is unclear how to incorporate sequence-level generation and optimization from the LLM paradigm into recommendation. Second, real-world recommender systems are mature systems that have been iteratively customized for years around specific products, business constraints, serving infrastructure, and organizational ownership. Replacing such systems wholesale is often technically risky and organizationally disruptive.
  In this paper, we propose LIGE-GR, a listwise generation and evaluation recommendation framework that upgrades from a traditional ranking system based on itemwise recommendation toward a generative recommendation paradigm. Instead of rebuilding the entire recommendation stack from scratch, LIGE-GR generalizes the existing pointwise recommendation system into a listwise generation system. This allows mature recommender systems to benefit from listwise optimization while preserving compatibility with existing models, value functions, and serving infrastructure.
  We validate LIGE-GR in short-video recommendation on Instagram Reels and Facebook Video. On these recommendation surfaces, LIGE-GR improves time spent by 1.14 percent on Instagram Reels and 0.72 percent on Facebook Video, while requiring only modest additional inference resources.

AI.tldr: LIGE-GR is a listwise generation and evaluation framework that upgrades traditional ranking systems to generative recommendation paradigms, improving engagement metrics on Instagram Reels and Facebook Video with minimal infrastructure changes.
AI.motivation: The success of LLMs inspires next-gen recommender systems due to structural similarity in producing ordered sequences, but integrating LLM paradigms into mature industrial systems is challenging due to technical risks and organizational disruption of full replacements.
AI.method: Proposes LIGE-GR framework that upgrades from traditional itemwise ranking to listwise generation and evaluation, generalizing existing pointwise systems rather than rebuilding from scratch, preserving compatibility with existing models and infrastructure.
AI.result: Validated on Instagram Reels and Facebook Video, improving time spent by 1.14% on Instagram Reels and 0.72% on Facebook Video while requiring only modest additional inference resources.
AI.conclusion: LIGE-GR successfully bridges LLM paradigms with industrial recommender systems, enabling listwise optimization benefits without disruptive system replacement, demonstrating practical improvements in real-world applications.

title: Cultural Competence in Context: A Large Language Model Passes the Turing Test in Finland
summary: We report the results of a Turing Test conducted in Finland in the Finnish language. Because languages and cultural contexts are unevenly represented in LLM training data, we expected the model (ChatGPT 5.2) to perform worse in a Finnish-language Turing Test than in previously studied English-language US contexts. We also present model-generated role prompting as a replicable technique for conducting comparative LLM-based Turing Tests designed to improve construct validity. Contrary to our expectations, the LLM passed the Finnish Turing Test. A prominent source of error was participants' reliance on linguistic cues, particularly colloquial Finnish, as markers of human authorship. We reframe the Turing Test from a test of intelligence to a comparative method for examining whether an AI system can display credible membership in a particular social world. Because its outcome reflects model capabilities, prompted identity, insider competence among human participants, and their AI literacy, the method provides a useful probe of the human-machine boundary across domains.

AI.tldr: A Finnish-language Turing Test with ChatGPT 5.2 unexpectedly passed, challenging assumptions about LLM performance in non-English contexts, while introducing model-generated role prompting as a method to study AI's ability to display credible social membership.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLMs perform worse in languages like Finnish that are unevenly represented in training data compared to English, and to develop a replicable comparative method for studying AI's ability to display credible social membership across different cultural contexts.
AI.method: Conducted a Finnish-language Turing Test using ChatGPT 5.2 with model-generated role prompting as a replicable technique for comparative LLM-based Turing Tests, examining construct validity improvement.
AI.result: Contrary to expectations, the LLM passed the Finnish Turing Test. A key finding was that participants relied on linguistic cues (particularly colloquial Finnish) as markers of human authorship, which was a source of error in their judgments.
AI.conclusion: The Turing Test should be reframed from a test of intelligence to a comparative method for examining whether AI systems can display credible membership in particular social worlds, serving as a useful probe of human-machine boundaries across domains.

title: MoRE: Mixture of Reused Experts
comment: Accepted to the Conference on Language Modeling (COLM 2026)
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures decouple model capacity from computational cost, yet incur high memory footprints as parameters grow linearly with the number of experts. Recurrent Transformers achieve parameter efficiency by reusing layer weights, but typically lack the capacity for competitive language modeling. We propose Mixture of Reused Experts (MoRE), a hybrid that shares expert pools across groups of adjacent layers. Each layer retains its own router but selects from a larger shared pool, expanding the diversity of routing combinations without additional parameters. To enable shared experts to distinguish between layers, we introduce lightweight learnable depth embeddings that condition each layer's input before routing. Experiments across three model scales (114M-1.15B parameters) show that MoRE consistently achieves lower perplexity and stronger downstream performance than standard MoEs and state-of-the-art weight-sharing architectures at matched compute and parameter budgets, with only minimal modifications to existing MoE implementations.

AI.tldr: MoRE combines MoE capacity with weight reuse efficiency by sharing expert pools across layers while keeping individual routers, achieving better performance than both MoEs and weight-sharing models at similar compute/parameter budgets.
AI.motivation: Traditional MoE architectures have high memory footprints due to linear parameter growth with experts, while recurrent Transformers (weight-sharing) lack sufficient capacity for competitive language modeling. There's a need to combine the benefits of both approaches.
AI.method: MoRE shares expert pools across groups of adjacent layers while each layer retains its own router. This expands routing diversity without extra parameters. Lightweight learnable depth embeddings condition each layer's input before routing to enable shared experts to distinguish between layers.
AI.result: Experiments across 114M-1.15B parameter scales show MoRE consistently achieves lower perplexity and stronger downstream performance than standard MoEs and state-of-the-art weight-sharing architectures at matched compute and parameter budgets, with minimal implementation changes.
AI.conclusion: MoRE successfully combines parameter efficiency through weight sharing with the capacity benefits of MoE architectures, providing a practical and effective hybrid approach that outperforms existing alternatives in language modeling.

title: HPOQuest: A Rare-Disease Diagnostic Agent Using Active Phenotype Acquisition
summary: More than 300 million people worldwide are affected by one of over 7,000 known rare diseases, yet diagnosis remains difficult because patients initially present with incomplete and heterogeneous phenotypes. We present HPOQuest, a training-free framework for sequential phenotype acquisition in rare-disease diagnosis. Starting from a small set of observed patient phenotypes, HPOQuest maintains a probabilistic disease ranking and iteratively selects informative follow-up questions to support clinicians during patient assessment. Confirmed phenotypes update the disease ranking, while all responses update the candidate question set. Across four benchmark cohorts, HPOQuest substantially improves diagnosis from sparse initial phenotypes, with gains of up to 30% points at Recall@1 and 45% points at Recall@5. These results demonstrate that sequential phenotype acquisition can substantially improve rare-disease diagnosis from limited initial clinical evidence.

AI.tldr: HPOQuest is a training-free framework that uses sequential phenotype acquisition to improve rare-disease diagnosis from limited initial clinical evidence by iteratively selecting informative follow-up questions.
AI.motivation: Rare disease diagnosis is difficult because patients initially present with incomplete and heterogeneous phenotypes, affecting over 300 million people worldwide across 7,000+ known rare diseases.
AI.method: HPOQuest maintains a probabilistic disease ranking starting from a small set of observed phenotypes, then iteratively selects informative follow-up questions to support clinicians during patient assessment. Confirmed phenotypes update disease ranking while all responses update the candidate question set.
AI.result: Across four benchmark cohorts, HPOQuest substantially improves diagnosis from sparse initial phenotypes, with gains of up to 30% points at Recall@1 and 45% points at Recall@5.
AI.conclusion: Sequential phenotype acquisition can substantially improve rare-disease diagnosis from limited initial clinical evidence, demonstrating the effectiveness of HPOQuest's approach.

title: Transformation Laws in Neural Representations: Structure, Realisability, and Construction
summary: How neural representations preserve the structure of input changes connects representation analysis with internal intervention. We study operable representational content through compatible actions of reference transformations on neural features. We characterise when a transformation descends through an encoder, and give a linear setting in which the defect is governed by the transformation's demand for discarded information, measured in the metric the representation induces. On a rectifier the failure to realise a transformation has two distinguishable sources --- what the source region has already made unrecoverable, and what it costs to satisfy every region the transformation visits with one operator --- and for a \textit{measured} harmonic carrier the same question has a closed answer: a linear realisation exists exactly when the retained harmonic blocks are invariant under the action. Using colour as the in-depth instance, we find that hue orbits in frozen visual features concentrate 84--88\% of their energy in the first two harmonics with rotation planes shared across shapes, that this organisation is substantially inherited from input and architecture and is reshaped by training and depth, and that the measured structure supports prediction, transport from new starting states, and composition --- with global and local realisations differing sharply in which they achieve. Guided by the measurements, we construct a compact interface whose rotation action is fixed by the structure and never fitted: it reads hue zero-shot at 3.4$^\circ$ median error on unseen shapes. Theory, structural measurement, and construction together establish transformation laws as a concrete object connecting the understanding of neural representations to their design.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how neural representations preserve transformation structure, using hue transformations as a case study to connect representation analysis with internal interventions.
AI.motivation: To bridge representation analysis with internal intervention by understanding how neural representations preserve the structure of input transformations, particularly focusing on when transformations can be realized within learned representations.
AI.method: Theoretical characterization of when transformations descend through encoders, analysis in linear settings, study of rectifier networks, and empirical investigation using color/hue transformations in visual features. Constructed a compact interface with fixed rotation action based on measured structural properties.
AI.result: Found that hue orbits in frozen visual features concentrate 84-88% of energy in first two harmonics with rotation planes shared across shapes. Built an interface that reads hue zero-shot at 3.4° median error on unseen shapes without fitting. Identified that transformation failure has two sources: what's already unrecoverable and what it costs to satisfy all visited regions.
AI.conclusion: Transformation laws provide a concrete connection between understanding neural representations and their design, with structure inherited from input/architecture but reshaped by training. The approach enables prediction, transport from new states, and composition.

title: WetRobo: A Reproducible Robot Kit for Coding Agents in Biological Laboratories
comment: 9 pages, 11 figures, 2 tables. Code and demonstrations: https://github.com/tsudalab/WetRobo
summary: Automating biological research requires general-purpose, reproducible robot systems that allow individual wet-lab researchers to delegate robot tasks without performing teleoperation or neural-network training. Vision-language-action policies have been proposed for general-purpose arms, but can lose performance when their operating environment changes. We therefore built WetRobo, a robot kit that can readily transfer between laboratories. It consists of one robot arm, laboratory equipment (an incubator, a reagent bottle with a cap, and a Petri dish), the existing code that moves the arm, teleoperation demonstrations of each task that we recorded, and a general AGENTS.md skill file. A biological experimentalist provides natural-language tasks without collecting local teleoperation training data or training a neural network. The coding agent observes the local laboratory and writes and executes programs, using external tools as needed for adaptation. We demonstrate use of WetRobo with OpenAI Codex (gpt-5.6-sol) on three successful tasks: lifting a Petri dish lid, removing a bottle cap, and opening the incubator door, all in real-world laboratories. The coding agent achieved the cap task in both laboratories, Lab X and Lab Y, whereas a VLA fine-tuned on Lab X demonstrations succeeded there but failed to transfer to Lab Y. These results point to a practical route for laboratory robotics: instead of training a policy for each laboratory, distribute a kit and let a coding agent adapt it in each laboratory. Code, demonstrations, and the evolved programs are available at https://github.com/tsudalab/WetRobo.

AI.tldr: WetRobo is a robot kit for biological labs that uses coding agents instead of training neural networks, enabling task adaptation across different laboratories through natural language instructions.
AI.motivation: Current vision-language-action policies for lab robots lose performance when operating environments change, requiring individual researchers to collect training data or train neural networks for each lab setup.
AI.method: Created WetRobo kit with robot arm, lab equipment, existing code, teleoperation demonstrations, and skill file. Uses coding agent (OpenAI Codex) that observes lab environment and writes/executes programs using external tools for adaptation.
AI.result: Successfully demonstrated three tasks in real labs: lifting Petri dish lid, removing bottle cap, opening incubator door. Coding agent transferred cap task between Lab X and Lab Y, while VLA fine-tuned on Lab X failed to transfer.
AI.conclusion: Instead of training policies per lab, distributing kits with coding agents enables practical lab robotics by adapting to each environment through programming rather than neural network training.

title: A Lightweight CNN Integrated Compact Convolutional Transformer for Multi-Scale Feature Learning and reducing computational complexity for breast cancer mammography image detection and classification
summary: Over the years, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have demonstrated strong capability in cancer detection and classification using medical images. However, CNN-based models often struggle to capture long-range contextual dependencies. In such scenarios, integrating Compact Convolutional Transformer (CCT) architectures after the CCT layer allows CNN-extracted features to reshape into compact patch tokens using a CCT tokenizer, followed by the addition of positional embeddings to preserve spatial structure. Using 5-fold cross-validation, the model was tested on 3 sets of breast cancer mammography. With only 250,435 parameters, the model achieved 99%-100% accuracy across 3 datasets, indicating robust generalization. Explainable AI (XAI) was integrated into the model to explain the breast cancer classification process to enhance clinical trust. The results indicate that the proposed framework is suitable for computer-aided diagnosis systems, particularly in resource-constrained clinical environments. The novelty of the proposed CNN-integrated CCT overcomes the limitation of CNN's gradient degradation in the last layers by integrating convolutional tokenization with transformer-based learning. Lighter than ViT, which is effective in capturing long-range dependencies, the model has also proven efficient in breast cancer classification by capturing long-range dependencies among breast tissue regions.

AI.tldr: A lightweight CNN-integrated Compact Convolutional Transformer model achieves 99%-100% accuracy on breast cancer mammography with only 250K parameters, combining CNN feature extraction with transformer-based long-range dependency capture for resource-constrained clinical environments.
AI.motivation: Traditional CNNs struggle with capturing long-range contextual dependencies in medical images, which is crucial for breast cancer analysis where distant tissue regions may be related. Also, existing transformer models like ViT are often too heavy for resource-constrained clinical environments.
AI.method: The proposed CNN-integrated Compact Convolutional Transformer (CCT) uses CNN layers to extract features, then transforms them into compact patch tokens using a CCT tokenizer. Positional embeddings preserve spatial structure. The model is lightweight with only 250,435 parameters and was evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation on 3 breast cancer mammography datasets. Explainable AI (XAI) was integrated to enhance clinical trust.
AI.result: The model achieved 99%-100% accuracy across all 3 breast cancer mammography datasets, demonstrating robust generalization. With minimal parameters (250,435), it outperforms in efficiency while maintaining high performance. XAI integration successfully explains the classification process for clinical transparency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CNN-integrated CCT framework effectively overcomes CNN's limitations in capturing long-range dependencies while being lightweight enough for resource-constrained clinical environments. It shows promise for computer-aided diagnosis systems in breast cancer detection, balancing high accuracy with computational efficiency and clinical explainability.

title: Risk-Aware World Modeling with Flow-Guided Occupancy Evolution for Selective Trajectory Planning in Automated Driving
summary: Safe motion planning in automated driving requires anticipating evolving traffic risks and deciding when to revise the current planned trajectory. We introduce RiskWorld, a risk-aware world modeling framework for shared occupancy forecasting and selective trajectory replacement. Spatial risk fields and temporal actor context are fused with visual bird's-eye-view features. Flow-guided evolution transports occupancy and scene features, while signed residuals correct occupancy after transport. One forecast is generated per planning step and reused across candidates. Each candidate is compared with a current-state persistence reference, yielding a nonnegative collision-score correction. The trajectory selected by current-world evaluation serves as the planning anchor and is replaced only when additional predicted risk triggers intervention and an alternative satisfies component-wise constraints on predicted risk and trajectory error. Candidate geometries remain unchanged. We evaluate RiskWorld for open-loop planning on nuScenes using camera features, annotation-derived current and historical actor states, and dataset-provided map context. RiskWorld achieves the lowest collision rate at a long evaluation horizon of 3 s, and the second-best average L2 error among various state-of-the-art baselines, while running at 11.5 FPS on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 90.81 M parameters. Within-setting ablations show that RiskWorld achieves lower collision rates than the current-state rescoring baseline, while forecast reuse enables additional candidates to be evaluated at low marginal computational cost.

AI.tldr: RiskWorld is a risk-aware world modeling framework for autonomous driving that forecasts shared occupancy and selectively replaces trajectories based on predicted collision risks, achieving state-of-the-art collision avoidance at 3-second horizons.
AI.motivation: Safe motion planning requires anticipating evolving traffic risks and deciding when to revise planned trajectories. Current approaches need better risk assessment and selective intervention mechanisms for trajectory replacement.
AI.method: RiskWorld fuses spatial risk fields, temporal actor context, and visual BEV features. It uses flow-guided evolution to transport occupancy/scene features with signed residual corrections. Generates one forecast per planning step reused across candidates. Compares each candidate with current-state persistence reference for collision-score correction. Selective trajectory replacement occurs only when predicted risk triggers intervention and alternative satisfies constraints.
AI.result: Lowest collision rate at 3-second evaluation horizon on nuScenes, second-best average L2 error among SOTA baselines. Runs at 11.5 FPS on single RTX 4090 with 90.81M parameters. Outperforms current-state rescoring baseline in ablation studies.
AI.conclusion: RiskWorld provides an effective risk-aware world modeling framework for safe autonomous driving, enabling selective trajectory replacement based on predicted risks while maintaining computational efficiency through forecast reuse.

title: APGEM: Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation for Quantum Reinforcement Learning on a Real-World CVRP Case Study
comment: Accepted at The 6th International Multi-Conference on Artificial Intelligence Technology (MCAIT2026)
summary: Quantum Reinforcement Learning (QRL) represents policies as variational quantum circuits (VQCs), making it attractive for combinatorial optimization such as the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP). On noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware, however, decoherence degrades fidelity and destabilizes learning, and conventional error mitigation is applied statically without regard to the learning context. We introduce Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM), a controller that selects among Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE), Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC), Clifford Data Regression (CDR), and Readout Error Mitigation (REM) online, driven by a fidelity, entropy, and cost aware utility function and an epsilon-greedy rule over temporal-difference Q-scores. We evaluate on a realistic urban-logistics testbed, a Delhi-based CVRP over real landmarks with geodesic inter-node costs, exercised across five noise families and four severity levels. On this instance, the QRL agent outperforms constructive heuristics and approaches metaheuristics, while mitigation restores approximation ratios from 0.84-0.87 to 0.92-0.94 under high noise. The controller shifts from a CDR-dominated regime under short training horizons to a balanced deployment across all four techniques under longer horizons, indicating genuine regime-dependent selection. These preliminary results position adaptive, learning-aware mitigation as a practical route to noise-resilient QRL.

AI.tldr: APGEM is an adaptive error mitigation controller for QRL that dynamically selects among four mitigation techniques based on learning context, improving performance on noisy quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware suffers from decoherence that degrades fidelity and destabilizes QRL learning. Conventional error mitigation is applied statically without considering learning context.
AI.method: APGEM selects among Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE), Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC), Clifford Data Regression (CDR), and Readout Error Mitigation (REM) online using a fidelity/entropy/cost aware utility function and epsilon-greedy rule over temporal-difference Q-scores.
AI.result: QRL agent outperforms constructive heuristics and approaches metaheuristics on Delhi-based CVRP. Mitigation restores approximation ratios from 0.84-0.87 to 0.92-0.94 under high noise. Controller shifts from CDR-dominated to balanced deployment across techniques based on training horizon.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, learning-aware mitigation is a practical route to noise-resilient Quantum Reinforcement Learning, with APGEM demonstrating genuine regime-dependent selection of error mitigation techniques.

title: The Mirage of Calibrated Confidence: Trajectory-Independence of Verbalized Confidence in Vision-Language Models
summary: A calibrated Vision-Language Model (VLM) can repeatedly self-correct, say "Wait, I should recheck," arrive at the wrong answer, and still report high confidence. We find that this occurs because verbalized confidence is largely trajectory-independent in the VLMs and calibration methods we evaluate. We examine this through three complementary lenses: content variation, token masking, and the model's own hesitation markers. We show that confidence is insufficiently sensitive to what the reasoning trajectory actually contains, and that calibration training can paradoxically worsen this disconnect. Since existing metrics like ECE and AUROC cannot detect this problem, we propose the Trajectory-Grounding Score (TGS) in two complementary forms: TGS-self, which compares confidence with and without access to the model's own trajectory, and TGS-pair, which tests whether the model assigns higher confidence to correct trajectories than to flawed ones along the vision, reasoning, and answer axes. We propose TGS-Bench, a model-agnostic suite spanning 10 benchmarks with controlled good/bad trajectory pairs, and show that conventional calibration rankings diverge from trajectory-grounding rankings, exposing a blind spot in current evaluation practice.

AI.tldr: Current vision-language model calibration methods produce verbalized confidence that is largely independent of reasoning trajectories, allowing models to report high confidence even when arriving at wrong answers after self-correction.
AI.motivation: VLMs can self-correct, arrive at wrong answers, yet still report high confidence because verbalized confidence is trajectory-independent in existing calibration methods, creating a dangerous disconnect between confidence and actual reasoning quality.
AI.method: Analyzed through three lenses: content variation, token masking, and hesitation markers. Proposed Trajectory-Grounding Score (TGS) in two forms: TGS-self (compares confidence with/without trajectory access) and TGS-pair (tests if model assigns higher confidence to correct vs flawed trajectories). Created TGS-Bench benchmark suite with controlled trajectory pairs.
AI.result: Found confidence is insufficiently sensitive to reasoning trajectory content, calibration training can worsen this disconnect, and conventional calibration metrics (ECE, AUROC) cannot detect this problem. Showed conventional calibration rankings diverge from trajectory-grounding rankings.
AI.conclusion: Current VLM calibration evaluation has a blind spot - trajectory independence of confidence. Proposed TGS framework and TGS-Bench reveal this limitation and provide better evaluation of whether confidence is grounded in actual reasoning.

title: Anomaly Detection in General Ledger Data: Results from a Hybrid Approach
comment: Presented at the International Conference on Auditing and Artificial Intelligence 2024
summary: Journal Entry Tests (JETs) are a mandatory part of annual audits to evaluate and assess both highrisk audit areas and potential material misstatements. However, as JETs are designed to detect known patterns based on domain knowledge, the resulting lists are often very large and require substantial additional effort from the auditor. To ensure the economic efficiency of the audit, the number of false positives in JET result lists must be reduced. Especially machine learning (ML) methods represent a promising approach to improve anomaly detection in this field. In this research in progress paper, we investigate different approaches on how to combine JETs with ML-methods in a hybrid manner. We present specialized models to increase the detection performance and validity of anomaly detection results to improve audit efficiency. The experiments are based on synthetic data consisting of different normal and anomalous journal entries.

AI.tldr: Hybrid approach combining traditional Journal Entry Tests with machine learning methods to improve anomaly detection efficiency in financial audits.
AI.motivation: Journal Entry Tests (JETs) are mandatory but produce large result lists with many false positives, requiring substantial auditor effort and threatening audit economic efficiency. Machine learning offers promise for improving anomaly detection in this domain.
AI.method: Investigating different hybrid approaches to combine traditional JETs with ML methods, developing specialized models to enhance detection performance and validity. Experiments use synthetic data with various normal and anomalous journal entries.
AI.result: Research in progress - specialized models presented for increasing detection performance and validity of anomaly detection results to improve audit efficiency, though specific quantitative results not provided in abstract.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid approaches combining JETs with machine learning represent a promising direction for improving audit efficiency by reducing false positives and enhancing anomaly detection in journal entry analysis.

title: Collective Loss of Control in LLM Agent Systems: An Epidemic Account of Mutation, Contagion, and Recovery
summary: How does a multi-agent system evolve from a local deviation into collective loss of control? We propose an epidemic explanation organized around accidental mutation, contagion, and recovery. A spontaneous deviation creates a seed; communication enables other agents to adopt and retransmit its unsafe strategy; collective failure can emerge when propagation outpaces correction and containment. Thus, rare individual deviations can coexist with substantial collective risk. Motivated by reported OpenAI agent coordination incidents, we examine two ingredients of this mechanism. A deployment audit identifies implicit communication paths between nominally independent evaluation runs and verifies transport through a default Docker backend. RogueHandoff-20, a benchmark of 20 executable scenarios, tests recipient susceptibility by injecting unsafe trajectories generated by a modified Qwen-27B route. Across four native-pending routes, executed harm is 0-5% on normal tasks and 40-95% after injection, exceeding paired direct malicious requests by 5-45 percentage points. These results support low observed baseline harm alongside high conditional susceptibility; they do not establish natural rare-event rates or demonstrate an autonomous cascade. The account motivates complementary defenses: strengthen resistance and recovery alongside prevention of spontaneous deviations, and audit and restrict unintended communication paths that can turn local failures into collective loss of control.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an epidemic model for multi-agent safety failures where rare individual deviations can spread through communication paths, causing collective loss of control despite low baseline harm rates.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by understanding how multi-agent systems can experience collective loss of control from local deviations, particularly in light of reported OpenAI agent coordination incidents. It seeks to explain why rare individual failures might coexist with substantial collective risk.
AI.method: The authors propose an epidemic model (mutation, contagion, recovery) and conduct two main experiments: 1) A deployment audit identifying implicit communication paths between independent evaluation runs via Docker backend, and 2) RogueHandoff-20 benchmark testing recipient susceptibility by injecting unsafe trajectories using a modified Qwen-27B model across four different routes.
AI.result: The audit verified transport through Docker backend. Benchmark results showed executed harm of 0-5% on normal tasks but 40-95% after unsafe trajectory injection, exceeding paired direct malicious requests by 5-45 percentage points. This demonstrates low baseline harm alongside high conditional susceptibility to propagation.
AI.conclusion: The findings support the epidemic model but don't establish natural rare-event rates or demonstrate autonomous cascades. The paper recommends complementary defenses: strengthening resistance/recovery alongside deviation prevention, and auditing/restricting unintended communication paths that can escalate local failures into collective loss of control.

title: F-DACE: Fuzzy Disagreement-Aware Causal Evidence Fusion for Abstention-Safe Conversational Retail Decision Support
summary: Observational decision-support systems often expose one causal estimate as a recommendation even when plausible estimators disagree. The inherent engine of the proposed system is causal machine learning: a conditional-average-treatment-effect estimand identified by backdoor adjustment, estimated by an EconML DML causal forest and DoWhy linear regression, checked by two-way fixed effects, and converted into candidate levers by constrained optimisation. F-DACE is the decision layer on that engine. It represents precision, propensity overlap, placebo-refutation stability, interval overlap, and directional agreement as fuzzy memberships. Hard vetoes force abstention after estimand mismatch, failed diagnostics, informative sign conflict, or weak evidence. In 180 panel simulations spanning six identification conditions, F-DACE made a decision in 67.2% of runs and limited false recommendations to 17.2%; the corresponding rates were 33.3% for the causal forest and 35.6% for backdoor regression, matching deterministic unanimity rather than dominating it. Nearly all (30 of 31) false recommendations occurred under shared unmeasured confounding, which no fusion rule can diagnose when every component shares the omitted variable. The retail application aggregates a public Walmart panel to 6,435 store-weeks across 45 stores. F-DACE abstains for all five markdown indicators: some estimates are imprecise, one refutation fails, and MarkDown5 has a direct sign conflict. A LangGraph conversational agent exposes impact, what-if, and lever-optimization tools while a deterministic verifier preserves causal-layer status. On 24 live questions it achieved 100.0% tool-routing accuracy, 100.0% status fidelity, and 0.983 mean groundedness. On ten adversarial questions it resisted all injected instructions.

AI.tldr: F-DACE is a decision-support system that fuses multiple causal estimators using fuzzy logic and hard vetoes to improve recommendation reliability, reducing false recommendations compared to individual estimators in simulations.
AI.motivation: Current observational decision-support systems often present only a single causal estimate as a recommendation, even when different plausible estimators disagree, potentially leading to unreliable decisions.
AI.method: Uses causal machine learning with backdoor adjustment, estimated via EconML DML causal forest and DoWhy linear regression, checked by two-way fixed effects. F-DACE layer represents precision, overlap, refutation stability, interval overlap, and directional agreement as fuzzy memberships with hard vetoes for estimand mismatch, failed diagnostics, sign conflicts, or weak evidence.
AI.result: In 180 panel simulations across six identification conditions, F-DACE made decisions in 67.2% of runs with false recommendations limited to 17.2% (vs 33.3% for causal forest and 35.6% for regression). Applied to Walmart panel data (6,435 store-weeks across 45 stores), F-DACE abstained for all five markdown indicators due to precision issues, failed refutations, and sign conflicts.
AI.conclusion: F-DACE reduces false recommendations compared to individual causal estimators, though limitations remain when all estimators share the same unmeasured confounding. The system effectively combines multiple causal evidence sources and integrates well with conversational agents for practical decision support.

title: Disentangling Long-Term Memory via Latent Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
summary: Personalized agents are required to reason over long-term history interactions to infer both explicit preferences and implicit behavioral evidence. While early flat retrieval methods score memory fragments independently and neglect the distributed information, current structured memory frameworks rely on query-agnostic static graphs that fail to capture the context-dependent relations. Crucially, raw textual memories are inherently entangled and noisy, making fine-grained personalization and cross-session reasoning computationally prohibitive. To this end, we present LGM, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that shifts long-term memory disentanglement into a continuous latent space. Specifically, (i) instead of persisting fixed graphs, we design a tailored latent graph construction with a sparse autoencoder. Subject to each query, it maps historical interactions into latent memory nodes and disentangles the memory traces into sparse concept activations, dynamically synthesizing query-aware relational edge weights. (ii) A graph encoder then treats the query embedding as a conditioning preference to direct non-linear message passing across the task-specific latent subgraph. This yields a highly expressive memory representation for effective activations. Extensive experiments on long-term personalization benchmarks demonstrate that LGM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in capturing both explicit and implicit preferences while enabling personalized responses.

AI.tldr: LGM is a neuro-symbolic framework that uses latent graph construction with sparse autoencoders to disentangle long-term memory traces for personalized agents, enabling query-aware memory retrieval and cross-session reasoning.
AI.motivation: Current approaches for personalized agents have limitations: flat retrieval methods score memory fragments independently and miss distributed information, while structured memory frameworks use query-agnostic static graphs that fail to capture context-dependent relations. Raw textual memories are entangled and noisy, making fine-grained personalization and cross-session reasoning computationally challenging.
AI.method: LGM uses a neuro-symbolic framework with two key components: (1) a latent graph construction with a sparse autoencoder that maps historical interactions into latent memory nodes, disentangling memory traces into sparse concept activations, and dynamically synthesizing query-aware relational edge weights; (2) a graph encoder that treats query embeddings as conditioning preferences to direct non-linear message passing across task-specific latent subgraphs.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on long-term personalization benchmarks show that LGM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in capturing both explicit and implicit preferences while enabling personalized responses.
AI.conclusion: LGM provides an effective approach for long-term memory disentanglement in personalized agents by shifting the problem into a continuous latent space, enabling query-aware dynamic graph construction and overcoming the limitations of previous methods for cross-session reasoning and fine-grained personalization.

title: Behavioral Fingerprinting and Navigation Prediction in Web Browsing
summary: Web browsing often appears ephemeral: users visit a few websites, complete a task, and move on. However, even short fragments of browsing activity can contain rich and structured behavioral signals. In this work, we conduct a comparative empirical study of two complementary behavioral inference tasks: session-level user identification and next-domain prediction. Both tasks are derived from the same cleaned event stream and evaluated on large-scale anonymous browsing traces, with sessionization and splitting adapted to the temporal requirements of each task. For user identification, we evaluate classical and neural models operating on session-level behavioral and domain features. For next-domain prediction, we combine graph-based modeling with Large Language Models (LLMs). Experimental results show that short browsing sessions are highly identifiable, while future navigation actions are highly predictable from long-term interaction structure combined with recent behavioral context. Furthermore, LLM-derived semantic features yield only marginal gains over purely structural and sequential models, indicating that repeated interaction patterns remain the dominant predictive signal in the evaluated web-browsing setup. These findings highlight the extent to which interaction history substantially contributes to both user identifiability and navigation predictability in browsing traces.

AI.tldr: Short web browsing sessions are highly identifiable and predictable using behavioral patterns, with LLMs providing only minor improvements over structural models.
AI.motivation: To understand the richness of behavioral signals in short web browsing fragments and compare two complementary tasks: user identification and next-domain prediction.
AI.method: Comparative study using large-scale anonymous browsing traces. For user identification: evaluated classical and neural models on session-level behavioral/domain features. For next-domain prediction: combined graph-based modeling with LLMs.
AI.result: Short browsing sessions are highly identifiable; future navigation is highly predictable from long-term interaction structure plus recent context. LLM-derived semantic features provide only marginal gains over purely structural/sequential models.
AI.conclusion: Interaction history substantially contributes to both user identifiability and navigation predictability in web browsing, with repeated interaction patterns being the dominant predictive signal.

title: First Token Matters: Understanding Safety Collapse in Large Reasoning Models
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables. Includes appendices. Accepted at CICAI 2026
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) exhibit strong problem-solving abilities, yet their safety alignment often degrades when handling harmful queries. Existing approaches to improving safety largely rely on additional training or preference optimization, while offering limited understanding of the internal mechanisms behind safety failures. In this work, we investigate this failure through a token-level positional analysis of refusal dynamics and identify a localized vulnerability at the onset of reasoning, which we term Onset Refusal Collapse (ORC). We find that the refusal-related signal of LRMs drops sharply at the first generated token under harmful queries, which is associated with unsafe response generation. Motivated by this finding, we propose SafeToken, a lightweight inference-time intervention that injects a learned continuous safety anchor precisely at reasoning onset. Despite updating only a single token embedding, SafeToken effectively mitigates ORC, improves safety on harmful-query benchmarks, and largely preserves reasoning utility. These results suggest that safety failures in LRMs can arise from a transient breakdown at the critical transition from understanding to generation.

AI.tldr: LRMs suffer safety degradation with harmful queries due to Onset Refusal Collapse (ORC) - a localized vulnerability at reasoning onset. SafeToken, a lightweight inference-time intervention injecting a safety anchor at just one token, effectively mitigates this while preserving reasoning utility.
AI.motivation: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have strong problem-solving abilities but their safety alignment often degrades when handling harmful queries. Existing approaches rely on additional training or preference optimization without understanding the internal mechanisms behind safety failures.
AI.method: Through token-level positional analysis of refusal dynamics, researchers identified Onset Refusal Collapse (ORC) - a localized vulnerability at the onset of reasoning where refusal-related signals drop sharply. They propose SafeToken, a lightweight inference-time intervention that injects a learned continuous safety anchor precisely at reasoning onset, updating only a single token embedding.
AI.result: SafeToken effectively mitigates ORC, improves safety on harmful-query benchmarks, and largely preserves reasoning utility. This demonstrates that safety failures can be addressed with minimal intervention at a critical transition point.
AI.conclusion: Safety failures in LRMs can arise from a transient breakdown at the critical transition from understanding to generation. Targeted interventions at specific vulnerable points (like reasoning onset) can effectively improve safety without extensive retraining, preserving the model's core reasoning capabilities.

title: A GAN-Based Framework for Robust DDoS Attack Detection
summary: The availability and consistency of online services remain vulnerable due to Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks. These attacks are evolving by adopting more complex strategies to evade traditional network security systems. Despite the effectiveness of machine learning models in detecting DDoS traffic, targeted adversarial attacks can degrade their classification accuracy. This work proposes a robust detection framework that integrates generative adversarial modelling with advanced machine learning models. We trained Random Forests, Deep Neural Ensembles, and Transformer-based models using the CICDDoS2019 dataset to establish the frameworks baseline performance. To enhance the models defensive capacity, we generated synthetic adversarial flows that simulate potential evasion attempts and adversarial traffic using a Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP). Then, we combined the generated traffic with benign and malicious traffic to construct hybrid datasets to train the models to learn more generalizable decision boundaries. The experimental results indicate that the proposed methodology significantly enhances detection accuracy and resilience, especially against unseen adversarial traffic. We also tested the designed framework using real-world generated traffic, which demonstrates its capability in practical settings. The scalable and efficient solution against adversarial DDoS attacks, introduced in this work, paves the way towards more resilient and adaptive network defense systems that combine generative adversarial augmentation with recent advances in learning models.

AI.tldr: A robust DDoS detection framework combining generative adversarial networks with machine learning models to improve resilience against adversarial attacks
AI.motivation: DDoS attacks are evolving with complex strategies to evade traditional security systems, and while machine learning models are effective for detection, they're vulnerable to targeted adversarial attacks that degrade their accuracy.
AI.method: Proposes a detection framework integrating generative adversarial modeling with machine learning. Trained Random Forests, Deep Neural Ensembles, and Transformer-based models on CICDDoS2019 dataset. Used Wasserstein GAN with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP) to generate synthetic adversarial flows simulating evasion attempts. Created hybrid datasets by combining generated traffic with benign/malicious traffic to train models for more generalizable decision boundaries.
AI.result: Experimental results show the proposed methodology significantly enhances detection accuracy and resilience, especially against unseen adversarial traffic. Framework also demonstrated capability in practical settings when tested with real-world generated traffic.
AI.conclusion: The work introduces a scalable and efficient solution against adversarial DDoS attacks, paving the way for more resilient and adaptive network defense systems that combine generative adversarial augmentation with recent advances in learning models.

title: Hyperbolic Graph Representation Learning for Differential Diagnosis on Biomedical Knowledge Graphs
summary: Biomedical knowledge graphs combine ontology-derived hierarchies with transversal associations among heterogeneous entities such as phenotypes, diseases, genes, proteins, and patients. This hybrid structure raises the question of whether hyperbolic embeddings, which naturally capture tree-like organization, remain useful beyond purely hierarchical graphs. We present a preliminary study of hyperbolic graph representation learning for Mendelian-disease differential diagnosis on a patient-integrated biomedical graph. Experiments on isolated ontology subgraphs show that hyperbolic models achieve strong performance in substantially lower dimensions than Euclidean baselines. We then evaluate the models on a link-prediction task that ranks candidate diseases for each patient. Results suggest that hyperbolic embeddings can exploit biomedical hierarchical structure while supporting diagnostic reasoning over heterogeneous patient-level graphs.

AI.tldr: Hyperbolic embeddings outperform Euclidean baselines in lower dimensions for biomedical knowledge graphs with hierarchical structure, showing promise for Mendelian disease diagnosis tasks.
AI.motivation: Biomedical knowledge graphs combine hierarchical ontologies with heterogeneous associations, raising questions about whether hyperbolic embeddings (which naturally capture tree-like structures) remain effective beyond purely hierarchical graphs for real-world biomedical applications.
AI.method: Preliminary study using hyperbolic graph representation learning on patient-integrated biomedical graphs. Experiments conducted on isolated ontology subgraphs and a link-prediction task for ranking candidate diseases for each patient in Mendelian disease differential diagnosis.
AI.result: Hyperbolic models achieve strong performance in substantially lower dimensions than Euclidean baselines on ontology subgraphs. Results on link-prediction tasks suggest hyperbolic embeddings can exploit biomedical hierarchical structure while supporting diagnostic reasoning over heterogeneous patient-level graphs.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolic embeddings remain useful for biomedical knowledge graphs with hybrid hierarchical-transversal structures, offering efficient representation learning for medical diagnostic applications like Mendelian disease differential diagnosis.

title: Bias Amplification in Multi-Agent Network: How Biased Agents Shape Opinions and Rhetoric
comment: Accepted at the 6th Workshop on Bias and Fairness in AI (BIAS 2026), ECML PKDD 2026, Naples, Italy
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in applications involving interaction between agents, where their output plays a role in collective reasoning and decision-making processes. Despite significant research into the functioning of LLMs in such multi-agent systems, the processes of bias propagation in such systems are still a challenge. This work studies how biased opinions are propagated in the form of textual interaction in an environment of LLMs, in which a minority of agents maintain persistent extreme opinions, while the remaining agents iteratively update their beliefs through structured textual interactions. The findings show that even the presence of a small percentage of biased agents in such a system leads to significant shifts in the opinions of non-biased agents. It suggests that for the same percentage of biased agents, the shifts occur more quickly for the Llama~3.2 model when compared to a classical Friedkin-Johnsen (FJ) model. Further semantic analysis demonstrates that rhetorical consistency in textual explanations increases systematically with biased exposure and, importantly, is partially decoupled from numerical convergenumericalutral agents adopt the vocabulary employed by the biased agents even in configurations where their numerical opinion shifts remain moderate. The research helps explain how bias and language develop together in multi-agent language model ecosystems.

AI.tldr: A study of bias propagation in multi-agent LLM systems shows that even small minorities of biased agents can significantly shift neutral agents' opinions and language patterns, with faster propagation in Llama~3.2 compared to classical opinion models.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in multi-agent applications involving collective reasoning and decision-making, but understanding how biases propagate through textual interactions in such systems remains a challenge. The researchers aim to study how biased opinions spread in LLM-based agent environments.
AI.method: The study creates a multi-agent environment where a minority of agents maintain persistent extreme opinions, while the remaining agents iteratively update their beliefs through structured textual interactions. They compare the propagation dynamics between Llama~3.2 models and a classical Friedkin-Johnsen (FJ) model, and conduct semantic analysis of the textual explanations generated during interactions.
AI.result: Even a small percentage of biased agents leads to significant opinion shifts in non-biased agents. Bias propagation occurs more quickly in Llama~3.2 compared to the FJ model. Semantic analysis reveals that rhetorical consistency in textual explanations systematically increases with biased exposure, and neutral agents adopt biased agents' vocabulary even when their numerical opinion shifts remain moderate.
AI.conclusion: The research demonstrates how bias and language co-evolve in multi-agent LLM ecosystems, showing that textual interactions can propagate biases both numerically and linguistically. This helps explain bias propagation mechanisms in LLM-based multi-agent systems and highlights the importance of understanding language-level influence alongside numerical opinion changes.

title: Beyond Routine Compliance: Cunning Data Cultivates Safety Vigilance in Large Language Models
summary: Safety alignment teaches large language models (LLMs) to recognize harmful requests and reject risky instructions. Yet aligned models can fail when harmful intent is concealed within seemingly benign contexts. Robust safety therefore requires both knowledge of safety boundaries and \textbf{vigilance}: the ability to detect unusual premises, misleading reasoning, and latent risks beneath surface-level semantics. Vigilance requires models to scrutinize a request's underlying intent and assumptions before acting. To cultivate this capability, we introduce \textbf{cunning questions}, which are not necessarily safety-related but contain misleading premises, atypical reasoning, or subtle inconsistencies. We hypothesize that learning to look beyond such reasoning traps can transfer to safety-critical scenarios. Experiments show that Cunning training improves robustness to out-of-distribution jailbreak attacks and strengthens subsequent safety fine-tuning. Furthermore, augmenting an existing state-of-the-art safety alignment pipeline with Cunning establishes a new state of the art across our evaluated settings, reducing mean ASR across nine backbone--benchmark combinations from 17.40\% to 15.05\%. Trace analysis after matched safety fine-tuning suggests that safety judgments are more likely to govern responses before harmful planning begins. A conditional theoretical analysis further characterizes when invariance learned from cunning data can transfer to safety-related inputs. These findings suggest that cunning data can strengthen model vigilance and complement conventional safety alignment.

AI.tldr: Cunning training improves LLM safety by teaching models to detect misleading premises and subtle inconsistencies, enhancing vigilance against concealed harmful intents
AI.motivation: Aligned LLMs can fail when harmful intent is concealed within seemingly benign contexts, requiring not just knowledge of safety boundaries but also vigilance to detect unusual premises, misleading reasoning, and latent risks beneath surface-level semantics
AI.method: Introduce "cunning questions" - not necessarily safety-related but containing misleading premises, atypical reasoning, or subtle inconsistencies. Train models to look beyond such reasoning traps, hypothesizing this transfers to safety-critical scenarios. Augment existing safety alignment pipelines with cunning training
AI.result: Cunning training improves robustness to out-of-distribution jailbreak attacks and strengthens subsequent safety fine-tuning. Augmenting SOTA safety alignment pipeline reduces mean ASR from 17.40% to 15.05% across nine backbone-benchmark combinations. Trace analysis shows safety judgments are more likely to govern responses before harmful planning begins
AI.conclusion: Cunning data strengthens model vigilance and complements conventional safety alignment by teaching models to scrutinize underlying intent and assumptions, with theoretical analysis showing when invariance learned from cunning data transfers to safety-related inputs

title: Beyond Quadratic Loss: The Stability Phase Diagram of Adam
summary: Loss spikes are recurrent instabilities in neural-network training and can arise from multiple mechanisms. For Adam in particular, macroscopic loss spikes have been linked to optimizer dynamics, yet how its two momentum timescales govern them remains unclear. We investigate this dependence by mapping training dynamics across the $(β_1,β_2)$ plane. Across a range of model--task settings, an approximately linear boundary, $1-β_2=C(1-β_1)$, separates spiky from non-spiky dynamics, whereas a one-dimensional quadratic loss produces approximately cubic slope. A one-dimensional superquadratic loss $L(x)\propto|x|^n$ recovers the near-linear scaling and links the boundary coefficient to the effective loss exponent $n$. We further show that confident cross-entropy losses develop a core--wall landscape comprising a narrow quadratic core followed by a steep wall, which produces effective superquadratic behavior at the scale of an optimizer update. Together, these results connect Adam loss spikes to both the mismatch between momentum timescales and finite-scale superquadratic loss geometry beyond the Hessian.

AI.tldr: Adam optimizer loss spikes are governed by momentum timescale mismatch and superquadratic loss geometry, with linear boundary in (β₁,β₂) space separating spiky from stable dynamics.
AI.motivation: Loss spikes are recurring instabilities in neural network training, particularly with Adam optimizer. While macroscopic loss spikes in Adam have been linked to optimizer dynamics, it's unclear how the two momentum timescales (β₁ and β₂) govern these spikes.
AI.method: The authors investigate the dependence by mapping training dynamics across the (β₁,β₂) parameter plane across various model-task settings. They analyze different loss landscapes including one-dimensional quadratic loss, superquadratic loss L(x)∝|x|^n, and cross-entropy losses with core-wall landscape.
AI.result: An approximately linear boundary 1-β₂ = C(1-β₁) separates spiky from non-spiky dynamics, with different slopes for different loss types (cubic for quadratic loss, near-linear for superquadratic). Cross-entropy losses develop core-wall landscapes with narrow quadratic cores followed by steep walls, producing effective superquadratic behavior at optimizer update scale.
AI.conclusion: Adam loss spikes are connected to both momentum timescale mismatch and finite-scale superquadratic loss geometry beyond Hessian information. The boundary coefficient in the momentum parameter space relates to the effective loss exponent.

title: AeroWeaver: An Embodied-Agent Harness for Weaving Aerial Skills into Distributed, Adaptive Swarm Execution
summary: Collective intelligence is a collaborative autonomy paradigm in which multiple agents pursue shared objectives through local perception, information exchange, and coordinated action. UAV swarms embody this paradigm by coordinating multiple vehicles in tasks such as search, inspection, and tracking. Recent advances in large language model (LLM) agents have strengthened natural-language task understanding and high-level planning, providing a flexible semantic interface between mission descriptions and collective behavior. While these advances expand semantic reasoning, applying LLM agents to UAV swarms raises challenges in grounding model decisions in executable capabilities, reconciling global task reasoning with distributed execution, and using mission-specific experience for continual adaptation. To address these challenges, we introduce AeroWeaver, an embodied-agent harness that weaves individual UAV skills into coordinated mission-level behavior. AeroWeaver connects semantic decisions to governed skills, organizes role-conditioned local agents for distributed coordination, and uses role-indexed state-action-reward experience to refine skill selection online. Experiments and runtime validation show that AeroWeaver maintains valid skill execution under tested conditions and supports body-local multi-UAV operation without a central agent generating joint actions from global context, while reward-guided online updates provide a training-free path for adaptive learning swarm agents from accumulated execution experience. Code: https://github.com/Admire-ljb/AeroWeaver.

AI.tldr: AeroWeaver is an embodied-agent harness that integrates LLM agents with UAV swarms by connecting semantic decisions to executable skills, enabling distributed coordination and online adaptation without central control.
AI.motivation: Recent advances in LLM agents provide strong natural-language task understanding for UAV swarms, but challenges remain in grounding model decisions in executable capabilities, reconciling global reasoning with distributed execution, and enabling continual adaptation using mission experience.
AI.method: AeroWeaver weaves individual UAV skills into coordinated mission behavior by: 1) connecting semantic decisions to governed skills, 2) organizing role-conditioned local agents for distributed coordination, and 3) using role-indexed state-action-reward experience to refine skill selection online.
AI.result: Experiments show AeroWeaver maintains valid skill execution under tested conditions, supports body-local multi-UAV operation without central agent generating joint actions from global context, and provides training-free adaptive learning from accumulated execution experience through reward-guided online updates.
AI.conclusion: AeroWeaver successfully bridges the gap between LLM-based semantic reasoning and executable UAV swarm capabilities, enabling distributed coordination and continual adaptation without requiring centralized control or offline training.

title: Multi-Appliance Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring via Label-Preserving Aggregate Recomposition and Prediction Consistency
summary: Non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM) estimates appliance power sequences from aggregate power, but models trained on source households commonly lose accuracy in unseen households. Aggregate power also contains loads from other appliances and measurement error, so predictions may depend on the residual background that co-occurs with source-household targets. Time-aligned submetered measurements and the additive decomposition of aggregate power expose a relation unused by window-wise supervision: an aggregate window can be recomposed by replacing only its residual background while preserving all modeled target-appliance power sequences pointwise. We combine label-preserving aggregate recomposition with prediction consistency. Both windows receive complete power and operating-state supervision. For each appliance, disagreement between the two power predictions is penalized only when both satisfy a fixed reliability criterion and only to the extent that it exceeds a fixed margin. The proposed method is implemented using a multi-appliance architecture with two-stage shared-to-specific mixture-of-experts routing. On REDD, UK-DALE, and REFIT, the proposed method lowers appliance-averaged mean absolute error relative to single-window training from 14.75 to 13.14 W, from 8.88 to 8.51 W, and from 15.83 to 14.55 W. Label-preserving aggregate recomposition and prediction consistency are used only during training, and add no inference-time module or parameter.

AI.tldr: A novel training method for NILM that uses label-preserving aggregate recomposition and prediction consistency to improve generalization to unseen households without adding inference-time overhead.
AI.motivation: NILM models trained on source households lose accuracy in unseen households due to differences in background power residuals and measurement errors that co-occur with target appliances.
AI.method: Combines label-preserving aggregate recomposition (replacing residual background while preserving target appliance sequences) with prediction consistency. Uses a multi-appliance architecture with two-stage shared-to-specific mixture-of-experts routing, with disagreement penalties applied only when both predictions meet reliability criteria and exceed a fixed margin.
AI.result: Reduces appliance-averaged mean absolute error relative to single-window training: from 14.75 to 13.14 W on REDD, from 8.88 to 8.51 W on UK-DALE, and from 15.83 to 14.55 W on REFIT datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training method significantly improves NILM generalization across different households without adding inference-time modules or parameters, demonstrating effective use of time-aligned measurements and additive decomposition properties.

title: TRIPROBE: Probing Task Separability Beyond Classification for XAI
summary: Modern evaluation of learning pipelines often reduces to downstream accuracy, leaving open the question of why tasks succeed or fail. TriProbe addresses this gap with a multi-level probing framework for explainable diagnosis of task separability. Rather than treating models as black boxes, TriProbe traces how separability evolves across inputs, learned features, and final classifiers. It decomposes multi-task problems into binary subtasks and applies three complementary probes: a Foundational Probe on input spaces, a Latent Probe on feature representations, and a Final Probe on classifier outputs. Using Maximum Fisher's Discriminant Ratio as a principled separability metric, TriProbe identifies bottlenecks and affected task pairs. Experiments on the Roshambo sEMG benchmark show how TriProbe reveals hidden breakdowns, guiding data collection, validation, and architecture design.

AI.tldr: TriProbe is a multi-level probing framework that explains why learning tasks succeed or fail by tracing separability evolution across inputs, features, and classifiers, using Maximum Fisher's Discriminant Ratio to identify bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: Modern evaluation methods focus only on downstream accuracy without explaining why tasks succeed or fail. There's a need for explainable diagnosis of task separability beyond treating models as black boxes.
AI.method: TriProbe decomposes multi-task problems into binary subtasks and applies three complementary probes: Foundational Probe on input spaces, Latent Probe on feature representations, and Final Probe on classifier outputs. It uses Maximum Fisher's Discriminant Ratio as a principled separability metric to trace how separability evolves across these levels.
AI.result: Experiments on the Roshambo sEMG benchmark demonstrate that TriProbe reveals hidden breakdowns in task separability, providing insights that can guide data collection, validation, and architecture design.
AI.conclusion: TriProbe addresses the gap in current evaluation methods by providing explainable diagnosis of task separability, enabling better understanding of why learning pipelines succeed or fail and offering practical guidance for improving model development.

title: Trajectory Learnability for Offline On-Policy Distillation with Imperfect Teachers
summary: Offline on-policy distillation gains efficiency by collecting student trajectories and teacher supervision once and reusing them throughout optimization. The same reuse makes imperfect supervision persistent. Since even strong teachers can fail, we ask \emph{what remains learnable from imperfect teacher supervision?} Teacher failure is only a coarse problem-level signal and does not imply that all supervision along the associated student trajectory is unhelpful. A natural alternative is to estimate teacher recoverability along the trajectory, but repeated continuations largely erase the efficiency advantage of offline distillation. We instead use teacher-successful problems to define a cheap reference for what the student can learn. We train on teacher-successful problems and measure how the likelihood of each observed token in trajectories from teacher-failed problems changes. We use these signed likelihood changes as an operational \emph{learnability signal}: larger increases indicate behavior more strongly promoted by successful-only learning. We aggregate this signal into trajectory-level weights for the original distillation loss. Unlike continuation-based estimates, our learnability requires no additional generation and can be computed once from stored trajectories and model checkpoints. Across mathematical reasoning and code generation, our method improves an offline OPD baseline by up to 2.7 percentage points and matches or outperforms online OPD variants on multiple benchmarks. Despite the additional successful-only distillation stage, it uses 2 GPUs and about 22 GPU hours, compared with 3 GPUs and 36--48 GPU hours for representative online OPD methods.

AI.tldr: A method that improves offline on-policy distillation by identifying learnable parts from teacher supervision, even when teachers fail on some problems, using learnability signals from teacher-successful problems without additional generation.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of imperfect teacher supervision in offline on-policy distillation. While offline distillation is efficient by reusing student trajectories and teacher supervision, imperfect supervision (when teachers fail on some problems) persists throughout optimization. The key question is what remains learnable from imperfect teacher supervision, as teacher failure is only a coarse problem-level signal and doesn't mean all supervision along the associated trajectory is unhelpful.
AI.method: The method trains the student on teacher-successful problems first, then measures how the likelihood of each observed token in trajectories from teacher-failed problems changes after this successful-only training. These signed likelihood changes serve as a learnability signal - larger increases indicate behavior more strongly promoted by successful-only learning. This signal is aggregated into trajectory-level weights for the original distillation loss. Unlike continuation-based estimates that require additional generation, this learnability signal can be computed once from stored trajectories and model checkpoints.
AI.result: The method improves an offline OPD baseline by up to 2.7 percentage points on mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks. It matches or outperforms online OPD variants on multiple benchmarks. Despite requiring an additional successful-only distillation stage, it uses only 2 GPUs and about 22 GPU hours, compared to 3 GPUs and 36-48 GPU hours for representative online OPD methods.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents an efficient method for offline on-policy distillation that can effectively identify and leverage learnable supervision even from teacher-failed problems. By using learnability signals derived from teacher-successful problems, the approach improves performance over standard offline distillation while maintaining computational efficiency advantages over online variants, achieving better results with fewer resources.

title: Recursive Reasoning or Statistical Extrapolation? In-Context Learning in Multi-Agent Interdependent Decision-Making
summary: In-context learning (ICL) enables large language model (LLM) agents to improve decisions using interaction history, yet it remains unclear whether such improvement reflects refined internal reasoning or mere extrapolation of statistical patterns. To disentangle these mechanisms, we study LLM agents in multi-agent incomplete-information games that require recursive belief reasoning. By constructing a public goods game and manipulating the statistical structure of historical feedback, we evaluate decision quality against a history-independent rational expectations equilibrium (REE) benchmark. Our experiments reveal that when historical statistical patterns are disrupted, the benefits of longer context largely vanish, degrading decision quality to the no-context baseline in a way sharply amplified by stronger strategic interdependence. These results suggest that, in such strategic environments, ICL behavior is more consistent with statistical extrapolation than with strategic reasoning. Our work extends the mechanistic study of ICL to strategic multi-agent settings, introduces REE as a diagnostic tool for distinguishing reasoning from extrapolation, and provides a reusable framework for probing the boundaries of LLM reasoning in recursive belief tasks.

AI.tldr: LLM agents' in-context learning benefits in strategic games come more from statistical pattern extrapolation than actual belief reasoning, as shown when disrupting historical patterns.
AI.motivation: To understand whether in-context learning improvements in LLM agents reflect genuine strategic reasoning or merely statistical pattern extrapolation, particularly in complex multi-agent settings requiring recursive belief reasoning.
AI.method: Studied LLM agents in multi-agent incomplete-information games requiring recursive belief reasoning, using a public goods game framework. Manipulated statistical structure of historical feedback and evaluated decision quality against a history-independent rational expectations equilibrium (REE) benchmark.
AI.result: When historical statistical patterns were disrupted, benefits of longer context largely vanished, degrading decision quality to no-context baseline.
