This paper introduces LightSleepX, a lightweight framework designed to deliver robust sleep analysis in resource-constrained environments. LightSleepX combines an Inception-style architecture with depthwise separable convolutions and Multi-scale Enhanced Attention for efficient multi-modal EEG/EOG feature extraction, and a Mamba encoder for rule-free long-range temporal modeling. On public benchmark datasets, LightSleepX achieves 85.9% accuracy and a 0.803 macro-F1 score on Sleep-EDF-20, and 81.8% accuracy and a 0.796 macro-F1 score on the cross-subject ISRUC-S3 dataset. With 0.049M parameters and 195.9 MFLOPs, the framework targets practical local deployment where computational cost and privacy are central constraints.

AI.tldr: LightSleepX is a lightweight deep learning framework for efficient sleep stage classification using EEG/EOG signals, achieving high accuracy with minimal computational resources for real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: Existing sleep staging methods face challenges: traditional approaches with hand-crafted features lack generalization, while state-of-the-art deep learning methods are too computationally heavy for resource-constrained environments. There's a need for practical, efficient sleep analysis suitable for real-world applications with privacy and computational constraints.
AI.method: LightSleepX combines an Inception-style architecture with depthwise separable convolutions for efficient multi-modal EEG/EOG feature extraction, incorporates Multi-scale Enhanced Attention, and uses a Mamba encoder for rule-free long-range temporal modeling. The framework is designed with computational efficiency as a primary consideration.
AI.result: Achieved 85.9% accuracy and 0.803 macro-F1 score on Sleep-EDF-20 dataset, and 81.8% accuracy with 0.796 macro-F1 score on cross-subject ISRUC-S3 dataset. The framework is extremely lightweight with only 0.049M parameters and 195.9 MFLOPs computational cost.
AI.conclusion: LightSleepX successfully addresses the computational efficiency challenge in sleep staging while maintaining competitive accuracy, making it suitable for practical local deployment in resource-constrained environments where computational cost and privacy are major concerns.

title: RLLBC-Lib: An Educational Code Library for Reinforcement Learning and Learning-Based Control
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an exciting concept as well as a remarkable success story worth sharing. However, RL builds on rather complex interactions between different objects that play out over several cycles. Such dynamics are often best explained with an easily accessible implementation. We present RLLBC-Lib, a carefully crafted code library with the goal of lowering the entry barrier for students and other learners of RL in the context of learning-based control. At its heart, RLLBC-Lib comprises a comprehensive library of tabular RL approaches to enforce a clear understanding of the theoretical foundations. A deep RL library follows the same design principles, underscoring the parallels between simple tabular and state-of-the-art deep RL approaches. Additionally, RLLBC-Lib provides a collection of implementations illustrating core RL principles and contrasting RL to other learning-based control approaches. Finally, RLLBC-Lib provides an ideal basis for creating programming assignments with automated grading.

AI.tldr: RLLBC-Lib is an educational code library designed to lower the entry barrier for learning reinforcement learning in control contexts, featuring both tabular and deep RL implementations with clear design parallels between them.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning has complex interactions and dynamics that are challenging for learners to understand. There's a need for accessible implementations that can help students and newcomers grasp RL concepts, particularly in the context of learning-based control applications.
AI.method: The authors developed RLLBC-Lib, a carefully crafted code library with: 1) comprehensive tabular RL approaches to enforce clear understanding of theoretical foundations, 2) deep RL library following the same design principles to show parallels between simple tabular and state-of-the-art deep RL, 3) implementations illustrating core RL principles and contrasting RL with other learning-based control approaches, and 4) support for creating programming assignments with automated grading.
AI.result: RLLBC-Lib provides a unified educational platform that bridges the gap between theoretical understanding and practical implementation of reinforcement learning, with particular focus on learning-based control applications.
AI.conclusion: RLLBC-Lib successfully addresses the need for accessible reinforcement learning educational tools by providing a well-designed code library that helps learners understand complex RL concepts through clear implementations and structured parallels between tabular and deep RL approaches.

title: Double descent is the principle of least action
summary: The test error of a model plotted against its number of parameters $d$ falls, peaks when the model can just fit the training data, and falls again, exhibiting the double descent phenomenon. We explain the phenomenon with statistical mechanics. The training trajectory of a stochastic gradient-based method is a particle wandering over the energy landscape of the training loss at an induced temperature $T$, and a run that has equilibrated visits every parameter vector of a given training loss equally often, the fundamental postulate of statistical mechanics, with probability given by the Boltzmann distribution. Because training starts at an initial point and has only finite time to diffuse, it carries an effective weight decay, which makes every parameter a quadratic degree of freedom. The equipartition theorem then distributes the energy among the $d$ degrees of freedom in shares of $T/2$, so at a fixed training loss adding parameters lowers the temperature and drives the Boltzmann distribution toward the stationary path. Finally, adding parameters can only lower the $L^2$ norm of the stationary path, so a solution sampled at fixed loss is less likely to be large with increasing $d$, effectively increasing weight regularization.

AI.tldr: The paper explains the double descent phenomenon in model test error using statistical mechanics, showing how training dynamics with finite time induce effective weight decay, and how adding parameters lowers temperature and increases regularization.
AI.motivation: The double descent phenomenon where test error first falls, then peaks when models can just fit training data, then falls again needs explanation beyond traditional bias-variance tradeoff.
AI.method: Using statistical mechanics framework: training trajectory as particle diffusing on energy landscape with induced temperature T; finite-time training induces effective weight decay; applying equipartition theorem and Boltzmann distribution analysis.
AI.result: Adding parameters at fixed training loss lowers temperature, drives distribution toward stationary path, and increases effective regularization by reducing L^2 norm of solutions, explaining the double descent pattern.
AI.conclusion: Double descent emerges naturally from statistical mechanical treatment of training dynamics, where finite-time diffusion induces weight decay-like effects and parameter addition increases implicit regularization.

title: Probabilistic Linear Explanations
summary: Formal explainability provides mathematically grounded justifications for individual predictions. However, abductive explanations often exceed human cognitive limits by involving too many features, while probabilistic relaxations have remained largely limited to categorical classification. We present a unified framework for probabilistic explainability based on sparse, anchored linear models, applicable to both binary classification and continuous regression. By mapping instances to the Boolean hypercube, our linear explanations strictly generalize subset-based approaches: they capture both the magnitude and direction of feature contributions while enforcing a prescribed sparsity budget $k$. We show that minimizing the relevance error for such explanations is \ClassNPPP-hard when the underlying model is a neural network, and we relate this intractable objective to a tractable surrogate---the fidelity error. For a parameterized family of local distributions, the relevance error of any $k$-sparse explanation is bounded by its fidelity error up to a multiplicative factor that remains small locally. We address the resulting empirical problem using two complementary approaches: a Mixed Integer Programming (MIP) formulation that yields provably optimal empirical solutions while maintaining polynomial sample complexity, and a polynomial-time Iterative Hard Thresholding (IHT) algorithm with provable approximation guarantees. Empirical evaluations show that, unlike state-of-the-art baselines such as LIME and MAPLE, our explanations satisfy both the anchoring and sparsity constraints by construction, while consistently achieving lower relevance error.

AI.tldr: A unified framework for probabilistic explainability using sparse anchored linear models for both classification and regression, with theoretical guarantees and practical algorithms.
AI.motivation: Existing formal explainability methods either produce too many features for human comprehension or are limited to categorical classification. There's a need for sparse probabilistic explanations applicable to both classification and regression tasks.
AI.method: Map instances to Boolean hypercube and use sparse anchored linear models that capture feature magnitude/direction with sparsity budget k. Provide theoretical analysis showing minimization is NPPP-hard for neural networks, relate to tractable surrogate (fidelity error), and offer two approaches: MIP for optimal solutions and IHT for polynomial-time approximations.
AI.result: Theoretical bounds show relevance error bounded by fidelity error with small multiplicative factor locally. Empirical evaluations demonstrate superior performance over LIME and MAPLE, satisfying anchoring and sparsity constraints while achieving lower relevance error.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a theoretically grounded, practical approach to probabilistic explainability that generalizes existing methods, handles both classification and regression, and delivers sparse, interpretable explanations with provable guarantees.

title: Evidence-Grounded Agentic Formulation Development in an Autonomous Laboratory
summary: Self-emulsifying drug delivery systems (SEDDS) can improve the oral bioavailability of poorly soluble drugs, but identifying high-performing formulations remains experimentally intensive. We present Andromeda 2, an agentic system that reasons over structured in-house experimental evidence and invokes computational and experimental tools to design and execute successive formulation batches. Using a miniaturized automated laboratory at a matched budget, we benchmark it against Andromeda 1, a probabilistic optimization model deployed across dozens of live development projects, and a wet-lab design-of-experiments (DoE) campaign. For paclitaxel, Andromeda 2 achieved a 50% high-performance hit rate versus 17% for Andromeda 1 and 2% for DoE, and identified 12 formulations meeting all four target product profile (TPP) objectives versus 6 and 0, respectively. Median $AUC_{10-240}$ was 70.1, 12.0, and 3.5 mg$\cdot$min/mL, while maximum AUC was comparable between Andromeda 2 and Andromeda 1. A selected full-TPP formulation achieved an apparent effective paclitaxel loading of $19 \pm 5\%$ w/w at the first FaSSIF measurement, approximately 3.3-fold higher than the 5.7% w/w loading reported for a published paclitaxel S-SEDDS. A controlled ablation showed that access to structured in-house experimental evidence increased mean AUC by 34%.

AI.tldr: Andromeda 2 is an agentic system that outperforms previous methods in designing self-emulsifying drug delivery systems for poorly soluble drugs like paclitaxel.
AI.motivation: Identifying high-performing SEDDS formulations is experimentally intensive, and existing methods like DoE campaigns and probabilistic optimization models have limited effectiveness.
AI.method: Andromeda 2 reasons over structured in-house experimental evidence and invokes computational and experimental tools to design and execute successive formulation batches using a miniaturized automated laboratory.
AI.result: Andromeda 2 achieved 50% high-performance hit rate (vs 17% for Andromeda 1 and 2% for DoE), identified 12 formulations meeting all TPP objectives (vs 6 and 0), and achieved median AUC of 70.1 mg·min/mL (vs 12.0 and 3.5).
AI.conclusion: Andromeda 2's agentic approach significantly outperforms previous methods for SEDDS formulation design, demonstrating the value of structured experimental evidence and integrated computational-experimental workflows.

title: How Model Growth, Recursion, and Boundary Operators Influence Scaling Exponents
summary: Scaling laws predict how loss decreases with increases in computation. We show, contrary to conventional wisdom, that architectural interventions can modify scaling exponents in pre-training, leading to exponential improvements in performance with increases in computation. As an anchoring point, we consider the architectural formulation of looped transformers. Although not typically used in this way, looping, also known as recursive depth, provides a mechanism for model growth, by increasing the number of loops during training. Model growth, with and without shared weights, provides the biggest changes to the scaling exponents. In particular, a 7.4B model growth architecture matches GPT-3 13B on CORE with roughly $20\times$ less compute, and has compute efficiency gains that increase with scale. Moreover, simply using a boundary operator in a vanilla transformer, which normalizes and injects an earlier block, also provides increasing compute-efficiency gains, although to a lesser extent. In the data-constrained, multi-epoch setting, standard looping has a useful regularizing effect, where we find it is compute-optimal to increase the number of loops with scale. These results can be understood through the lens of computational depth: for a given computational budget, we wish to increase the usable depth of the transformer, which can lead to efficiency gains that increase with scale.

AI.tldr: Architectural interventions like looped transformers and model growth can modify scaling exponents, leading to exponential performance improvements with compute. A 7.4B growth architecture matches GPT-3 13B with 20x less compute, showing increasing efficiency gains with scale.
AI.motivation: Conventional scaling laws assume fixed scaling exponents with increased computation. The paper challenges this by exploring whether architectural interventions can modify these exponents, potentially leading to more efficient scaling and better performance per compute unit.
AI.method: The authors use looped transformers (recursive depth) as an architectural intervention. They explore model growth through increasing loops during training (with and without shared weights), and also test a boundary operator in vanilla transformers that normalizes and injects earlier blocks. They analyze these approaches in both compute-constrained and data-constrained multi-epoch settings.
AI.result: A 7.4B model growth architecture matches GPT-3 13B on CORE benchmark with roughly 20x less compute. Both model growth and boundary operator approaches show increasing compute-efficiency gains with scale. In data-constrained settings, standard looping acts as a useful regularizer, and it's compute-optimal to increase loops with scale.
AI.conclusion: Architectural interventions can modify neural scaling exponents, leading to exponential performance improvements with increased computation. By increasing usable transformer depth for a given computational budget, these techniques create efficiency gains that scale with model size, challenging conventional wisdom about fixed scaling relationships.

title: Exponential Hardness of Off-Policy Evaluation under History-Dependent Logging
summary: Can a logged dataset visit every hidden state frequently and still be exponentially uninformative about a target policy's value? We show that it can when the logger depends on history. For every horizon $H \ge 3$, we construct two POMDPs with at most two latent states per stage, three actions, and a common logger with three memory states. Action coverage, belief coverage, and two behavior-marginal outcome-revealing conditions all have constants independent of $H$. Nevertheless, evaluating a known deterministic target policy to accuracy $1/8$ requires $Θ((3/2)^H \log(1/δ))$ logged episodes at confidence $1-δ$, for $0 < δ\le 1/4$, even when both candidate models are known. The mechanism is simple: a reset erases the unknown transition that determines the target value. We characterize the resulting statistical experiment exactly and obtain a matching optimal estimator. A directed two-lane gridworld realizes the construction, and trajectory simulations agree with its finite-sample prediction. The result establishes intractability for the history-dependent-logging, model-based case posed by Zhang and Jiang (2025, arXiv:2503.01134), under their behavior-marginal definition of revealing.

AI.tldr: A paper showing that even with good coverage and revealing conditions, evaluating a deterministic policy can require exponentially many logged episodes when the logger depends on history, due to reset mechanisms erasing transition information.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to investigate whether logged datasets with frequent state visitation can still be uninformative for policy evaluation when the logging mechanism depends on history, addressing open questions from Zhang and Jiang (2025) about the tractability of offline reinforcement learning with history-dependent logging.
AI.method: The authors construct two POMDPs (Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes) with specific properties: horizon H≥3, at most two latent states per stage, three actions, and a common logger with three memory states. They demonstrate that despite good coverage conditions (action coverage, belief coverage, and behavior-marginal outcome-revealing conditions), evaluating a deterministic target policy requires exponentially many logged episodes. The key mechanism involves reset operations that erase transition information determining the target value.
AI.result: The main result shows that evaluating a known deterministic target policy to accuracy 1/8 requires Θ((3/2)^H log(1/δ)) logged episodes at confidence 1-δ, for 0<δ≤1/4, even when both candidate models are known. This establishes exponential sample complexity in the horizon H. The authors characterize the statistical experiment exactly, obtain a matching optimal estimator, demonstrate the construction on a directed two-lane gridworld, and show trajectory simulations agree with finite-sample predictions.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion establishes intractability for the history-dependent-logging, model-based case under behavior-marginal revealing definitions, showing that offline RL with history-dependent logging can suffer from exponential sample complexity despite apparently favorable coverage conditions, due to the reset mechanism that erases crucial transition information.
